airstream_properties: Elevated near-dry-adiabatic layer from the Spanish tableland, theta about 36 C, base 850 mb and top near 700 mb, low theta-w 17-18 C; overlies shallow moist layer in which theta-w rises to 21-24 C
diagnostic_variables: Potential temperature theta, wet-bulb potential temperature theta-w, saturation potential temperature theta-s; isentropic relative-flow charts; tephigram soundings (Chateauroux, Bordeaux, Brussels); condensation level; vertical wind shear; screen-level maps
origin_and_transport_claim: Deep dry convective layer over the elevated arid Spanish plateau (about 1 km) is advected north in a southerly airstream ahead of an approaching Atlantic trough to lie aloft over SW France, the Channel and southern England; analogous Mexican plume in the USA
origin_evidence: DIRECT: isentropic relative-flow trajectory analysis on several theta surfaces plus climatological screen-level theta maps and soundings identifying Spanish adiabatic air at 850-700 mb
capping_or_instability_mechanism: Plume acts as a lid confining small-scale convection to the lowest 1-2 km so theta-w rises abnormally, storing potential instability; lid rendered ineffective when French soil is parched
capping_or_instability_evidence: DIRECT: soundings show the Spanish layer and lid at 850 mb; null case of 29 August 1961 shows storms fail when the lid is destroyed
initiation_mechanism: Instability released where the backed low-level moist flow passes beyond the western edge of the restraining plume, aided by large-scale baroclinic ascent in the frontal confluence zone; castellanus grow to cumulonimbus which then propagate on a squall front
initiation_evidence: DIRECT: case-by-case isentropic and sounding analysis of Horsham, Wokingham and Brussels storms plus the null case
hazards_locations_and_event_types: Severe local storms with giant hail, squalls and tornadoes; Horsham 5 Sep 1958, Wokingham 9 Jul 1959, Brussels 12 Jul 1961 (southern England, Channel, Belgium, France); Geary 4 May 1961 and 26 May 1962 in the US Great Plains
prefrontal_trough: UNCLEAR: reports a shallow low-level trough across central France with backed winds ahead of the front but does not identify it as a prefrontal trough
key_supporting_quote: beneath a plume of very warm air lying downwind of an extensive arid plateau (Spain or Mexico)
limitations_or_uncertainty: Trajectories rely on a steady-state assumption; soundings do not show saturation at castellanus bases, possibly unresponsive humidity sensors; dry-line processes stated to lack a satisfactory explanation; gradients near the dry-line may be stronger than smoothed synoptic data indicate

airstream_properties: Area of potentially very warm air at 850 mb (less so 700 mb) over parts of Spain and France, overlying surface air of abnormally high wet-bulb potential temperature (25 C in the lee of the Pyrenees, 23 C over France, versus a summer average near 14 C)
diagnostic_variables: Surface wet-bulb potential temperature (WBPT), 850 and 700 mb dry-bulb potential temperature, Camborne tephigram ascents, 300 mb charts and jet axis, 500-300 mb vertical wind shear, 300 mb vorticity analysis, Rackliff, Boyden and Showalter indices
origin_and_transport_claim: Potentially warm air present over Spain and France at 850 mb forms a plume acting as a lid over France; the high surface WBPT beneath it was advected from the Mediterranean, and instability was released when that air escaped from beneath the plume
origin_evidence: INDIRECT: inferred from 850 mb potential temperature charts and a time sequence of surface WBPT charts, with the plume concept attributed to Carlson and Ludlam (1968); no trajectory computation
capping_or_instability_mechanism: Plume of potentially warm air at 850 mb acted as a lid; French maxima near 30 C were insufficient to break it whereas 35 C in Spain allowed deep convection
capping_or_instability_evidence: DIRECT: contrast of Spanish and French thunderstorm occurrence with 850 mb potential temperature and surface WBPT analyses and Camborne ascents
initiation_mechanism: Escape of high-WBPT surface air from beneath the plume as the surface gradient backed in response to falling surface pressure (initially diurnal), allowing convection beyond 300 mb; storms maintained by strong 500-300 mb shear
initiation_evidence: DIRECT: chart sequence of surface WBPT relative to the 850 mb warm air, plus Camborne ascent evolution
hazards_locations_and_event_types: Exceptionally heavy rainfall (over 100 mm in 24 h in Gloucestershire), severe thunderstorms, rapid cyclogenesis and gales; SW England, southern England, East Anglia and the Wash, 9-11 July 1968
key_supporting_quote: Thus convection in France was minimal because there was a plume of potentially warm air which effectively acted like a lid.
limitations_or_uncertainty: Rackliff and Boyden indices over-estimated the area of thundery activity when used objectively; techniques gave no accurate indication of severity; Benwell 500 mb jet criterion only marginally satisfied

airstream_properties: A reservoir of hot air over Iberia flanked by a zone of strong low-tropospheric temperature gradient (850 mb wet-bulb potential temperature), initially dynamically inactive; the sharpening thermal ridge becomes the effective main frontal zone
diagnostic_variables: Mean sea-level pressure, 850 mb wet-bulb potential temperature, 500 mb geopotential height and 1000-500 mb thickness, maximum winds and jet, layer-mean thermal advection and vertical velocity (850-500 mb), quasi-geostrophic omega reasoning, Meteosat imagery, forecast convective cloud tops
origin_and_transport_claim: Plume is generated by dynamical interaction between a slowly advancing mid-latitude upper trough and a pre-existing hot air mass over Iberia; cyclonic curvature causes ascent and falling pressure, thermal advection sharpens the thermal ridge, and the plume then advances north into western France and the UK
origin_evidence: DIRECT: author's own quasi-geostrophic diagnosis illustrated with Met Office 15-level model initialized fields, satellite imagery and surface reports for 19-20 May 1986
capping_or_instability_mechanism: Convective instability is released by organised dynamical ascent ahead of the trough; no capping inversion or lid is described
capping_or_instability_evidence: ASSERTED_ONLY: convective instability of the air is raised only as a forecasting doubt, with no sounding or lid analysis presented
initiation_mechanism: Positive vorticity advection and warm advection ahead of the advancing upper trough produce strong ascent, focused at the discontinuity of thermal advection over Iberia; ascent then spreads north-east with the plume
initiation_evidence: DIRECT: composite charts of thermal advection and vertical velocity from analyses and T+12 to T+36 forecasts, verified against Meteosat cloud and surface weather
hazards_locations_and_event_types: Widespread thunderstorms and thundery rain over Iberia, western France and the UK with convective tops above FL300-FL400; case of 19-20 May 1986
key_supporting_quote: This weather pattern, which usually occurs at least once or twice during the summer months between May and September, is known as the 'Spanish plume'.
limitations_or_uncertainty: Timing error in the forecast movement of rain across northern England and southern Scotland; a curious phase difference between analysed ascent and observed weather; data assimilation may introduce spurious local solutions; model forecasts are not always accurate

airstream_properties: Plume of very warm moist low-level air with 850 mb theta-w generally above 18 C covering France and Iberia, capped by warm very dry air near 850 mb (about 1500 m); the plume later becomes the main frontal zone while the original cold front weakens
diagnostic_variables: 850 mb contours and theta-w, 300 mb contours and isotachs with jet axis, surface analyses and streamlines, Brest tephigram, Crawley hodograph, CAPE, directional and speed shear, Meteosat and NOAA imagery, rainfall radar
origin_and_transport_claim: Hot air from the Spanish plateau is lifted ahead of an eastward-moving upper trough over Biscay; a feedback loop tightens the thermal gradient, strengthens upper winds and increases vorticity advection and ascent over the warm plume
origin_evidence: INDIRECT: origin over Iberia and the Spanish plateau asserted following Morris (1986) and supported by 850 mb theta-w fields, but no trajectory or origin computation is presented
capping_or_instability_mechanism: Very warm moist low-level air trapped beneath a capping inversion of warm very dry air near 850 mb ('loaded gun' profile) stores CAPE until enough is available for severe development
capping_or_instability_evidence: DIRECT: Brest 1100 GMT tephigram showing the loaded-gun profile, with the Crawley hodograph confirming differential thermal advection
initiation_mechanism: First showers formed in a marked low-level convergence zone over Brittany with sea-breeze and orographic contributions; broad-scale positive vorticity and warm advection ahead of the upper trough then sustained repeated MCS development, with new cells favoured ahead of parent cells
initiation_evidence: DIRECT: surface streamline analysis, satellite and radar sequences and the location of the first MCS near the frontal wave tip
hazards_locations_and_event_types: Widespread violent thunderstorms and a mesoscale convective system with over 40 mm rain and rates to 100 mm per hour; SE England (Sussex, Kent, East Anglia), 20-21 July 1992; other 1992 European cases noted
prefrontal_trough: PRESENT: surface pressure fell over Iberia and France with formation of a trough or shallow surface low ahead of the pre-existing cold front
key_supporting_quote: This synoptic situation is known colloquially as the ‘Spanish plume’.
limitations_or_uncertainty: MCS development is not explicitly predicted by operational numerical models; detailed timing and distribution varied greatly between limited-area model runs; the model cannot advect showers; forecasters remained dependent on satellite and radar imagery

airstream_properties: Plume of very warm air with 850 mb wet-bulb potential temperature above 16 C (later above 18 C), containing a warm 'nose' near 800 mb that produces a temperature inversion; the cold front lay near the 13 C WBPT contour
diagnostic_variables: 850 mb WBPT from the limited-area model, mean sea-level pressure, 250 mb height, Herstmonceux upper-air ascents, CAPE, wind veer with height, Fawbush and Miller downdraught gust technique, mesoscale model convergence lines, infra-red satellite and radar composites
origin_and_transport_claim: The plume of very warm air had originated from the Spanish plateau the previous day and was carried north over Biscay and France; it is lifted by positive vorticity advection ahead of the eastward-moving upper trough and quickly becomes the effective cold front
origin_evidence: INDIRECT: origin from the Spanish plateau asserted from model 850 mb WBPT fields and synoptic continuity rather than demonstrated by trajectory analysis
capping_or_instability_mechanism: Warm 'nose' near 800 mb caps surface-based convection and stores substantial CAPE until removed by differential thermal advection, precipitation cooling or air-mass ascent, after which CAPE is released explosively
capping_or_instability_evidence: DIRECT: Herstmonceux 0600 GMT ascent showing the nose and the 1800 GMT ascent showing its removal and deep instability
initiation_mechanism: Arrival of a pre-existing small cyclonic circulation over Brittany combined with sea-breeze reinforcement of low-level convergence triggered the first cells; large-scale ascent ahead of the upper trough and daughter-cell generation then built an MCS
initiation_evidence: DIRECT: surface convergence analysis, mesoscale model convergence line, satellite and radar sequences and comparison of forecast and observed soundings
hazards_locations_and_event_types: Severe thunderstorms and a large MCS with 44 mm rain in one hour at Wokingham, hail, gusts to 56 kn and flash flooding at Great Dunmow; SE England, East Anglia and Kent, 24 June 1994
prefrontal_trough: PRESENT: a well marked trough in the surface isobars containing a small depression lay ahead of the cold front over the Bay of Biscay, beneath the plume
key_supporting_quote: In this article it is shown how the synoptic pattern conformed very well with the ‘Spanish plume’ conceptual model (Morris 1986)
limitations_or_uncertainty: The limited-area model failed to produce showers over southern England near the plume axis and its forecast profile was too dry between 700 and 500 mb; numerical guidance is often unreliable in such situations; it is unclear whether the observed 84 kn maximum wind was representative; no tornado reports were confirmed

airstream_properties: High 1000-500 mb thicknesses above 564 dam and high wet-bulb potential temperature across southern Britain, with 850 mb theta-w above 17 C forming a warm conveyor belt from the Bay of Biscay; a slight warm 'nose' at 770 mb on 24 July
diagnostic_variables: 1000-500 mb thickness, 500 mb height, 850 mb theta-w, dew point, Aughton, Hemsby, Herstmonceux and Camborne ascents, CAPE, Rackliff, modified Jefferson and potential instability indices, rainfall radar, hyetograph and barograph traces
origin_and_transport_claim: Very warm moist low-level air was advected northwards from the Bay of Biscay as a warm conveyor belt ahead of a weak cold front; the 'Spanish plume' label is applied to the high-thickness, high theta-w air already present over southern Britain
origin_evidence: ASSERTED_ONLY: the plume label is attached to the thickness and theta-w pattern with no origin analysis, trajectory or citation of a plume source region
capping_or_instability_mechanism: On 24 July a slight warm 'nose' at 770 mb capped the boundary layer until surface heating and forced ascent broke it; on 3-4 August cool polar air overrunning above 600 mb destabilised middle levels for elevated convection
capping_or_instability_evidence: DIRECT: Aughton 0600 GMT tephigram showing the 770 mb nose and CAPE, Herstmonceux 1800 GMT ascent showing 30 C would have been needed for surface-based convection, and tabulated eastward wind components
initiation_mechanism: 24 July storms triggered where sea-breezes converging into a heat low formed a marked convergence line west of Birmingham; 3-4 August storms were elevated, triggered ahead of a weak cold front with destabilisation aloft aided by radiative cooling of cloud tops after sunset
initiation_evidence: DIRECT: surface wind convergence analysis, tephigrams, upper-wind tables and radar imagery for both episodes
hazards_locations_and_event_types: Severe thunderstorms with 15 mm hail, 21.0 mm rain in under an hour, gusts to 33 kn and about 30 lightning flashes per minute; three lightning deaths reported in the region; Birmingham and the West Midlands, 24 July and 3-4 August 1994
key_supporting_quote: values were present across southern Britain in the form of a ‘Spanish plume’
limitations_or_uncertainty: Thunderstorm indices gave a mixed picture for 3 August and the second episode was less predictable; the tilting-syphon gauge under-recorded (19.5 mm against a corrected 21.0 mm); mesoscale variations invoked to explain differences from an earlier comparable case

airstream_properties: Only the thermodynamic signature is reported: an inversion below 830 mb with strong potential instability above it in the Bordeaux sounding
diagnostic_variables: Bordeaux 1100 UTC upper-air sounding (inversion and potential instability), surface synoptic chart, barograph traces from Jersey, Guernsey and French stations, tide gauge and eyewitness sea-level estimates, Merian's formula, inverted-barometer and dynamic sea-level response equations
origin_and_transport_claim: NR: no origin or transport of the plume is described; only a shallow low moving north-east from west of Iberia and an upper trough crossing Iberia and Biscay are noted
origin_evidence: CITED_ONLY: the plume identification rests on a single sounding described as typical of Morris (1986), with no origin analysis of the paper's own
capping_or_instability_mechanism: Inversion below 830 mb with strong potential instability above, described as typical of Spanish plume formation
capping_or_instability_evidence: DIRECT: the Bordeaux 1100 UTC sounding is reported by the author, although only in one sentence
initiation_mechanism: NR: no convective initiation mechanism is analysed; a possible MCS is noted moving north from France
initiation_evidence: NR
hazards_locations_and_event_types: Seiche (meteotsunami) in Saint Aubin's Bay and Saint Helier Harbour, Jersey, with sea-level oscillations of at least 50 cm and over 1 m, caused by a meso-depression or wake low; thunderstorms over Brittany, the Channel Islands, Kent and East Anglia, 17 September 1992
prefrontal_trough: UNCLEAR: an associated upper trough is described as lying ahead of the cold front, but no surface prefrontal trough is identified
key_supporting_quote: The Bordeaux upper air sounding for 1100 UTC indicated an inversion below 830mbar with strong potential instability above
limitations_or_uncertainty: The Saint Helier tide gauge was out of service so amplitudes rest on eyewitness estimates; the observed nodal line lay closer to shore than theory predicted; the harmonic (third or fifth) could not be resolved; the event year is given inconsistently in the text

airstream_properties: Warm very moist air in a conveyor belt from the south-south-west with a long sea track over a still-warm Mediterranean; 850 mb wet-bulb potential temperature around 15 C and over 17 C over Corsica, against below 10 C behind the front
diagnostic_variables: Surface and 850 mb height analyses, 850 mb wet-bulb potential temperature, 500 mb height and isotherms for a comparison case, freezing-level height, Meteosat imagery, radar, automatic rain-gauge network
origin_and_transport_claim: The rainfall occurred on the forward side of a sharp slow-moving upper trough with Piedmont flooded by warm very moist air in a quasi-stationary conveyor belt from the SSW; the Spanish Plume is invoked only as an analogy, with no Iberian source claimed
origin_evidence: ASSERTED_ONLY: the analogy to the Spanish Plume is stated and illustrated only by the 850 mb theta-w contrast across the front; no origin or trajectory analysis

capping_or_instability_evidence: NR

initiation_evidence: INDIRECT: inferred from successive surface and 850 mb analyses and the persistence of the flow; short-wave enhancement offered only as a possibility
hazards_locations_and_event_types: Catastrophic flooding with cumulative totals up to about 600 mm, record 24-hour falls, about 65 deaths and about 6400 billion lira damage; Piedmont, Liguria and Lombardy in NW Italy, with Spain, Morocco and southern France also affected, 4-6 November 1994
key_supporting_quote: The situation is somewhat analogous to the ‘Spanish Plume’, except that less deep convection was involved.
limitations_or_uncertainty: Few automatic stations hold historical hourly rainfall data so hourly rates cannot be compared over a long period; an absence of dredging is raised as a possible contributory cause of the floods; authorities' response was late

origin_evidence: ASSERTED_ONLY: both the Spanish plume link and the proposed South France plume are asserted, supported only by reference to satellite images and general observation
configuration: OTHER: a proposed north-eastward South France plume analogue crossing the western Alps, distinct from the UK Spanish plume
capping_or_instability_mechanism: Elevated dust layers store anomalous heat and shift radiative effects upward, giving a larger than normal initial heat trigger and a sharp temperature discontinuity of 10 degC or more between cold air below the cloud and warmer air around it
capping_or_instability_evidence: ASSERTED_ONLY: mechanisms are asserted from selected cases and computed air tracks, with dust concentrations described as enormous but unknown

key_supporting_quote: Similar rainfall events often occur following an event known in the UK as a ‘Spanish plume’.
limitations_or_uncertainty: Dust concentrations in elevated layers are stated to be unknown; attribution of rainfall maxima to specific power stations is correlational; the author notes such events could remain hidden even with a relatively dense rainfall network; long-term climatologies said to have little meaning

initiation_evidence: NR

airstream_properties: Warm and moist air from the Iberian Peninsula carried to central Europe on southwesterly winds in the warm sector of a depression; the paper's own composites show a layer near 850 hPa 3-6 degC warmer on thundery days and a humid layer at 600-700 hPa
diagnostic_variables: Payerne radiosoundings; Showalter, SWEAT, K, TT, KO, Boyden, DCI, HI and surface lifted indices; CAPE variants and the new SWISS and CS indices; vertical wind shear over 0-3, 3-6 and 0-6 km; helicity; hodographs; dewpoint depression; lightning counters; hail damage reports; radar
origin_and_transport_claim: On severe Swiss hail days a trough or cut-off low lies over the Bay of Biscay with a shallow lee depression over France, and warm moist air from the Iberian Peninsula is carried into central Europe by southwesterly winds while cold advection occurs aloft

capping_or_instability_evidence: DIRECT: mean temperature soundings, dewpoint-depression differences and CAPE composites for no, isolated and widespread thunderstorm days over 1985-89
initiation_mechanism: Especially strong developments are expected if the cold front reaches Switzerland in the late afternoon or evening; a pronounced low-level jet near 3 km, wind shear and orography organise and initiate convection
initiation_evidence: DIRECT: five-year skill-score, probability-distribution and composite sounding and hodograph analysis, with independent verification on 1990, 1992 and 1993 data

airstream_properties: Very warm 'Spanish plume' air over south-east England with 0900 GMT dew points locally above 20 C and temperatures above 31 C; a moist layer near 800 mb capped by markedly drier air at 400-600 mb; freezing level near 3500 m over East Anglia against 1500 m behind the front
diagnostic_variables: Surface synoptic analysis, radiosonde ascents (Herstmonceux, Aberporth, Camborne), lapse rate, freezing level, dew point, wind veer and shear, 1200 GMT Larkhill pilot balloon 500 mb wind, rainfall radar, ATD sferics lightning fixes, thermograph and autographic records, TORRO hail scale, eyewitness and press reports
origin_and_transport_claim: The contrasting airmasses originated from Spain and Greenland respectively, with a thundery low moving north-north-east from northern Spain over 24 hours to reach southern East Anglia; a shallow heat low formed over central southern England
origin_evidence: INDIRECT: the Spanish source is stated from the surface synoptic analysis and airmass contrast and from the tracked low, but no trajectory or upstream sounding analysis is presented
capping_or_instability_mechanism: A moist layer around 800 mb capped by markedly drier air at medium levels (400-600 mb), with a particularly steep lapse rate from cloud base to the 0 C level, described as a classic precursor of severe British hailstorms
capping_or_instability_evidence: DIRECT: Herstmonceux 1800 GMT ascent, compared with the Horsham 1958 and Essex 1985 hailstorm soundings
initiation_mechanism: East Anglian storms began through convergence between a sea-breeze front and a pre-frontal trough from storm outflow, aided by the London heat island; the severest storms formed just ahead of the cold front fed by warm inflow on the flank of Low S and heat low Y, with rightward propagation carrying them ahead of the front
initiation_evidence: DIRECT: surface charts with converging winds and temperature contrasts, radar and sferics sequences, and station autographic records
hazards_locations_and_event_types: Giant hail over 30 mm and up to cricket-ball size in eight damaging swaths, tornadoes at Basingstoke and Sherborne, a 44 kn squall, 73.9 mm rain at East Lockinge and flooding; Dorset, Wessex, Berkshire, Oxfordshire, Buckinghamshire, Cambridgeshire, Norfolk and Suffolk, 7 June 1996
prefrontal_trough: PRESENT: a pre-frontal trough associated with outflow from the storm area further west converged with a sea-breeze front over East Anglia; two troughs also appear in the surface analysis
key_supporting_quote: Cold front CY represented the major boundary between the contrasting airmasses, which originated from Spain and Greenland respectively.
limitations_or_uncertainty: The ATD sferics system locates only about 25 per cent of discharges; peak rainfall rests partly on radar accumulations; much of the damage record relies on eyewitness accounts and press appeals; the western boundary of heavy precipitation was very sharp and poorly sampled

airstream_properties: Plume of relatively dry and warm air formed over the Spanish plateau at levels between 900 and 700 hPa; its eastern part undergoes subsidence and becomes still warmer; recognisable as a dent in the isentropes near 1 W in the 45 N cross-section, with potential instability above
diagnostic_variables: Meteosat infrared and visible imagery; three-hourly surface observations of pressure, temperature, dew point and wind; six-hourly ECMWF analyses on 11 pressure levels; potential and equivalent potential temperature cross-sections; slope of isentropes as a new frontal-intensity measure; Q-vector divergence; relative vorticity and specific humidity; surface moisture flux convergence; 700 and 300 hPa isotachs and jetstreaks
origin_and_transport_claim: The plume forms over the Spanish plateau at 900-700 hPa and, under an approaching Atlantic trough, is advected northward over the Bay of Biscay and France; water vapour then accumulates in the boundary layer beneath it
origin_evidence: INDIRECT: the Spanish plateau source at 900-700 hPa is taken from Carlson and Ludlam (1968) and Morris (1986), while the paper's own ECMWF fields locate the plume as the low-level warm-advection region over Iberia and France without trajectory calculation
capping_or_instability_mechanism: The plume acts as a capping inversion preventing deep convection while boundary-layer moisture accumulates, creating high potential static instability above (the 'loaded gun'); the cross-frontal circulation in the warm-advection region further destabilises mid-tropospheric levels through tilting and stretching
capping_or_instability_evidence: DIRECT: ECMWF equivalent potential temperature cross-sections at 42 N show potential instability to at least 8 km east of the front against only 3 km behind it, supported by the derived frontal-intensity equation
initiation_mechanism: The squall line is triggered in the updraught of the cross-frontal circulation, seen at the surface as a line of mass convergence or confluence over 1000 km long from southern Iberia to northern France; a surface moisture flux convergence maximum in the upper Ebro valley and a very low LCL where cool humid Biscay air meets hot humid south-west French air localise first development
initiation_evidence: DIRECT: objectively analysed surface pressure and moisture flux convergence fields, Meteosat visible sequences over the Basque country, and ECMWF cross-sections for 8 August 1992
hazards_locations_and_event_types: Severe prefrontal squall-line thunderstorms within a thundery low; Spanish Basque country, western Pyrenees, upper Ebro valley, Bay of Biscay and south-west France, 8 August 1992; Mediterranean flash-flood MCSs and alpine hailstorms noted as other European types
prefrontal_trough: PRESENT: a thundery (heat) low with a line of surface convergence or confluence more than 1000 km long forms ahead of the cold front and is the seat of the prefrontal squall line
key_supporting_quote: because the Spanish plume acts as a capping inversion preventing deep convection
limitations_or_uncertainty: The origin of the thundery low and its associated confluence line is stated to be not clear; the Rossby number exceeds 0.5 over a large area so quasi-geostrophic theory gives only an approximate first-order explanation; diabatic contributions to frontal intensification are difficult to quantify; the frontal-intensity measure diverges where the vertical potential temperature gradient vanishes

airstream_properties: Warm and moist air from the Mediterranean or from central Spain advected across southern France; a low-level inversion at a typical height of about 1.5 km limits vertical mixing so low-level equivalent potential temperature rises from day to day
diagnostic_variables: CAPE, bulk Richardson number, storm-relative helicity, energy-helicity index, equivalent potential temperature, hodographs, Stuttgart rawinsonde with 200 m mast data, C-band Doppler radar reflectivity and velocity, echotops
origin_and_transport_claim: Warm moist air from the Mediterranean or central Spain is advected across southern France and channelled through the Rhone valley, the Swiss Jura mountains and the Belfort Gap into the Rhine valley
origin_evidence: CITED_ONLY: stated as a generalisation from past-decades tornado data citing Morris (1986) and Dessens and Snow (1989); the studied case was driven by a deep low originating from ex-hurricane Iris, not by a plume
configuration: OTHER: a Mediterranean and central-Spanish route channelled through the Rhone valley and Belfort Gap into the Upper Rhine valley, not the classic Iberia-to-UK track
capping_or_instability_mechanism: Low-level inversion near 1.5 km caps the moistening boundary layer so equivalent potential temperature accumulates; it is removed by frontal lifting or positive vorticity advection with a short-wave upper trough
capping_or_instability_evidence: ASSERTED_ONLY: described generically in the background section with no sounding evidence; the case sounding gave only 440 J/kg CAPE with the near-surface mast data included
initiation_mechanism: Removal of the inversion by a cold front from W-NW or by short-wave trough vorticity advection; for the studied case a mid-tropospheric trough increased instability and orographic channelling produced a convergence line between southerly boundary-layer flow and enhanced westerly flow above the Saverne depression, with convergence-driven vortex stretching initiating the tornado
initiation_evidence: DIRECT for the case: Doppler radar vortex, convergence and divergence signatures, echotop evolution, hodograph, CAPE, SRH and EHI; the plume-related route itself is asserted
hazards_locations_and_event_types: A weak T2/F1 tornado near Oberkirch-Nussbach uprooting trees and damaging buildings and cars over a swath 1 km by 50 m, within severe thunderstorms and hail in the Upper Rhine valley, 9 September 1995; historical tornadoes including Pforzheim 10 July 1968
prefrontal_trough: NR: a weak cold front had already passed and a mid-tropospheric trough crossed at noon, but no prefrontal trough is reported
key_supporting_quote: warm and moist air from the Mediterranean or from central Spain is advected across southern France (the “Spanish plume” (Morris 1986))
limitations_or_uncertainty: No hook echo was observed, possibly because of the storm's small size or limited radar resolution; three other mesocyclones on the same day produced no reported tornadoes; CAPE was strongly sensitive to near-surface data (70 against 440 J/kg); the authors state the results are preliminary and need further research

airstream_properties: Warm humid air advected from the Spanish plateau creating a stable layer around 900 mb, with low-level warm advection over northern France and/or southern England and cold advection aloft into Iberia supplying large CAPE
diagnostic_variables: Daily Weather Reports (lightning, rainfall and cloud cover), archived polar-orbiter and later continuous satellite imagery, radar, surface temperature as a CAPE proxy, 500 mb height charts, anvil and rain areas, storm tracks and centroid paths
origin_and_transport_claim: The three main components are cold advection into Iberia, low-level warm advection over northern France and/or southern England, and an eastward-propagating upper trough to the west of the UK usually associated with a weak cold front; the warm humid air is advected from the Spanish plateau
origin_evidence: INDIRECT: the components are established by the authors' own synoptic classification of 32 archived cases from Daily Weather Reports and 500 mb charts, but the Spanish plateau source is asserted following Morris (1986) without trajectory analysis
configuration: CLASSIC: with noted variants including a cut-off low in a third of cases, cold advection from a southward-drifting cut-off low in one case, and strongly blocked flow with a westward-drifting cut-off low in others
capping_or_instability_mechanism: Warm humid air advected from the Spanish plateau creates a stable layer around 900 mbar so that the large CAPE generated by cold advection aloft cannot be released spontaneously
capping_or_instability_evidence: ASSERTED_ONLY: the stable layer is stated as the mechanism without soundings, and the authors note it is impossible to calculate CAPE from the available data
initiation_mechanism: Warm advection coupled with eastward propagation of the upper trough creates an area of ascent ahead of the surface cold front which destabilises the profile and releases the CAPE; weak short-wave troughs can assist; systems propagate by new cell growth on downdraught outflow boundaries
initiation_evidence: INDIRECT: inferred from synoptic charts for the case sample, with the short-wave contribution described only as something that may have assisted development
hazards_locations_and_event_types: Mesoscale convective systems bringing heavy rain, hail, strong gusts, local flooding and occasionally tornadoes; 32 MCSs over the UK 1981-97, most frequent over south-east England, central southern England and East Anglia, mid-May to end of August, mostly advected in from France
key_supporting_quote: Of the 32 MCSs studied, 25 are associated with a Spanish plume.
limitations_or_uncertainty: CAPE could not be calculated from the available data; the list is described as highly probable MCSs and may exclude events with insufficient evidence; satellite images do not always coincide with the storm time over the UK; more systems may have been identified in 1997 because of better data; the apparent El Nino correspondence is attributed to coincidence given the small sample

airstream_properties: Warm air lying east of the forward cold front, separated from cooler air further east by a warm front; associated more generally with warm air advected northward at levels between 900 and 700 hPa ahead of an approaching cold front in spring and summer over western Europe
diagnostic_variables: Slope of isentropes as a frontal-intensity indicator, potential and equivalent potential temperature vertical cross-sections, ECMWF analyses, Meteosat infrared imagery, and the frontogenetic terms (tilting, stretching, confluence, shear, advection)
origin_and_transport_claim: Warm air is advected northward between 900 and 700 hPa in advance of an approaching cold front; no source region is identified in this paper
origin_evidence: CITED_ONLY: the plume label and its characteristics are taken from Van Delden (1998); the paper's own analysis only locates the warm air east of the forward cold front
capping_or_instability_mechanism: The forward cold front is characterised as a cold front of reduced static stability leaning toward the warm air, whose forward tilt is caused by the cross-frontal circulation and may lead to severe thunderstorms; no capping inversion or CAPE analysis is presented
capping_or_instability_evidence: INDIRECT: based on isentrope-slope and frontogenesis diagnostics of the 8 August 1992 ECMWF analyses, with the link to thunderstorms carried by citation
initiation_mechanism: NR: no convective initiation mechanism is analysed; the forward tilt is only said to possibly lead to severe thunderstorms
initiation_evidence: CITED_ONLY: the thunderstorm connection rests on Van Delden (1998)
hazards_locations_and_event_types: Severe thunderstorms in western Europe are mentioned only in passing; the analysed case covers Iberia, the Bay of Biscay and France on 8 August 1992
key_supporting_quote: there is a warm front separating the warm air associated with the so-called ‘‘Spanish plume’’
limitations_or_uncertainty: The frontal-intensity measure diverges where the vertical potential temperature gradient vanishes, and worse when equivalent potential temperature is used; determining the front speed is stated to be very difficult if not impossible; a broad upright zone is judged more intense than a narrow one; the new frontogenetic terms play only a secondary role

airstream_properties: NR for the plume itself; the associated conditions reported are a strong horizontal temperature gradient over France and a cold airmass with its upper trough to westward towards Biscay and Iberia
diagnostic_variables: Historical account based on surface synoptic charts, aeroplane, kite and balloon upper-air temperature and humidity observations, lapse rate, upper-cloud drift and thermal wind reasoning; for the storm passage, the horizontal temperature gradient over France and westward decrease of upper-air temperature
origin_and_transport_claim: NR: no origin or transport is described; only that the typical thundery front develops over Biscay or western France when upper-air temperature decreases westward, often ahead of an Atlantic front
origin_evidence: CITED_ONLY: the plume is invoked retrospectively as something Douglas and Harding (1946) anticipated, with no supporting analysis
capping_or_instability_mechanism: NR
capping_or_instability_evidence: NR
initiation_mechanism: NR
initiation_evidence: CITED_ONLY: the development of a thundery front over Biscay or western France is reported from Douglas and Harding (1946) rather than analysed
hazards_locations_and_event_types: The thunderstorm of 14-15 July 1945, described as the most severe to affect England since 9-10 July 1923, with heaviest rainfall in Sussex, London, the Home Counties and the east Midlands
prefrontal_trough: UNCLEAR: a typical thundery front developing ahead of an Atlantic front is described, and Douglas is said to have noted that troughs lie further west aloft, but no prefrontal trough is identified
key_supporting_quote: Douglas and Harding’s (1946) observations contain a pre-science of the phenomenon known as the ‘Spanish plume’.
limitations_or_uncertainty: This is a biographical profile rather than an analysis; the attribution of pre-science is the author's retrospective interpretation, and the paper stresses the primitive methods and the lack of adequate upper-air observations near fronts in Douglas's era

airstream_properties: Very warm air over the Iberian plateau (about 1000 m high) at levels between 900 and 700 hPa, appearing at 850 hPa as a zone of warm advection from Iberia over the Bay of Biscay and western France, with high potential static instability created above it
diagnostic_variables: Four-year six-hourly synoptic thunderstorm reports from over 200 stations; radiosonde potential instability (925 minus 500 hPa equivalent potential temperature per unit height); dew point statistics; ECMWF 850 hPa height, temperature and temperature advection; Q-vector divergence; 700 hPa winds and jetstreaks; isentropic potential vorticity and layer divergence; surface moisture flux convergence; Meteosat imagery
origin_and_transport_claim: When a trough or cut-off low approaches Iberia from the west in summer, the very warm air over the Iberian plateau at 900-700 hPa is set in motion and travels north over the Bay of Biscay and western France; comparable warm plumes can also form over northern Africa or the European continent
origin_evidence: DIRECT: the author's own ECMWF 850 hPa temperature and temperature-advection analyses for 20 July 1992 and two further 1992 cases identify the warm-advection zone, supported by a four-year sounding climatology of potential instability
configuration: CLASSIC: with explicit variants in which the warm plume originates over northern Africa (22 September 1992) or the European continent (20 August 1992)
capping_or_instability_mechanism: High levels of potential static instability are created above the plume, giving the 'loaded gun' state; elsewhere potential instability is aided by orographic blocking of low-level cold advection and by high low-level moisture
capping_or_instability_evidence: DIRECT: potential instability computed from radiosondes at six stations over 1996-1999 and mapped for the three 1992 severe thunderstorm cases
initiation_mechanism: Frontogenesis, driven by the intense horizontal gradient of temperature advection over Iberia, forces the vertical circulation that lifts boundary-layer air to its level of free convection and forms the thundery low along a convergence line; upper-level potential vorticity advection, lee cyclogenesis, sea and land breezes and thermally forced upslope flow supply additional lift
initiation_evidence: DIRECT: Q-vector divergence, 700 hPa vertical velocity, 925 hPa height and temperature, moisture flux convergence, jetstreak and potential vorticity or divergence fields computed for the three 1992 cases
hazards_locations_and_event_types: Severe thunderstorms and convective complexes across western Europe, with three preferred regions (Massif Central to southern Germany, the Po valley and south-east Alps, and the Gulf of Genoa); cases of 20-21 July 1992 (Spain, France, southern England, Benelux), 20 August 1992 (Germany) and 22 September 1992 (southern France)
prefrontal_trough: PRESENT: the convergence line runs through the axis of a trough (the thundery low) formed by mass convergence, and a separate lee-trough is identified north of the Alps
key_supporting_quote: Above the Spanish plume, high levels of potential static instability are created.
limitations_or_uncertainty: Thunderstorm reports are subjective and observer-dependent; the data sets for Italy and much of Spain and Portugal are relatively incomplete; a four-year period may not represent longer-term averages; stations reporting only in working hours were excluded; the Corsican land and sea breeze effect remains to be investigated

airstream_properties: NR: the paper's 'plume' is a cloud-top layer of small ice crystals (effective radius 4-7 micrometres, optical depth 2-8) above a cumulonimbus anvil, not a tropospheric warm airstream
diagnostic_variables: AVHRR channel 2, 3, 4 and 5 reflectances and brightness temperatures, brightness temperature differences, multispectral colour composites, and Streamer one-dimensional plane-parallel radiative transfer simulations with varied ice crystal habit, optical depth and effective radius
origin_and_transport_claim: NR: the term 'Spanish' plume in this paper denotes the storm-top ice-crystal plume observed over south-eastern Spain on 28 August 1991, and no synoptic Spanish Plume origin or transport is described
origin_evidence: NR
capping_or_instability_mechanism: NR: no capping or tropospheric instability mechanism is treated; storm-top plume formation is attributed by cited work to strong updraughts, overshooting domes and gravity waves
capping_or_instability_evidence: CITED_ONLY: the plume formation mechanism is attributed to Wang (2001) and Fujita (1982) and is not tested here
initiation_mechanism: NR
initiation_evidence: NR
hazards_locations_and_event_types: A multicell storm over south-eastern Spain on 28 August 1991 with a cloud-top plume; no surface hazards are reported
key_supporting_quote: The 28 August 1991 ‘‘Spanish’’ plume
limitations_or_uncertainty: Simulations could not reproduce brightness temperatures as low as 216 K so the assumed underlying cloud structure probably does not fit the real scenario; the ice crystal habit could not be unambiguously retrieved; the scene was assumed aerosol free, an assumption the authors note may not be justified; more cases are needed to generalise

airstream_properties: Hot humid air with 850 mbar wet-bulb potential temperature above 18 C and maximum temperatures around 30 C on the preceding day
diagnostic_variables: 850 mbar wet-bulb potential temperature, maximum temperature, 500 mbar col, Meteosat visible imagery, European and UK rainfall radar, rainfall totals and rates
origin_and_transport_claim: NR for an Iberian source: the paper reports only a frontal system over the west of the British Isles and through the Bay of Biscay, an upper trough approaching from the west and surface heat lows over land under a 500 mbar col
origin_evidence: ASSERTED_ONLY: similarity to the Spanish plume is asserted from the presence of certain ingredients with a citation to Morris (1986), and no origin or transport analysis is given
configuration: MODIFIED: only some of the ingredients are said to match a Spanish plume, with surface heat lows under a 500 mbar col rather than a clear Iberian plume beneath an advancing trough
capping_or_instability_mechanism: NR: no capping layer is described; the air is stated to be unstable to surface temperatures, with decreasing stability in the upper troposphere and overnight cooling aloft
capping_or_instability_evidence: ASSERTED_ONLY: instability inferred from 850 mbar theta-w and surface maxima with no soundings presented
initiation_mechanism: Insolation, low-level convergence and overnight cooling of the upper atmosphere, with orographic triggering over the Lincolnshire and Yorkshire Wolds, the Pennines, the north-western slopes of the Massif Central and several southern British uplands
initiation_evidence: INDIRECT: inferred from the position of cumulonimbus lines and radar rainfall lines relative to high ground in satellite and radar imagery
hazards_locations_and_event_types: Heavy thundery rain with 100 mm in under 24 hours near Halifax, 82 mm in under 17 hours near King's Lynn, day darkness in Manchester and rainfall rates over 16 mm/h in central France; UK and western Europe, 30-31 July 2002
key_supporting_quote: Many of the ingredients for the development of these storms were similar to those seen in the so-called `Spanish plume’
limitations_or_uncertainty: This is a short image note; mechanisms are stated as likely or as appearing to have been the trigger, and are inferred from satellite and radar imagery rather than demonstrated

airstream_properties: NR
diagnostic_variables: Cloud genus and species identification, atmospheric profiles and tephigrams, satellite imagery; for the plume mention only the obscuring effect of a low cloud layer is relevant
origin_and_transport_claim: NR: only that heavy thundery rain moves north into the British Isles in a Spanish plume
origin_evidence: CITED_ONLY: supported solely by citations to Galvin et al. (1995) and Young (1995)
capping_or_instability_mechanism: NR
capping_or_instability_evidence: NR
initiation_mechanism: NR
initiation_evidence: NR
hazards_locations_and_event_types: Heavy thundery rain moving north into the British Isles, with low cloud obscuring much or all of the sky for the observer
key_supporting_quote: heavy thundery rain moves north into the British Isles in a `Spanish plume’
limitations_or_uncertainty: This is an observational guide rather than an analysis; the author notes that classical frontal cloud sequences are rare and most cases are exceptions, and that the cloud-base formula is accurate only to within about 20 per cent

airstream_properties: A tongue of warm and moist boundary-layer air flowing northward from Spain and the Mediterranean Sea, usually capped by an elevated inversion creating the 'loaded gun' situation
diagnostic_variables: Composite C-band radar reflectivity at 500 m (pseudo-CAPPI) with 18, 40 and 50 dBZ thresholds, MCS duration, tracks, times of initiation, dissipation and maximum intensity, and national lightning statistics
origin_and_transport_claim: A tongue of warm moist boundary-layer air flows northward from Spain and the Mediterranean Sea ahead of an approaching upper-level trough, allowing a strong MCS to develop over France and the United Kingdom; a comparable southerly or south-easterly warm moist inflow is noted for Finland
origin_evidence: CITED_ONLY: the description is a literature summary citing Browning and Hill (1984), McCallum and Waters (1993), Young (1995), Gray and Marshall (1998) and van Delden (1998), and the Finnish analogue rests on forecasting experience
configuration: CLASSIC: for the western European description; the Finnish analogue is said only to have some similarities
capping_or_instability_mechanism: The boundary-layer air is usually capped by an elevated inversion creating the 'loaded gun' situation
capping_or_instability_evidence: CITED_ONLY: stated as background from the western European literature, with no soundings analysed in this study
initiation_mechanism: NR for the plume: the study does not analyse initiation mechanisms, reporting only that intense MCSs are modulated by the diurnal heating and cooling cycle while spring and autumn systems appear driven by baroclinic disturbances
initiation_evidence: INDIRECT: initiation times and seasonality are derived from radar statistics rather than from mechanism analysis
hazards_locations_and_event_types: Mesoscale convective systems and heavy convective precipitation, with reflectivities above 50 dBZ noted as carrying an increased threat of hail, downbursts, lightning and flash floods; Finland and nearby regions, April to September 2000 and 2001; strong MCSs over France and the UK cited for the plume
key_supporting_quote: A tongue of warm and moist boundary layer air flows northward from Spain and the Mediterranean Sea in front of an approaching upper-level trough.
limitations_or_uncertainty: Only a two-year sample, so climatic conclusions are described as very preliminary; 5.3 per cent of radar images were missing; bright banding can both over- and under-estimate reflectivity and extend MCS duration, with the total effect stated to be unknown; incompletely tracked systems bias durations and paths; the MCS definition allows fairly weak precipitation areas to qualify

airstream_properties: A tongue of warm low-level air with anomalously large equivalent potential temperature at low and mid levels, with a thermal inversion just below 850 mb where the warm tongue from the Spanish plateau resides and large CAPE above
diagnostic_variables: Met Office Unified Model at 12 km with 38 levels; 850 hPa equivalent potential temperature; model-derived tephigrams with CAPE and CIN; AVHRR infrared images and model pseudo-infrared images; passive tracers of 3 h and 24 h lifetime and the derived age of air; 310 K isentropic analyses; EXPORT aircraft hydrocarbon measurements
origin_and_transport_claim: A tongue of warm low-level air is advected from the Spanish plateau on the forward side of an eastward-propagating upper-level trough, usually associated with a weak cold front; the modelled tracer plume emanates from the Iberian Peninsula and is advected toward north-east Europe
origin_evidence: DIRECT: the model tracer experiments show a plume emanating from the Iberian Peninsula with age increasing downstream, supported by 850 hPa equivalent potential temperature fields, while the definition itself is attributed to Morris (1986)
capping_or_instability_mechanism: A thermal inversion just below 850 mb inhibits low-level convection and allows gradual formation of a large CAPE reservoir; CAPE was created by boundary-layer moistening while convective inhibition was reduced by cooling, presumably from turbulent surface fluxes, with cold advection aloft between 450 and 350 hPa adding upper-level CAPE
capping_or_instability_evidence: DIRECT: model tephigrams at 7.5E 47.5N showing convective inhibition below 600 hPa and its later reduction to below 900 hPa, compared with an ascent 11 hours earlier
initiation_mechanism: Ascent ahead of the surface cold front due to the advancing upper-level trough together with orographic forcing destabilised the profile, releasing CAPE and triggering the MCSs; a separate upper cold front dry intrusion overran moist air creating potential instability and mid-level convection
initiation_evidence: DIRECT: model tephigram evolution, comparison of pseudo-infrared and AVHRR imagery, and tracer age fields for 1-2 August 2000
hazards_locations_and_event_types: Mesoscale convective systems ahead of a weak cold front over western and central Europe on 1-2 August 2000; the paper's emphasis is on boundary-layer ventilation and pollutant export rather than surface hazards
prefrontal_trough: NR: a weak cold front, an upper-level trough and an upper cold front are described, but no surface prefrontal trough is reported
key_supporting_quote: The other characteristic feature of the Spanish plume is a thermal inversion which can be observed just below 850 mb
limitations_or_uncertainty: Modelled MCS positions are displaced west and south and the forecast lags the observations by a few hours; the tracer age estimate carries a bias of up to 6 hours; implicit diffusion in the advection scheme can cause unrealistic phase speeds and age inaccuracies; convective detrainment at 600 hPa was absent in the model; representativity cannot be assessed without more case studies

airstream_properties: NR: no properties are given; the plume is likened only to prefrontal warm anomalies produced by intense surface heating over continents or by downsloping in the lee of orography
diagnostic_variables: NR for the plume; the review's general diagnostics are surface pressure, wind shift, temperature gradient, vorticity, convergence and the mean temperature of the overlying column
origin_and_transport_claim: NR: no origin or transport is described; the plume is suggested only to be a warm anomaly in the prefrontal air over western Europe capable of producing a second front ahead of the primary front
origin_evidence: CITED_ONLY: invoked by citation to Morris (1986) and van Delden (1998), with the author stating that this mechanism remains undiagnosed using real data
capping_or_instability_mechanism: NR for the plume; the review notes generally that prefrontal stable layers inhibit deep moist convection and that adiabatic cooling at a front may help remove them
capping_or_instability_evidence: NR
initiation_mechanism: NR for the plume; the review notes that prefrontal troughs may be one mechanism by which prefrontal squall lines form and are used operationally as boundaries for convective initiation
initiation_evidence: CITED_ONLY: the convective relevance of prefrontal troughs is drawn from the cited literature rather than analysed here
hazards_locations_and_event_types: NR for the plume; the review associates prefrontal troughs generally with heavy rains, convective storms, dust storms, dry gusty winds favouring wildfires and extratropical cyclones, mainly in Australian and United States examples
prefrontal_trough: PRESENT: prefrontal troughs are the subject of the paper, and the Spanish plume is proposed as a similar prefrontal warm-anomaly feature over western Europe
key_supporting_quote: The Spanish plume (Morris 1986; van Delden 1998) may also be a similar feature over western Europe.
limitations_or_uncertainty: The author states that this mechanism remains undiagnosed using real data; more broadly, many of the ten mechanisms have been identified from theory or observation but not both, other self-consistent taxonomies are possible, and further mechanisms may exist or remain undiscovered

airstream_properties: A plume of warm dry air of high potential temperature from the arid Spanish plateau, formed as a relatively deep dry mixed boundary layer; afternoon screen-level theta about 36 C over the plateau against 26-28 C over France, overlying cooler moister air of lower theta but higher theta-w as an elevated mixed layer with a strong inversion at its base
diagnostic_variables: Wet-bulb potential temperature theta-w and potential temperature theta, CAPE and CIN on tephigrams, Bowen ratio and sensible-to-latent heat flux ratio, water vapour satellite imagery and potential vorticity for dry intrusions, radar clear-air echoes, sferics
origin_and_transport_claim: The warm lid originates from a deep dry mixed boundary layer generated over the arid Spanish plateau and advects northwards in a southerly airstream to overlie the cooler moister boundary layer of south-west France as an elevated mixed layer
origin_evidence: CITED_ONLY: the mechanism and the quoted screen-level potential temperatures are attributed to Carlson and Ludlam (1968), Ludlam (1980) and Carlson (1991), and the review presents no new analysis of the plume
capping_or_instability_mechanism: The warm dry elevated mixed layer acts as a strong lid confining small-scale convection to the lowest 1-2 km so that theta-w rises by about 2.5 degC per 24 hours and large CAPE accumulates beneath large CIN
capping_or_instability_evidence: CITED_ONLY: presented from Carlson and Ludlam (1968) and Carlson (1991) with schematic thermodynamic diagrams; the one real tephigram shown is an unrelated Nottingham example of a stable layer
initiation_mechanism: Instability is released most often where the low-level flow, backed from southerly to more easterly, reaches the western edge of the dry plume aloft, a boundary marked by a cold front; colder air aloft and strong vertical wind shear then favour severe storms and possibly an MCS, with evaporation from high-based castellanus further cooling aloft
initiation_evidence: CITED_ONLY: attributed to the isentropic analysis of Carlson and Ludlam (1968) and to Ludlam (1963)
hazards_locations_and_event_types: Severe storms and mesoscale convective systems over the UK with flood-producing heavy rain, hail and lightning; 25 of 32 UK MCSs between 1981 and 1997 are reported (after Gray and Marshall 1998) as associated with Spanish Plume events, mainly May to August and advected in overnight from continental Europe
prefrontal_trough: NR: a split-front structure with an upper cold front running ahead of the surface cold front is described, but no prefrontal trough is reported
key_supporting_quote: The warm lid of the Spanish Plume originates from a relatively deep mixed boundary layer generated over the arid Spanish plateau.
limitations_or_uncertainty: The review states that the mechanisms initiating convective cells are inadequately understood and that forecasting skill for such events is low; current observation resolution cannot resolve the small-scale pre-storm environment; even high-resolution soundings are described as only marginally useful for precise forecasts of initiation

airstream_properties: A warm moist plume below 750 mb with 850 mb wet-bulb potential temperature above 289 K tracking north beneath cooler drier mid- and upper-level south-westerly flow, its front edge becoming elevated above a low-level easterly flow below 850 mb
diagnostic_variables: Model 850 mb geopotential height and wet-bulb potential temperature, off-line CAPE and CIN from pseudo-adiabatic parcel ascent, area-average CAPE and convective adjustment timescale, Meteosat infrared imagery, network radar rainfall, potential vorticity and 250 mb wind perturbations
origin_and_transport_claim: A warm moist plume below 750 mb tracked north beneath cooler drier south-westerly flow aloft, becoming elevated above a low-level easterly flow; no Iberian source region is traced
origin_evidence: INDIRECT: the plume is identified from model 850 mb theta-w and height fields for 28-29 May 1999 and named after Morris (1986), with no origin or trajectory analysis
capping_or_instability_mechanism: The elevated front edge of the plume above the low-level easterly flow created a large-scale unstable region with significant vertical shear; in this case most of the CAPE region was collocated with almost zero CIN so convection was free to act, in contrast to the second, non-equilibrium case where CAPE lay under high CIN
capping_or_instability_evidence: DIRECT: model CAPE and CIN fields prior to initiation, plus time series of area-average CAPE and of the estimated convective adjustment timescale
initiation_mechanism: Convection was triggered on the elevated plume over the Bay of Biscay at 0000 UTC 29 May and again near southern England between 0330 and 0400 UTC, within high CAPE and outside high CIN, evolving into a coherent MCS that tracked north-eastward with the mid-level flow
initiation_evidence: DIRECT: Meteosat infrared triggering locations compared with model CAPE and CIN fields and with radar-derived rainfall
hazards_locations_and_event_types: Organized convection and a mesoscale convective system over southern England moving to the North Sea, with propagating parallel lines of convection; 28-29 May 1999
prefrontal_trough: NR: warm and cold fronts at 850 mb are analysed, but no prefrontal trough is reported for this case
key_supporting_quote: The meteorological situation known as the Spanish plume, described by Morris (1986), occurred during 28 and 29 May 1999
limitations_or_uncertainty: CAPE and CIN were computed off-line with buoyancy assumptions differing from the model and omitting unresolved-scale contributions, so the fields are offered only as general stability information; the convective timescale calculation ignores convective modification of the boundary layer and significantly overestimates the timescale; the squall-line-like propagation late in case 1 complicates the equilibrium interpretation and was not reproduced at 12 km grid spacing

airstream_properties: NR: no plume properties are given, and the authors state that a Spanish plume was not present in their case
diagnostic_variables: NR for the plume; the paper's own diagnostics are potential vorticity and the 2 PVU tropopause, an online stratospheric tracer passed through or withheld from the convection scheme, CAPE, a De Bilt skew-T sounding, Meteosat water vapour imagery, Nimrod radar rainfall and sferics
origin_and_transport_claim: NR: no origin or transport of a plume is described
origin_evidence: CITED_ONLY: the plume is invoked only through Gray and Marshall (1998) as the environment in which UK MCSs most often form, and is explicitly stated to have been absent on 27 June 2004
capping_or_instability_mechanism: NR for the plume; the case's own potential instability came from a warm moist near-surface layer capped by a deep dry mid-tropospheric layer beneath a tropopause fold, with 191 J/kg of CAPE
capping_or_instability_evidence: DIRECT for the case: De Bilt 1200 UT skew-T sounding and Meteosat water vapour imagery, but this instability is attributed to a tropopause fold and not to a plume
initiation_mechanism: NR for the plume; convection formed near the leading edge of an eastward-propagating upper-level potential vorticity anomaly, with upper-level PV advection judged crucial to initiation and maintenance
initiation_evidence: DIRECT for the case: sferics timing, satellite imagery, radar rainfall and model potential temperature on the 2 PVU surface
hazards_locations_and_event_types: A mesoscale convective system with peak radar rainfall rates of 16-32 mm/h over south-east England and the North Sea on 27 June 2004; the paper's focus is stratosphere-to-troposphere transport rather than surface hazards
key_supporting_quote: are most likely to form within a so-called ‘‘Spanish plume’’ [Gray and Marshall, 1998], although this was not present on 27 June 2004
limitations_or_uncertainty: The analysis retains the uncertainty of the convective parameterization, whose suitability at 4 km is described as somewhat suspect; at 1 km the resolved convection does not produce the full turbulence spectrum so the simulated mass flux cannot be fully trusted; deeply transported tracer concentrations are three orders of magnitude below those of shallow transport

airstream_properties: Warm humid air advected from the Atlantic and the Mediterranean from a south-westerly direction; associated tornado days show precipitable water mostly 15-25 mm, 700 hPa wind direction 220-260 degrees, 500 hPa temperature -16 to -12 C, 850 hPa temperature 8-12 C and 850 hPa dewpoint 0-5 C
diagnostic_variables: DWD objective weather-type classification (700 hPa wind direction, cyclonality from the Laplacian of geopotential at 950 and 500 hPa, precipitable water), thunderstorm days, Essen radiosonde 850 and 500 hPa temperature and 850 hPa dewpoint, Fujita scale ratings, binomial significance testing
origin_and_transport_claim: Warm humid air is advected to Germany from the Atlantic and the Mediterranean from a south-westerly direction, labelled the Spanish plume; no Iberian plateau source is claimed
origin_evidence: ASSERTED_ONLY: the label is attached in the discussion, with a citation to Morris (1986), to the statistically identified south-westerly wet weather types, with no origin or trajectory analysis
configuration: OTHER: the airstream is described as advected from the Atlantic and the Mediterranean toward Germany rather than as an elevated Iberian plume
capping_or_instability_mechanism: NR: no capping layer or instability mechanism is described; instability enters only through weather-type humidity and the preferred aerological ranges
capping_or_instability_evidence: NR
initiation_mechanism: Warm humid south-westerly advection combined with orogenic low-level wind shear is said to intensify thunderstorms and thus also to lead to tornadoes, especially in summer
initiation_evidence: ASSERTED_ONLY: offered in the discussion as an explanation for the statistical preference, without dynamical analysis
hazards_locations_and_event_types: Tornadoes in Germany, 468 reported over 1950-2003 including one F4 (Pforzheim, 10 July 1968) and thirteen F3 events; maxima in north-western and south-western Germany with a July peak; about one tornado day per 50 thunderstorm days at most
key_supporting_quote: the warm humid air which is advected from the Atlantic and the Mediterranean from south-westerly direction to Germany (the “Spanish plume”, Morris, 1986)
limitations_or_uncertainty: Tornado reports are incomplete, with underreporting varying with population density and with time, so no absolute probabilities should be drawn; the weather-type series begins only in 1980, giving 24 years; 23.5 per cent of tornadoes have no intensity rating; the audible-thunder definition of thunderstorm days is acknowledged as problematic; thunderstorm days and precipitable water are found not to be useful predictors

airstream_properties: A tongue of warm relatively dry low-level air advected northward from the Spanish plateau, which caps the moister surface air
diagnostic_variables: NR for the plume; the paper's own diagnostics are wet-bulb potential temperature surfaces, idealized tracers of 3 h and 24 h lifetime, age of air, tracer budgets, infrared satellite imagery and modelled boundary layer height
origin_and_transport_claim: A tongue of warm relatively dry low-level air is advected northward from the Spanish plateau on the forward side of an eastward-propagating upper-level trough
origin_evidence: CITED_ONLY: the definition is given from Morris (1986) and the earlier finding from Agusti-Panareda et al. (2005); neither of the two cases analysed here is a Spanish plume event
capping_or_instability_mechanism: The warm relatively dry plume air caps the moister surface air so that convective instability can build; once released it can lead to mesoscale convective systems and thunderstorms
capping_or_instability_evidence: CITED_ONLY: stated from Morris (1986) with no sounding or CAPE analysis in this paper
initiation_mechanism: Release of the accumulated convective instability, leading to mesoscale convective systems and thunderstorms; in the earlier study this convection ahead of a kata-cold front dominated boundary-layer ventilation
initiation_evidence: CITED_ONLY: taken from Morris (1986) and Agusti-Panareda et al. (2005)
hazards_locations_and_event_types: Mesoscale convective systems and thunderstorms; the earlier summer kata-cold front case is contrasted with the spring case here, in which no boundary-layer ventilation by convection occurred where the dry intrusion overran the warm conveyor belt
prefrontal_trough: NR: convection in the earlier plume case is described as occurring ahead of the kata-cold front, but no prefrontal trough is reported
key_supporting_quote: a tongue of warm relatively dry low-level air is advected northward from the Spanish plateau
limitations_or_uncertainty: The authors note that the earlier kata-cold front result might have been influenced more by summer conditions than by the frontal type itself; the age diagnostic is biased toward larger ages near the surface, requiring the tracer sink to be removed in the lowest five levels; the 3 h tracer lifetime is longer than the 0.5-1 h typical of convection because of numerical dispersion; only two cases are analysed

airstream_properties: A warm moist conditionally unstable low-level plume (theta-w above about 289-290 K) advected north-eastwards or northwards from Iberia, capped near 850 hPa (about 1500 m) by a stable elevated mixed layer of warmer but very dry air (lower theta-w, higher theta) originating over the Spanish plateau
diagnostic_variables: Met Office ATD lightning, radar, Meteosat 7 and 9 imagery, surface analyses, 12 km MetUM analyses, NCEP GFS, NCEP/NCAR reanalysis composites of MSLP, 500 hPa height and 300 and 200 hPa winds, 850 hPa theta-w and geopotential, CAPE and CIN, quasi-geostrophically forced 700 hPa vertical velocity, Trappes and Bordeaux radiosondes, potential temperature on the 2 PVU surface
origin_and_transport_claim: An upper-level trough propagating toward Biscay and Iberia with a surface cold front, together with a low-level zone of strong temperature gradient over Iberia, generates warm advection that sharpens that gradient into a plume of convectively unstable air moving north toward northern France and southern England, which becomes the main frontal zone; a modified variant has a forward-tilted or cut-off trough, and a third type has a plume advected westwards across northern continental Europe
origin_evidence: DIRECT: an extended 1998-2008 climatology of 25 UK MCSs, two detailed case studies using MetUM analyses and radiosondes, and NCEP/NCAR composites of each environment, although the classical description itself is drawn from Carlson and Ludlam (1968), Morris (1986), Gray and Marshall (1998) and Bennett et al. (2006)
configuration: CLASSIC: this paper defines the three-way classification, assigning 9 of 25 MCSs to the classical Spanish plume, 10 to the modified Spanish plume and 5 to the European easterly plume, with one unclassified
capping_or_instability_mechanism: Large CAPE builds because warm humid surface air of high theta-w is capped near 850 hPa by a stable layer of warmer but very dry air from the Spanish plateau acting as a convective lid, allowing boundary-layer theta-w to rise on sunny days; cooling aloft ahead of the advancing trough further enhances CAPE
capping_or_instability_evidence: DIRECT: the Bordeaux 0000 UTC 19 June 2007 ascent shows warm dry air near 900 hPa above a convective lid, with model CAPE reaching about 2400 J/kg and CIN up to about 100 J/kg in the triggering region
initiation_mechanism: Ascent forced by low-level warm advection together with upper-level positive differential vorticity advection releases the CAPE; alternatively triggering occurs where the low-level flow reaches the western edge of the convective lid; in case II the cap was eroded from west to east by an upper front with secondary cells on the south-east flank, and in case I the plume was lifted isentropically over a shallow cold pool over southern England
initiation_evidence: DIRECT: quasi-geostrophically forced 700 hPa vertical velocity, CAPE and CIN fields, cross-sections of theta-w and vertical velocity, and radar and satellite sequences for both cases
hazards_locations_and_event_types: Mesoscale convective systems over the UK with radar rain rates above 50 mm/h (case I) and above 80 mm/h with small hail (case II), over 1200 lightning strikes per hour, and flash flooding; about 2.3 MCSs per year over 1998-2008, most frequent over south-east England, central southern England and East Anglia, mid-May to mid-September
prefrontal_trough: UNCLEAR: a pre-frontal convergence line or upper-level front is reported as a locus for further development in the modified Spanish plume, and a trough line was analysed with the case I MCS, but no synoptic prefrontal pressure trough is identified as such
key_supporting_quote: a warm moist plume of air advected northeastwards from Iberia that is capped by warmer, but very dry air, from the Spanish plateau
limitations_or_uncertainty: The identification criteria are described as somewhat arbitrary, and the lightning criterion excludes significant MCS-like events such as 20 July 2007; archive radar and sferics before 2004 were not readily available, potentially excluding events, and four further events were discounted for lack of evidence; compositing is less appropriate for small samples and the categorisation is subjective; caution is urged in comparing environment frequencies

airstream_properties: Warm and moist air advected from south-westerly directions; on 59 of 65 hail days the mid-tropospheric flow lay between south and west, with mean surface-based CAPE 1080-1250 J/kg, mixed-layer CAPE 500-610 J/kg, CIN50 mostly above -110 J/kg, a mean 0-2 km wind of 4.1 m/s and dry Brunt-Vaisala frequency 0.013 per s
diagnostic_variables: C-band 3D radar reflectivity with the TRACE3D cell-tracking algorithm, building insurance loss frequency, ESWD hail reports, Stuttgart 1200 UTC radiosondes with CAPE, CIN, K, Lifted and Showalter indices, 850 and 500 hPa wind direction, surface and 500 hPa charts, generalized Pareto extreme-value statistics and the Froude number
origin_and_transport_claim: An extended trough centred over the West European Basin or the Bay of Biscay with a ridge over the Mediterranean advects warm moist air from south-westerly directions into south-west Germany
origin_evidence: INDIRECT: based on the authors' inspection of surface and 500 hPa charts for all 65 hail days, with the plume label attached by citation to Morris (1986) and no origin or trajectory analysis
configuration: CLASSIC: a trough over the West European Basin or Bay of Biscay with a Mediterranean ridge and south-westerly advection, though directed at south-west Germany rather than the UK
capping_or_instability_mechanism: NR for a plume lid; convective inhibition on most hail days (CIN50 above -110 J/kg) was judged likely to be eroded in the early afternoon by boundary-layer mixing or synoptic-scale lifting, with frontal passage or strong large-scale lifting assumed on the few days with CIN below -150 J/kg
capping_or_instability_evidence: DIRECT: 1200 UTC Stuttgart and composite soundings for the 65 selected hail days, although the inhibition is not linked to a plume-derived elevated mixed layer
initiation_mechanism: Low Froude number flow (mean 0.32) diverted around the southern Black Forest produces downstream horizontal convergence near Stuttgart, and flow deviation at the sharply angled north-western edge of the Swabian Jura explains the sharp gradient in track density
initiation_evidence: INDIRECT: a conceptual Froude-number argument supported by sounding-derived wind and stability statistics and by the observed spatial pattern of tracks, with the authors stating that the flow regime and lee convergence need further evaluation
hazards_locations_and_event_types: Severe hailstorms with hailstones of 2-7 cm damaging buildings, vehicles and crops; about 40 per cent of building damage in Baden-Wuerttemberg over 1986-2008 was hail related with a mean annual loss near EUR 50 million, and a hot spot lies south of Stuttgart; 65 hail days over 1997-2007
key_supporting_quote: warm and moist air is advected from southwesterly directions in the area under investigation, frequently referred to as the “Spanish plume”
limitations_or_uncertainty: The 55 dBZ threshold is only a potential indicator of hail rather than proof; radar attenuation and a wet radome interrupt tracks and tracks within the outermost 10 km of range are unreliable; insurance data depend on population density and vulnerability and the hail-day thresholds are acknowledged as arbitrary; ESWD reports show a strong observational trend and only 14 give hailstone sizes; small samples give high uncertainty at long return periods

airstream_properties: NR for the plume itself; the airmass is described only as warm, humid and stagnant, with the 0900h Oxford dew point rising from 11 C to 16 C and temperatures reaching 26-28 C
diagnostic_variables: Daily Weather Report surface charts, Twentieth Century Reanalysis 500 mbar charts, dew point and temperature records, rain-gauge and hail observations, historical newspaper and British Rainfall accounts, TORRO hail scale
origin_and_transport_claim: NR: the identification rests on the 500 mbar pattern of a cut-off cold vortex south-west of the British Isles within a deep upper trough, with no plume origin or transport described
origin_evidence: INDIRECT: pattern matching of the reanalysis 500 mbar chart to the modified Spanish Plume scenario of Lewis and Gray (2010), with no analysis of a plume airstream
configuration: MODIFIED: explicitly identified as corresponding closely to the modified Spanish Plume of Lewis and Gray (2010)
capping_or_instability_mechanism: NR: no capping layer is described; the violence of the storms is attributed to destabilisation of a very humid air mass by surface heating
capping_or_instability_evidence: ASSERTED_ONLY: stated in the concluding remarks without sounding or stability data
initiation_mechanism: Destabilisation of a very humid air mass by surface heating, local convergence and general ascent ahead of a major upper trough; a north-easterly surface wind may have undercut the advancing warm humid air on 7 June
initiation_evidence: INDIRECT: inferred from historical surface charts, the near-simultaneity of the evening downpours (taken as indicative of a convergence zone) and reanalysis upper-level fields
hazards_locations_and_event_types: Violent thunderstorms with hail of 20-35 mm (at least H4 on the TORRO scale), daily rainfalls of 108-132 mm including over 100 mm in one hour at Wheatley, street flooding to 45-180 cm and extensive lightning damage and injuries; Thames Valley, Oxfordshire, Berkshire and the south Midlands, 7 and 9 June 1910
prefrontal_trough: NR: pressure was uniform on the morning of the 9th with a very shallow low tracking into the eastern English Channel; no prefrontal trough is reported
key_supporting_quote: This corresponds closely to the scenario of the ‘modified Spanish Plume’ described by Lewis and Gray (2010).
limitations_or_uncertainty: Two of the highest rainfall readings came from a non-standard gauge and a gauge in an unorthodox exposure; the Waterstock gauge was choked by hail and overflowed; the Kidmore End reading has little support from adjacent stations; hard hailstones can bounce out of standard gauges; the account depends heavily on historical newspaper and observer reports

airstream_properties: Very warm air moving northwards across the Spanish Plateau from Africa, with moist unstable air typically rising to around 10 000 feet (medium level) by the time it reaches the UK; 1000-850 mbar thickness 1409 m, 1000-500 mbar thickness 5697 m and 850 mbar theta-w near 18 C in the south-east
