diagnostic_variables: Synoptic analyses, Herstmonceux radiosonde ascent with 1000-850 and 1000-500 mbar thicknesses and 850 mbar theta-w, T+12 thickness forecasts, rainfall radar, Met Office lightning detection network, MSG visible imagery, NAME III and NOAA HYSPLIT backward trajectories, rainfall and temperature records
origin_and_transport_claim: Very warm air moves northwards across the Spanish Plateau from Africa; backward trajectories indicate an origin around Morocco on 23-24 June with the track passing over or near western Spain, Portugal and France
origin_evidence: DIRECT: two independent backward-trajectory models (NAME III and HYSPLIT) at 1000, 2000 and 3000 m indicate a Moroccan origin with a track over western Iberia and France, corroborated by Saharan dust deposits on 27 and 28 June
configuration: CLASSIC: an African source crossing the Spanish Plateau and reaching the UK ahead of troughs and waving cold fronts
capping_or_instability_mechanism: NR: no capping layer is described; a pre-existing zone of instability stretching from the Isle of Wight to the Wash is noted, with an approaching upper trough overrunning the surface front and increasing instability
capping_or_instability_evidence: ASSERTED_ONLY: a Herstmonceux ascent is shown but no capping layer or CAPE analysis is presented, and the instability zone is described qualitatively
initiation_mechanism: Thunderstorms broke out just ahead of the leading surface cold front, where a narrow trough lay slightly ahead of the fronts, as an approaching upper trough from the west began to overrun the surface front and intensify convection
initiation_evidence: INDIRECT: inferred from surface analyses, rainfall radar frames and lightning detection sequences rather than from computed forcing
hazards_locations_and_event_types: Intense lightning with widespread damage to houses, railway signalling and airport operations, one person struck but not seriously injured, four cattle killed, localised deluges (34.5 mm at Flempton), flooding in Kent, Essex and Suffolk and disruption to sporting fixtures; south-east England and East Anglia, 28 June 2011
prefrontal_trough: PRESENT: at 1200 UTC on 28 June the fronts lay across south-east England with a narrow trough slightly ahead of them, and troughs and small lows had earlier moved north across Spain and France ahead of waving cold fronts
key_supporting_quote: This is characterised by very warm air that moves northwards across the Spanish Plateau from Africa
limitations_or_uncertainty: The two trajectory models agree on a Moroccan origin but show differences in detail; the dust is described only as probably Saharan; rainfall totals were high but not exceptional because cells moved quickly; the closing remark that Spanish Plume events have been rare in recent years is unquantified

airstream_properties: High values of equivalent potential temperature at 850 hPa advected from the Spanish plateau toward western Europe, often with an Elevated Mixed Layer providing a cap; in this case an 850 hPa theta-e tongue reaching 68 C over south-east Belgium with modelled CAPE above 2000 J/kg
diagnostic_variables: 500 hPa charts and trough tilt, surface mesoanalysis at 1 hPa isobar intervals, 850 hPa equivalent potential temperature, C-band Doppler radar (PCAPPI and VVP wind profiles), CAPE, storm-relative helicity over 0-1 and 0-3 km, Bulk Richardson Number shear, Energy Helicity Index, a modified Supercell Composite Parameter and an MCS index, ETA and ALARO model forecasts, damage surveys and press reports
origin_and_transport_claim: Warm humid air with high equivalent potential temperature was advected from the Iberian Peninsula, producing a clear mid-level theta-e tongue over France; the flow is generated ahead of an upper-level trough west of the European continent
origin_evidence: INDIRECT: the plume is identified from the paper's own 500 hPa and 850 hPa theta-e analyses for 14 July 2010, with the Iberian source stated rather than traced by trajectories
capping_or_instability_mechanism: An Elevated Mixed Layer commonly accompanies a Spanish plume and inhibits spontaneous deep convection through the accompanying cap, so that a well-defined triggering mechanism is required
capping_or_instability_evidence: ASSERTED_ONLY: the elevated mixed layer and cap are described generically in the introduction, and the case analysis presents CAPE and shear but no cap analysis, the 1200 UTC Brussels sounding being judged unrepresentative
initiation_mechanism: A negatively tilting short-wave upper trough with concentrated differential positive vorticity advection and mid-level warm advection ahead of it, cold advection aloft increasing latent instability, the right entrance of an anticyclonically curved jetstreak over northern France, and a thermal trough deepening into a mesolow at the top of the theta-e wedge
initiation_evidence: DIRECT: 500 hPa trough evolution at three times, hourly surface mesoanalysis with radar overlays, VVP wind profiles showing backing low-level flow and strong shear, and model index fields for the case
hazards_locations_and_event_types: A derecho and quasi-linear convective system with widespread straight-line wind damage up to EF2 and gusts to 36 m/s, at least one tornado in the northern Netherlands, two fatalities and several injuries, 45 000 insurance claims and about EUR 133 million damage; France, Belgium, the Netherlands and Germany, 14 July 2010
prefrontal_trough: PRESENT: a thermal trough developed over the interior of France ahead of the trailing cold front and deepened into a closed mesolow at the top of the theta-e wedge, with a pronounced pre-squall mesolow also analysed ahead of the QLCS
key_supporting_quote: A spanish plume is a configuration where high values of equivalent potential temperature at 850 hPa are advected from the Spanish plateau toward western Europe.
limitations_or_uncertainty: Velocity folding and a low signal quality index produce empty holes in the velocity data and can falsely suggest vortices, making the analysis extremely difficult; many affected regions could not be surveyed so press and local reports were used; caution is urged in applying the Enhanced Fujita scale outside the continental United States; the 1200 UTC Brussels sounding was not representative of conditions near the system

airstream_properties: NR: the authors state that the 2011 outbreaks were not the Spanish plume scenario, the common theme instead being a slow-moving slack low under an upper cold vortex with local surface temperatures of 19-21 C
diagnostic_variables: NR for the plume; the paper uses Met Office surface analyses, NCEP reanalysis 500 mbar charts, radar reflectivity converted to rainfall intensity, satellite imagery, rain-gauge and automatic weather station records and the Bilham classification
origin_and_transport_claim: NR: no origin or transport is described
origin_evidence: ASSERTED_ONLY: the plume scenario is named only to contrast it with the observed pattern of a slack low beneath a cold upper vortex
capping_or_instability_mechanism: NR for the plume; convection in these cases was attributed to slack low pressure beneath an upper cold vortex with relatively high surface temperatures and surface convergence
capping_or_instability_evidence: NR
initiation_mechanism: NR for the plume; the observed storms formed on surface convergence zones (for example south of the Moray Firth and near the Firth of Forth), near occlusions and under upper cold vortices
initiation_evidence: INDIRECT: inferred from surface wind plots showing convergence together with satellite and radar imagery
hazards_locations_and_event_types: Severe thunderstorms with torrential rain, hail to 20 mm, flash flooding, lightning damage and two police officers struck; 50-60 mm in two hours in Edinburgh, 80 mm in two hours at Falkirk and 94 mm in a day; Edinburgh, Inverness, Falkirk, Renfrewshire and East Lothian, July and August 2011
prefrontal_trough: UNCLEAR: a trough is identified on the 8 July surface analysis and confirmed by a veer in surface winds, but it is not described as prefrontal
key_supporting_quote: Though not the ‘Spanish plume’ scenario for widespread severe thunderstorms, the above weather patterns do produce some of the UK’s most thundery spells
limitations_or_uncertainty: Radar-derived rainfall accumulations may be over-estimated when precipitation contains appreciable hail; the Bilham classification is 75 years old and a modern analysis would probably give different results; several rainfall figures come from private automatic weather stations and personal communications; hail sizes are inferred from reflectivity

airstream_properties: A bulge of very warm air over western Europe ahead of a sharpening upper trough, with very humid air over southern and eastern England (0800 GMT temperatures 21-22 C and dew points 16-18 C) and afternoon maxima above 27 C, reaching 32 C at Brixton
diagnostic_variables: NCEP reanalysis 500 mbar contour chart with surface isobars, Daily Weather Report surface charts, station temperature and dew point observations, historical rainfall and hail reports and eyewitness accounts
origin_and_transport_claim: A bulge of very warm air lay over western Europe ahead of a sharpening upper trough approaching Ireland and Biscay, with a brisk south-westerly flow at 500 mbar and a shallow surface depression over north-west France; no Iberian source is traced
origin_evidence: INDIRECT: identified by matching the reanalysis 500 mbar and surface charts to a classic Spanish Plume scenario and to the 24 June 1994 case described by Young (1995)
capping_or_instability_mechanism: NR: no capping layer or instability mechanism is described
capping_or_instability_evidence: NR
initiation_mechanism: NR: no triggering mechanism is analysed; shallow low centres moved across eastern England and screen temperatures rose rapidly above 27 C before the storms
initiation_evidence: INDIRECT: inferred from the surface analyses and the observed temperature rise
hazards_locations_and_event_types: Violent squalls and hailstorms with stones of 45-60 mm, a hail swath 115 km long and up to 15 km wide from Slough to Brightlingsea, uprooted trees, stripped roofs and a wrecked windmill, 42 mm in 20 minutes at Luton, 80 mm at West Oaks and two lightning deaths at Norwich; Essex, Bedfordshire, London, the Thames Valley and Surrey, 24 June 1897
prefrontal_trough: NR: a shallow surface depression over north-west France and shallow low centres over eastern England are described, but no prefrontal trough
key_supporting_quote: shows a classic ‘Spanish Plume’ scenario (quite similar to the severe storms of 24 June 1994 described by Young (1995))
limitations_or_uncertainty: The account relies on historical newspaper, society and British Rainfall reports; the 32 C Brixton reading came from a site described as probably slightly sheltered; hailstone diameters are inferred from reported weights assuming spheroidal stones of typical density

airstream_properties: Hot, humid air moving into southern Britain from France and converging on cooler air aloft advancing from the Atlantic
diagnostic_variables: Thunder-day counts from climatological stations, England and Wales rainfall series, NOAA/NCEP reanalysis weather charts, satellite imagery and rainfall reports
origin_and_transport_claim: When the flow is fairly slack, tending to blocking patterns, pre cold-frontal thunderstorms move into southern Britain from France, or develop there, as hot humid air converges on cooler air aloft advancing from the Atlantic; in summer 2011 such developments often headed from northern France across the Low Countries instead
origin_evidence: ASSERTED_ONLY: a general climatological statement offered without analysis or citation
capping_or_instability_mechanism: NR
capping_or_instability_evidence: NR
initiation_mechanism: Convergence of hot humid air with cooler air aloft advancing from the Atlantic ahead of a cold front; elsewhere the article attributes storms to diffuse cold frontal features, thundery troughs ahead of fronts and sea-breeze convergence zones
initiation_evidence: ASSERTED_ONLY: described in general climatological terms, with the author noting that the June 1982 triggers were difficult to analyse with any certainty
hazards_locations_and_event_types: An exceptionally thundery month with thunder on 14 days at some stations, about 200 houses flooded at Loughton, 79 mm in 90 minutes there and 114 mm in 100 minutes at Brodenham, deep hail accumulations, several lightning deaths and three children drowned; England, Wales and Scotland, June 1982
prefrontal_trough: PRESENT: on 17 June a thundery trough was carried northwards into south-west Britain and Ireland ahead of the fronts of a deep depression, and cold frontal troughs are described edging in from the Atlantic
key_supporting_quote: hot, humid air – the ‘Spanish plume’ – converges on cooler air aloft advancing from the Atlantic
limitations_or_uncertainty: The author stresses that no conclusions can be drawn from short periods of deviation and that thunderstorm climatology variations are complex; the June 1982 triggers are described as difficult to analyse with any certainty, with several mechanisms offered only as possibilities

airstream_properties: NR: no plume properties are given; the two days labelled Spanish plume had 0 C levels of 4.2 and 3.6 km, 600 hPa winds of 21 m/s from 222 degrees and 22 m/s from 231 degrees, and CAPE of 596 and 47 J/kg
diagnostic_variables: Hailpad measurements of frequency, kinetic energy per hailfall and per station, the ANELFA hail scale, radiosoundings (0 C level, 600 hPa wind, maximum tropospheric wind, CAPE), WRF-NMM simulations giving MUCAPE, HCAPE, 0-6 km shear, BRN shear, 0-3 km storm-relative helicity and the Supercell Composite Parameter, and radar-checked storm trajectories
origin_and_transport_claim: NR: no origin or transport is described; the paper's own classification is by the position of the primary low (Portugal or north-west Spain, Ireland, or the Mediterranean)
origin_evidence: ASSERTED_ONLY: the term appears only as a mesoscale-pattern table entry for two of the twelve major hail days, with no supporting description or citation
configuration: UNCLASSIFIED: the paper classifies the cases as SW, NW and Mediterranean types by the position of the primary low rather than by plume configuration
capping_or_instability_mechanism: NR
capping_or_instability_evidence: NR
initiation_mechanism: For all twelve days the simulations show simultaneous high-level potential vorticity advection with divergent upper flow, mid-level cyclonic flow with positive vorticity advection, and convergent low-level flow associated with a secondary surface low, with the interaction of large-scale and mesoscale forcing judged the key factor
initiation_evidence: DIRECT: WRF-NMM simulations at 30 to 5 km resolution initialised from CDAS/NCEP-NCAR reanalysis for each of the twelve major hail days
hazards_locations_and_event_types: Extreme hail days with hailstones of 5-8 cm, F1 downbursts, ruined vineyards and crops, flash floods, injuries and fatalities (two killed in an aircraft crash, one drowned); the Atlantic and Midi-Pyrenees regions of south-western France, 1988-2010
key_supporting_quote: Spanish plume
limitations_or_uncertainty: The sample of twelve days is small; a ranking bias remains from the geographical layout of the hailpad networks; correlations of the freezing level and winds with hail parameters are low; CAPE may be unrepresentative in frontal situations and no sounding station lies inside the Midi-Pyrenees area; the three synoptic types are described as a precondition rather than a forecasting tool; interpretation remains uncertain partly because aerosol content is not considered

airstream_properties: Air at intermediate heights (700 hPa) originating over the dry hot Iberian Peninsula, forming a dry elevated mixed layer with steep mid-level lapse rates that caps moisture-rich Mediterranean air beneath, with cooler Atlantic air aloft at 300 hPa; 850 hPa temperatures of 18-20 C and 850 hPa theta-e of 328-333 K in this case
diagnostic_variables: COSMO-7, COSMO-2 and ECMWF model fields, 500 and 300 hPa flow and jet streaks, 850 hPa temperature and equivalent potential temperature, MLCAPE, MUCAPE and CIN, Payerne and Lyon soundings and hodographs, storm-relative helicity, C-band Doppler radar imagery and TRT cell-tracking attributes, MSG satellite imagery, lightning data, surface stations, eyewitness reports and a damage survey
origin_and_transport_claim: Low-level moist air is most often of Mediterranean maritime-tropical origin, the 700 hPa air originates over the dry hot Iberian Peninsula and the 300 hPa flow is westerly and of Atlantic origin; in this case very warm relatively dry air was advected over south-eastern France and western Switzerland ahead of an Iberian trough
origin_evidence: INDIRECT: the three-layer origin structure is taken from isentropic back-trajectory work by Hernandez et al. (1998) and other cited studies, while the case identification rests on COSMO-7 and ECMWF fields and the Payerne sounding rather than the author's own trajectories
configuration: CLASSIC: a closed upper low or broad trough over Biscay and Iberia with a Saharan or Mediterranean ridge, here directed at south-eastern France and Switzerland
capping_or_instability_mechanism: The Iberian air at 700 hPa introduces a warm layer or cap over the moisture-rich Mediterranean air beneath, giving a dry elevated mixed layer with steep mid-level lapse rates; on the day the boundary layer was already well mixed by 1200 UTC with the capping lid eroding quickly and CIN decreasing
capping_or_instability_evidence: DIRECT: the modified 1200 UTC Payerne rawinsonde shows a well-mixed boundary layer, an eroding cap and falling CIN with MLCAPE of 1000-1500 J/kg and MUCAPE near 2000 J/kg, and a typical Spanish plume sounding from Nimes is also shown
initiation_mechanism: Strong large-scale ascent in the left-exit region of an upper-level jet streak, locally a double-jet left-exit and right-entrance configuration, impinging on the warm sector while abundant morning sunshine eroded the cap; tornadogenesis was aided by inflow winds channelled around mountains that locally raised low-level shear and helicity
initiation_evidence: DIRECT: model jet-streak analyses, soundings and hodographs recalculated with channelled winds, radar evolution of the splitting storm, SwissMetNet surface observations and a COSMO-2 reanalysis
hazards_locations_and_event_types: A supercell tracking over 300 km with golf-ball hail over a 1200 km2 swath damaging about 15 000 vehicles, a microburst gust of 161 km/h, two confirmed tornadoes (EF1 and EF2), destroyed vineyards, eight injuries and over 100 million dollars of damage; Lyon to the Lake Geneva region and Swiss Alpine foothills, 18 July 2005
prefrontal_trough: NR: the conceptual model shows low-level equivalent potential temperature maxima ahead of a surface cold front, but no prefrontal trough is reported
key_supporting_quote: The air masses at intermediate heights (700 hPa) tend to originate over the dry and hot Iberian Peninsula
limitations_or_uncertainty: Base velocity data were missing for a 30-minute period and part of a rotational couplet had to be estimated because of mountain interference; radar software could not determine echo tops above 12 km; COSMO-2 could not resolve the storm-scale wind field and no plots were available at the time of the second tornado; the exact tornadogenesis mechanism is stated to be beyond the model's simulating capability

airstream_properties: NR for the plume; the analogous Mediterranean profile shows an elevated mixed layer of warm dry air capping a very moist maritime boundary layer, with a mean 850 hPa theta-e of 52 C (no case below 30 C) and mean precipitable water of 36 mm
diagnostic_variables: MSG SEVIRI imagery (10.8 micrometre, HRV and Severe Convection RGB), ECMWF operational analyses of 500 hPa geopotential, 300 and 850 hPa winds, 850 hPa equivalent potential temperature, precipitable water, mean sea level pressure and the 2 PVU dynamical tropopause height, MERRA reanalysis climatology, ESWD reports and radiosoundings
origin_and_transport_claim: The paper's own claim is that the 500 hPa disturbances advect sub-tropical air from northern Africa toward the Mediterranean so that very warm air overtops a moisture-rich maritime boundary layer; no Iberian plume origin is claimed
origin_evidence: ASSERTED_ONLY: the resemblance to the Spanish plume conceptual model is asserted from inspection of soundings within the theta-e plumes, with the elevated mixed layer attributed to Carlson et al. (1983) and no trajectory or origin analysis
configuration: OTHER: a north African source advected over the Mediterranean, described only as similar to the Spanish plume conceptual model
capping_or_instability_mechanism: An elevated mixed layer with warm dry air capping a very moist Mediterranean boundary layer gives a 'loaded gun' profile, which appears more often in the 12-24 h preceding convective initiation
capping_or_instability_evidence: INDIRECT: inferred from inspection of soundings at listed stations located within the theta-e plumes, with the profiles not shown and no quantification given
initiation_mechanism: Convection triggers in the south-eastern portion of a diffluent 500 hPa disturbance, at the leading eastern edge of an approaching dynamical tropopause anomaly where 850 hPa theta-e and precipitable water are maximum, usually with low- and upper-level jets present
initiation_evidence: DIRECT: synoptic precursor statistics computed from ECMWF analyses for all 269 detected systems and compared with a 28-year MERRA climatology
hazards_locations_and_event_types: Long-lasting deep convective systems producing heavy rain, tornadoes, large hail, straight-line winds and funnel clouds, with 94 of 269 systems matched to ESWD severe weather reports; western and central Mediterranean, mainly around the Balearic Islands, the Ionian Sea and the Sicilian Channel, 2007-2010 and chiefly in autumn
key_supporting_quote: with warm and dry air capping very moist Mediterranean boundary layer, a situation similar to the Spanish plume conceptual model
limitations_or_uncertainty: The four-year record is short in a climatological sense; the detection procedure is deliberately simple and cannot follow complex dynamics; 850 hPa theta-e showed no obvious relationship with the detection extremes and needs deeper investigation; no clear correlation was found between mid-tropospheric disturbance type and vertical profile; ESWD reports are biased toward land

airstream_properties: Warm moist air with surface dew points above 16 C, reaching 20.8 C at Church Lawford, beneath a capping inversion associated with a warm layer between 900 and 850 mbar; surface-based CAPE of 2741 J/kg and a lifted index of -6.3 C
diagnostic_variables: Surface analysis and 500 mbar charts, the Larkhill 0900 UTC radiosonde modified with Church Lawford surface observations, 0-4 and 0-6 km shear, Met Office 1.5 km model CAPE and lifted index, satellite water vapour and visible imagery, ATDNet lightning locations and density, Doppler radar velocity couplets and composite reflectivity, ground-truth hail reports and photographs, TORRO intensity scales
origin_and_transport_claim: A 500 mbar trough west of the British Isles moved slowly east with 40-50 kn south-westerlies on its eastern flank; the mid-level airflow appears to have been just sufficiently backed to carry the plume of continental air further north-west than usual
origin_evidence: INDIRECT: identified by matching the surface and 500 mbar analyses to the classic Spanish Plume scenario of Lewis and Gray (2010), with the plume airstream itself not traced
configuration: CLASSIC: explicitly identified as the classic scenario and contrasted with the modified Spanish Plume of Lewis and Gray (2010)
capping_or_instability_mechanism: A capping inversion associated with a warm layer between 900 and 850 mbar, which the surface temperature and dew-point combination was only just sufficient to overcome; ascent and cooling below the level of maximum cyclonic vorticity advection gradually weakened it while surface temperatures rose
capping_or_instability_evidence: DIRECT: the modified Larkhill sounding shows the inversion and the marginal parcel curve, and a comparison of the 0000 and 1200 UTC Watnall soundings shows mid-level cooling largest at 580 mbar (1.5 degC)
initiation_mechanism: Storms developed near the leading north-eastern edge of an area of high potential vorticity collocated with strong 300 mbar diffluence several hundred kilometres ahead of the trough axis, where cyclonic vorticity advection weakened the cap; strong deep-layer shear (48 kn over 0-4 km) then supported supercells with deviant rightward motion into warmer air
initiation_evidence: DIRECT: satellite water vapour imagery, modified soundings, model CAPE fields, Doppler radar mesocyclone tracks and interpolated surface temperature and wind analyses
hazards_locations_and_event_types: A 110 km hail swath with stones above 20 mm and up to 80-90 mm (heaviest 81 g), two tornadoes including a T4 near Leicester and one near Sleaford, flash flooding with one fatality in Shropshire, about 23 000 properties losing power and railway closures, and 64 mm daily rain at Whitley Bay; the English Midlands, Lincolnshire and north-east England, 28 June 2012
prefrontal_trough: PRESENT: trough lines are analysed within the warm sector ahead of the double-structured cold front and mark the locations of the larger thunderstorm clusters
key_supporting_quote: The situation is consistent with the ‘classic’ Spanish Plume scenario of Lewis and Gray (2010).
limitations_or_uncertainty: Several hail sizes are estimated from damage descriptions rather than measured; reports were gathered through public appeals and personal communications; the routinely available model output caps CAPE contours at 1500 J/kg; many stones were very oblate and knobbly, complicating diameter estimates; one supercell crossed sparsely populated country and may be under-reported

airstream_properties: NR for the plume itself; the analogous case anomaly had 850 mbar wet-bulb potential temperature above 12-14 C, surface dew points of 13-15 C and integrated water vapour of 20-23 mm
diagnostic_variables: Met Office NAE (12 km) and UKV (1.5 km) model output, 300 mbar geopotential height and relative vorticity, 850 mbar wet-bulb potential temperature, surface analyses and dew-point isopleths, Nottingham and Albemarle tephigrams, radar rainfall and HYRAD accumulations, Meteosat infrared and water vapour imagery, GPS integrated water vapour, sferics and rain gauges
origin_and_transport_claim: A lower-tropospheric warm anomaly generated by diurnal heating can be transported elsewhere by the ambient flow and influence the weather at a very different location the following day; in the Spanish Plume the upstream heat source is the elevated ground of the Iberian plateau
origin_evidence: ASSERTED_ONLY: the plume is cited as a generic example of this process, while the paper's own anomaly was generated over southern England and verified with GPS integrated water vapour
configuration: OTHER: the analysed case is described as a much smaller-scale analogue with the heat source over southern England rather than Iberia
capping_or_instability_mechanism: The atmosphere was initially well capped in the region of the warm anomaly, with convection restricted to about 750 mbar by an inversion surmounted by dry air aloft; strong cooling between 750 and 450 mbar with deep moistening subsequently removed the cap
capping_or_instability_evidence: DIRECT: the Nottingham 0000 UTC and Albemarle 1200 UTC tephigrams show the initial cap and its removal, giving deep instability to surface temperatures by 1200 UTC
initiation_mechanism: Coupling of upper-tropospheric positive vorticity advection advancing from the Atlantic with the pre-existing low-level warm moist anomaly and its co-located weak cyclonic circulation, with storms developing ahead of the upper-level forcing feature marked by a dry tongue in water vapour imagery; strong veering shear aided mesoscale organisation
initiation_evidence: DIRECT: NAE 300 mbar vorticity forecasts, radar and satellite sequences, tephigram evolution and GPS integrated water vapour fields
hazards_locations_and_event_types: Heavy thunderstorms with 6-hour gauge totals of 33-39 mm and radar-derived peaks above 50 mm, local flooding of homes and roads, houses struck by lightning and an abandoned football match; northern and north-east England including Durham, Consett, Newcastle and Northumberland, 6 August 2011
prefrontal_trough: NR: the surface pattern was slack with a small heat-induced cyclonic circulation; no prefrontal trough is reported
key_supporting_quote: The ‘Spanish Plume’ is one such example in which the upstream heat source is the elevated ground of the Iberian plateau.
limitations_or_uncertainty: Total accumulations were not exceptional and no gauge exceeded the Extreme Rainfall Alert threshold; the source of the additional column moisture is only partly attributed, much of it appearing to have been advected from the west; extensive cloud obscured individual cell development on satellite imagery; a major false alarm subsequently developed across several models for the Edinburgh area on 7 August

airstream_properties: NR: the plume is named only as a synoptic situation and no airstream properties are given; regional summer instability is described generally as arising over warmer land
diagnostic_variables: 1981-2010 climatological averages for days of thunder at Ely and Horsham, days of hail, days of sleet or snow falling and lying at Ely, Hampstead and Chichester, together with rainfall, temperature, sunshine, visibility and wind statistics and descriptions of individual events
origin_and_transport_claim: Significant summer thunderstorms in the region are either home-grown or imported from the near-Continent, the latter sometimes in Spanish plume synoptic situations
origin_evidence: ASSERTED_ONLY: a single clause within a regional climatology, with no trajectory, chart, sounding or citation offered in support
capping_or_instability_mechanism: NR for the plume; instability in the region is attributed generally to heating over the warmer land in summer and to particularly unstable polar maritime air in spring
capping_or_instability_evidence: NR
initiation_mechanism: NR for the plume; other storms in the region are attributed to convergence lines, storm outflow boundaries and the sea-breeze front
initiation_evidence: NR
hazards_locations_and_event_types: Significant summer thunderstorms and hail imported from the near-Continent, with most of the region averaging five to eight hail days a year and about one day with hailstones larger than 5 mm, and the prolonged-hail Bracknell storm of 7 May 2000 cited separately; South East England and East Anglia
key_supporting_quote: The risk of significant thunderstorms increases everywhere in summer – either ‘home-grown’ or imported from the near-Continent, the latter sometimes in ‘Spanish plume’ synoptic situations.
limitations_or_uncertainty: A descriptive regional climatology rather than an analysis, and no evidence is presented for the plume attribution; the authors caution that exact hail frequencies at individual sites may reflect the vigilance of observers as much as climatological differences

airstream_properties: NR for the plume; the tropical continental air mass it is said to destabilise is described as arriving on south-easterly winds from central or southern Europe, usually stable, very warm or hot in summer and rare in winter
diagnostic_variables: 1981-2010 Met Office and Climatological Observers Link averages of rainfall, temperature and sunshine, the North Atlantic Oscillation index, annual and monthly rainfall anomaly scatterplots for Western Scotland and South East England, cumulative rainfall radar images and a summary table of air-mass characteristics
origin_and_transport_claim: Tropical continental air reaching the British Isles from central or southern Europe can be destabilised by Spanish plume events; no origin, source region or transport path is described for the plume itself
origin_evidence: ASSERTED_ONLY: the statement appears only as a table cell in an air-mass summary, with no analysis, chart or citation
capping_or_instability_mechanism: NR for the plume mechanism; the normally stable tropical continental air mass is simply said to be capable of being destabilised by Spanish plume events, with no capping or lapse-rate process described
capping_or_instability_evidence: ASSERTED_ONLY: asserted in the air-mass table only, with no sounding, stability index or model output shown
initiation_mechanism: NR
initiation_evidence: NR
hazards_locations_and_event_types: NR for the plume specifically; the article notes only the greater contribution of thunderstorms to total rainfall in the south-east in summer and the tendency for a larger proportion of rain in the south and east to fall on occasional very wet days; British Isles-wide introduction
key_supporting_quote: Can be destabilised by Spanish plume events
limitations_or_uncertainty: An introductory overview article in which the plume appears only as a table entry with no supporting evidence; the authors caution that the NAO index measures mid-latitude airflow over only a small sector of the Northern Hemisphere so that blocking over a major continental area may go undetected

airstream_properties: An elevated warm plume advected from Iberia or France on south or south-westerly upper flow, elevated enough to be relatively insensitive to the diurnal temperature range and so detectable in overnight CAPE; associated with the largest simulated CAPE of the ten-year record, locally above 3000 J/kg over north Wales and 2700-3000 J/kg in a narrow track from the Channel Islands and Cherbourg Peninsula to Dorset, weakening as plumes move offshore
diagnostic_variables: WRF-ARW v3.3.1 maximum CAPE on nested 27, 9 and 3 km grids for 1 June 2002 to 31 May 2012, surface-based CAPE from Albemarle, Nottingham Watnall and Herstmonceux soundings computed with RAOB, skew-T comparisons, simulated 850 hPa temperature and geopotential height, 2 m temperature as a proxy for land and sea surface temperatures, CAPE threshold exceedance frequencies by day and overnight (2100-0900 UTC), and infrared satellite imagery; CIN is deliberately omitted
origin_and_transport_claim: Mean upper-level winds are often south or south-westerly, allowing warm air to be advected from Iberia or France and giving S-N or SSW-NNE oriented plume traces; on 5-6 August 2003 a Spanish plume migrated north-eastwards across the British Isles, and plume position depends on how quickly and how far west the upper trough approaches Iberia
origin_evidence: INDIRECT: the plume is identified from the model's own 850 hPa temperature and geopotential fields and from the orientation of simulated CAPE maxima, with the concept attributed to Morris (1986) and the schematic adapted from ESTOFEX (2010); no trajectory or air-mass origin analysis is carried out
configuration: CLASSIC: a single generic Spanish plume schematic with an upper trough approaching Iberia and warm advection ahead of it is reproduced, and sensitivity to trough speed and longitude is discussed, but no classic-versus-modified typology is applied
capping_or_instability_mechanism: Plume events yield the highest CAPE in Britain but are infrequent, and because they are elevated they persist overnight; on 6 August 2003 the zone of highest CAPE shifted east across central and eastern Britain but produced no thunderstorms because of high CIN once the trough had cleared, demonstrating that high CAPE alone is insufficient
capping_or_instability_evidence: DIRECT: simulated maximum CAPE fields, annual and seasonal threshold-exceedance maps and overnight CAPE frequencies are the authors' own WRF output verified against three radiosonde stations, although CIN is not calculated anywhere in the study so the 6 August CIN explanation is asserted
initiation_mechanism: On 5 August 2003 the passage of a shortwave trough destabilized the plume, providing sufficient CAPE for scattered thunderstorms, while on 6 August the clearance of the trough removed the necessary forcing; lift is identified as the third required ingredient for deep moist convection alongside instability and moisture
initiation_evidence: INDIRECT: inferred from simulated 850 hPa fields, CAPE maps and infrared satellite imagery for 5-6 August 2003, with no lift, vorticity advection or ascent diagnostic computed
hazards_locations_and_event_types: Scattered thunderstorms across south-west England in the early morning of 5 August 2003 and more widely over Northern Ireland, south-west Scotland and adjacent Irish Sea coasts that afternoon and evening, with no storms on 6 August despite the highest modelled CAPE; mesoscale convective systems are noted as most commonly associated with Spanish plumes at about two per year; Great Britain, June 2002 to May 2012
prefrontal_trough: UNCLEAR: the schematic legend lists a trough alongside surface fronts and the 500 mb height contour, but the text describes only the upper trough and does not state whether a prefrontal surface trough is present
key_supporting_quote: During this 2-day event, a Spanish plume, as first described by Morris (1986), gradually migrated northeastwards across the British Isles
limitations_or_uncertainty: CIN is omitted throughout, so CAPE is explicitly not a direct predictor of thunderstorm incidence; the model uses maximum CAPE while observations use surface-based CAPE; WRF frequently exaggerates dewpoint and the 9 km grid spuriously maintains low-level inversions, biasing CAPE; Ireland and western Scotland lie outside the domain; ten years is short and thirty would be preferable; the urban CAPE deficit is unexplained and merits further investigation

airstream_properties: NR
diagnostic_variables: Thunder-day totals for 2013 mapped and tabulated against 1981-2010 means, duration of thunder in storm hours and counts of overhead thunder days at selected stations, reported lightning incidents by month, radar reflectivity for one storm and a visible satellite image
origin_and_transport_claim: NR
origin_evidence: NR: the term Spanish plume does not appear anywhere in the article
capping_or_instability_mechanism: NR
capping_or_instability_evidence: NR
initiation_mechanism: NR
initiation_evidence: NR
hazards_locations_and_event_types: Thunderstorms and lightning damage with 94 reported incidents including eight involving people struck and one fatality at Port Appin on 27 January, severe flooding at Southwell near Nottingham with 93 mm of rain in 75 minutes on 23 July, and 20 mm hail with a violent squall from a probable elevated supercell crossing the Isle of Wight on 2 August; Britain and Ireland, 2013
key_supporting_quote: NOT_FOUND
limitations_or_uncertainty: The author notes the usual caveats on thunder-frequency maps, namely the distribution of observers, whether observations rest on a 24-hour watch and the arguably increasing impact of background noise; reported lightning incidents are assumed to be only a proportion of the total and subject to future review; thunderstorm severity is said to be difficult to define precisely

airstream_properties: NR: no plume properties are given and the authors state the case was not typical of a classic Spanish Plume; the case profile itself was a relatively moist air mass with wet-bulb potential temperature near 15 C at 950 hPa and 12 C at 700 hPa and only about 300 J/kg of CAPE
diagnostic_variables: Met Office surface and mid- and upper-level synoptic analyses, wind-flow streamline analysis, rainfall radar at 1, 2 and 5 km resolution with integrated hourly returns, Meteosat Second Generation water vapour, visible and infrared imagery, the 1400 UTC Larkhill radiosonde with wet-bulb potential temperature, CAPE and lifted index, surface temperature and dew point, Met Office and Environment Agency rain gauges and a return-period model
origin_and_transport_claim: A trough was analysed from south-west England into northern France linked to medium-level convective and dynamic rain moving north-north-westwards from France, and upper-level potential vorticity forcing was advected northwards from the south of France, but no plume airstream is traced
origin_evidence: ASSERTED_ONLY: the Spanish Plume is invoked only in order to be excluded, on the stated ground that the cells bringing the heaviest rainfall formed locally along low-level convergence areas; no plume diagnosis, chart or trajectory is offered
configuration: NR: the event is explicitly said not to be typical of a classic Spanish Plume and no configuration is assigned
capping_or_instability_mechanism: NR for the plume; in the case itself there was some limitation to vertical ascent from higher wet-bulb potential temperature above about 400 hPa with potential instability in the middle of the profile, later deepened by positive vorticity advection and cold advection aloft
capping_or_instability_evidence: DIRECT for the case: the 1400 UTC Larkhill radiosonde with about 300 J/kg CAPE and a lifted index of -1 to -2 degC, supported by water vapour imagery; none of this is attributed to a plume
initiation_mechanism: NR for the plume; convection formed locally along low-level convergence lines over the Dorset Downs with only moderate surface heating, strengthened by afternoon sea breezes and a discrete low-pressure centre over Dorset, then enhanced by upper-level positive vorticity advection from France, with significant deep-layer shear allowing back-building of successive quasi-stationary cells
initiation_evidence: DIRECT for the case: the 1600 UTC streamline analysis showing the convergence line, surface observations at Yeovilton and Bournemouth Airport, 1730-1800 UTC radar sequences showing back-building on the southern flank, and water vapour imagery correlated with potential vorticity
hazards_locations_and_event_types: Flash flooding from slow-moving thundery downpours, with over 50 mm in one or two hours including 55.7 mm at Shillingford Abbot, 54.1 mm at Hemyock and a radar-estimated 51 mm in 45 minutes at Crewkerne (a 142-year return period), broken road surfaces, overturned walls, cars moved by debris, a landslide at Westown, inundated properties in Hemyock and four people rescued from a car near Honiton; Somerset and Devon, 29 May 2008
prefrontal_trough: UNCLEAR: a trough is analysed from south-west England into northern France, but no front is described in relation to it so it cannot be established whether it is prefrontal
key_supporting_quote: The convective activity, however, was not typical of a classic ‘Spanish Plume’ event because the thundery cells that brought the heaviest rainfall formed locally
limitations_or_uncertainty: The combined Met Office and Environment Agency gauge network failed to capture the rain that caused the Crewkerne flooding, so amounts rest on radar whose beam does not always sample the most intense rain and was found to under-read near Shepton Mallet; local reports of more than 70 mm in an hour are considered unreliable; the Larkhill ascent is only the most representative available and had to be subjectively modified for the Somerset event

airstream_properties: A hot and humid air mass imported from the continent within which thunderstorms develop; by explicit contrast, the air mass in this case was warm air with 850 hPa wet-bulb potential temperature of 14 C being advected slowly southwards from Scotland
diagnostic_variables: Nottingham radiosonde ascents at 1100 and 2300 UTC on 13 June, Met Office 250 and 300 hPa trough and vorticity forecasts, MSLP and 850 hPa wet-bulb potential temperature charts, Meteosat water vapour imagery interpreted through the water vapour and potential vorticity correlation, UKV 1.5 km CAPE and six-hour rainfall, total column precipitable water of 25-30 mm, post-processed lightning rate prognostics, the 12-member 2.2 km MOGREPS-UK ensemble, infrared satellite and radar imagery and sferics
origin_and_transport_claim: In a classic Spanish Plume thunderstorms develop within a hot and humid air mass imported from the continent, whereas in this event a warm air mass was advected slowly southwards from the north while an upper trough approached from the north-north-west
origin_evidence: CITED_ONLY: the plume is defined only by reference to Morris (1986), with Sibley (2012) given as an example case, and is used purely as a contrast; no plume origin or trajectory analysis is performed
configuration: CLASSIC: named only in the phrase a classic Spanish Plume event applied to other summer 2014 episodes, with no configuration described or analysed for the event studied
capping_or_instability_mechanism: NR for the plume; in this case the 1100 UTC Nottingham ascent showed a warm nose above 800 hPa that would inhibit convection in a steady-state environment, and this was removed by a large amount of mid-tropospheric cooling by 2300 UTC as the upper trough and cold advection aloft arrived
capping_or_instability_evidence: DIRECT for the case: the superimposed 1100 and 2300 UTC Nottingham ascents and a T+18 forecast vertical profile beneath the upper vorticity maximum, none of it attributed to a plume
initiation_mechanism: NR for the plume; destabilisation here came from residual diurnal heat at low levels, dynamical ascent by potential vorticity advection on the forward side of the advancing upper trough, and cold advection aloft running ahead of an intensifying PV maximum marked as an upper cold front, with cold advection compensating the PVA so that surface pressure fell only slowly
initiation_evidence: DIRECT for the case: real-time water vapour imagery compared with model equivalents, 300 hPa vorticity forecasts, the radiosonde evolution, sferics timing and infrared and radar sequences
hazards_locations_and_event_types: A slow-moving overnight mesoscale convective system with 700-800 recorded sferics and local rainfall over 50 mm, lightning strikes to overhead cables cutting power to 144 homes in Oxford and 400 in Reading, five fires, drivers rescued from localised surface-water flooding and a lightning-caused power cut at Gatwick Airport delaying 14 flights; central and southern England, overnight 13-14 June 2014
prefrontal_trough: NR: an upper cold front was analysed across south-east England and an upper trough approached from the north-north-west, but no prefrontal surface trough is described
key_supporting_quote: a classic ‘Spanish Plume’ event (Morris, 1986), where thunderstorms develop within a hot and humid airmass imported from the continent
limitations_or_uncertainty: The surface pressure pattern alone gave little indication that the event would occur; MOGREPS-UK members showed a large spread in detail even at nine hours; the same high-resolution runs produced a false alarm of heavy rain over north-east England earlier that day, denting confidence; a yellow warning for southern England was discussed but not issued; the authors state that lightning frequency and intensity remain beyond current capability and that cumulonimbus development does not guarantee lightning

airstream_properties: An air mass originating from the Spanish Plateau, characterised by steep lapse rates in the mid-troposphere and dry air in a shallow layer around 850 hPa; in this case the Trappes sounding showed a steep lapse rate from 900 to 300 hPa with dry air between 900 and 800 hPa, 2 m dewpoints reaching 20 C, a 0-6 km bulk wind difference of 17 m/s, an equivalent potential temperature difference of 18.8 K and CAPE of only 160 J/kg at 0000 UTC rising to a forecast 1500 J/kg by 1500 UTC
diagnostic_variables: ECMWF 500 hPa geopotential analysis, ALARO mean sea level pressure, 2 m specific humidity and 10 m wind analyses, the 0000 UTC Trappes radiosonde with CAPE, bulk wind difference, DCAPE and the surface-to-midlevel equivalent potential temperature difference, single-polarization C-band Doppler radar from De Bilt and Wideumont, 10-minute automatic weather station temperature, pressure and precipitation, infrared and visible satellite imagery, and ALARO runs at 4 km with the 3MT convection scheme and at 1 km without
origin_and_transport_claim: Thunderstorms are often associated with a Spanish plume, an air mass originating from the Spanish Plateau; on the day a southerly flow advected unstable air northward into the warm sector of a weak frontal system over Belgium and France
origin_evidence: CITED_ONLY: the Spanish Plateau origin is attributed to Carlson and Ludlam (1968) and van Delden (1998), and the plume in this case is identified only by matching the vertical structure of the Trappes sounding; no trajectory or air-mass origin analysis is performed
configuration: UNCLASSIFIED: the plume is described generically with no classic, modified or other configuration named, the synoptic setting given being an Atlantic upper trough with its axis south of Ireland and a deepening thermal low over France
capping_or_instability_mechanism: A shallow layer of dry air around 850 hPa, sometimes combined with a weak inversion, prevents moist shallow convection so that large amounts of water vapour accumulate in the boundary layer, favouring the development of large cumulonimbus if a forcing mechanism is present, with steep mid-tropospheric lapse rates above
capping_or_instability_evidence: DIRECT: the 0000 UTC Trappes sounding is shown and its steep 900-300 hPa lapse rate and dry layer between 900 and 800 hPa are explicitly stated to correspond to the Spanish plume, with CAPE, shear and equivalent potential temperature difference quantified
initiation_mechanism: A thermal surface low formed in the warm sector over France and moved northward while deepening under solar heating and the approaching upper-level trough, thunderstorms in western Europe being said often to form in such thermal lows; the plume itself is said to require a forcing mechanism before the accumulated boundary-layer moisture can be released
initiation_evidence: INDIRECT: inferred from the ECMWF and ALARO analyses and the radar evolution of cells developing near the French-Belgian border, with the thermal-low mechanism attributed to van Delden (1998) rather than diagnosed here
hazards_locations_and_event_types: Convective cells merging into a bow echo with bookend vortex that struck the Pukkelpop music festival, with 1-2 cm hail, up to 70 mm of accumulated rain, estimated gusts of 29-37 m/s and a downburst less than 100 m across, killing five people and injuring at least 140, uprooting trees, knocking down light towers and video screens and collapsing a concert tent; northern France and Belgium, 18 August 2011
prefrontal_trough: NR: the case is placed in the warm sector of a weak frontal system with a thermal surface low over France, and no prefrontal trough is described
key_supporting_quote: thunderstorms are often associated with a ‘‘Spanish plume,’’ which is an air mass originating from the Spanish Plateau
limitations_or_uncertainty: No observations of vertical velocity or mass flux were available during the event, so the downdraft scheme had to be calibrated on the secondary cold-pool effect; both 4 km runs predicted too high 2 m dewpoints and too warm cold pools and the observed cold pool strength could not be fully matched without microphysical changes such as explicit hail; radar signals beyond 200 km were discarded; the authors state that further tests, for example in winter, are needed and that DCAPE is less useful for downdrafts than CAPE is for updrafts because the strongest downdrafts violate parcel theory

airstream_properties: NR: no plume properties are given; the paper's only related statement is that north-western Europe had a precipitation surplus while Central Europe was hot and dry
diagnostic_variables: E-OBS 10.0 gridded daily mean and maximum temperature at 0.25 degree resolution, ECA&D station maximum temperature series from eight Central European stations with over 100 years of record, summed excesses above the 90th percentile (TS90 and HW90), effective precipitation as a soil-moisture proxy, and NCEP/NCAR reanalysis sea level pressure and 500 hPa geopotential height
origin_and_transport_claim: The precipitation surplus over north-western Europe was probably linked to intense mesoscale convective systems that hit France, the United Kingdom and Germany at the end of July, and these were related to the so-called Spanish Plume; no plume origin or transport is described
origin_evidence: CITED_ONLY: the attribution rests entirely on a citation to Holley et al. (2014), with no plume diagnosis, chart or airstream analysis of the authors' own
capping_or_instability_mechanism: NR
capping_or_instability_evidence: NR
initiation_mechanism: NR
initiation_evidence: NR
hazards_locations_and_event_types: Intense mesoscale convective systems with thunderstorms and associated hailstorms at the end of July 2013 that caused record-breaking economic losses running to billions of Euro across Germany, contributing to a precipitation surplus over north-western Europe; France, the United Kingdom and Germany
key_supporting_quote: These thunderstorms and associated hailstorms were related to the so-called ‘Spanish Plume’ (Holley et al., 2014)
limitations_or_uncertainty: The plume is invoked only in passing within a heat-wave climatology and no supporting analysis is offered; more broadly the authors note that most ECA&D stations show inhomogeneities, that an early instrumental warm bias affected Kremsmuenster at least until 1870, that some stations are influenced by urban heat islands, and that effective precipitation is only weakly affected by values early in the analysed period

airstream_properties: A strong southerly flow advecting very warm and moist air from the Iberian Peninsula and the Mediterranean Sea to Benelux and western Germany, with 850 hPa equivalent potential temperature above 65 C in northern Germany and along the convergence line, surface dew points of 19-22 C, precipitable water of 30-40 mm and observed CAPE of 1041 and 1312 J/kg at Essen and Idar-Oberstein rising to a simulated 1500-2800 J/kg during the morning
diagnostic_variables: COSMO analyses of 500 hPa geopotential height and 850 hPa equivalent potential temperature, COSMO 4.21 simulations at 2.8 km with the HYMACS hybrid convection scheme and four passive fluid tracers initialised in layers 0-2, 2-4 and 4-6 km, DWD radar precipitation rates, Essen and Idar-Oberstein radiosoundings with CAPE and precipitable water, simulated surface pressure, storm-relative wind at 925, 700 and 500 hPa, vertical cross-sections of storm-relative wind and equivalent potential temperature, and synoptic station rainfall and gust reports
origin_and_transport_claim: A strong southerly flow advected very warm and moist air from the Iberian Peninsula and the Mediterranean Sea to Benelux and the western part of Germany, a synoptic situation commonly referred to as a Spanish Plume weather event
origin_evidence: INDIRECT: the origin is inferred from the COSMO analysis of the 500 hPa long-wave trough and the 850 hPa equivalent potential temperature field, with the label attributed to common usage and the situation type to van Delden (1998); no trajectory or air-mass origin calculation is made
configuration: UNCLASSIFIED: given only as a long-wave trough over the North Atlantic and Western Europe with an embedded north-west to south-east tilted short-wave trough over southern England, with no named plume configuration
capping_or_instability_mechanism: NR for a plume cap: no capping inversion, dry intrusion or elevated mixed layer is described; the paper reports instead a potentially unstable prestorm layer with equivalent potential temperature decreasing with height up to about 5 km
capping_or_instability_evidence: DIRECT for the case: simulated vertical cross-sections of equivalent potential temperature showing potential instability to 5 km, plus observed and simulated CAPE and precipitable water; no cap is diagnosed anywhere
initiation_mechanism: A line of convergence developed during the early morning hours ahead of the surface cold front in a region of relatively low surface air pressure and shifted eastwards, and the squall line formed along this prefrontal convergence line; orographic effects then weakened the system in the lee of the Eifel and reinforced deep convection over the Bergisches Land
initiation_evidence: DIRECT: the convergence line was located from the divergence of the simulated near-surface wind field and checked against the DWD surface pressure analysis, with DWD radar and simulated precipitation sequences documenting initiation and evolution
hazards_locations_and_event_types: A fast-propagating bow-shaped squall line moving north-eastwards at more than 20 m/s with a continuous line of heavy convective precipitation, intense hail-producing presquall thunderstorms over the southern and eastern Netherlands, station rainfall of 20-64 mm in the northern Netherlands and along the East Frisian Islands, and widespread damaging gusts of 17-29 m/s along the weak part; France, Benelux and Germany, 12 July 2010
prefrontal_trough: PRESENT: a line of convergence that developed ahead of the cold front in a region of relatively low surface air pressure is analysed on the synoptic chart and from simulated near-surface divergence, though it is called a convergence line rather than a trough
key_supporting_quote: This synoptic situation is commonly referred to as a ‘Spanish Plume’ weather event.
limitations_or_uncertainty: The simulated squall line is displaced about 100 km to the south-west and is more zonally oriented, attributed to spin-up or inaccurate reanalyses; simulated precipitation intensities are locally too strong and the trailing stratiform region is missing because of excessive rainwater evaporation inherent to one-moment cloud schemes; the split between grid-scale and subgrid-scale mass flux depends on the convection scheme and grid spacing and is not generalisable; no soundings were available once the squall line had passed, preventing a 1200 UTC comparison; the authors state the article is not aimed at quantitative model verification

airstream_properties: NR: no plume properties are given; the paper notes only that the British Isles is often subject to convection that has initiated on the European continent
diagnostic_variables: Convective adjustment timescale computed from MetUM UKV 1.5 km operational forecasts coarse-grained to 60 km for JJA 2012-2014, CAPE lifted from the lowest 30 model levels, three-hourly precipitation accumulations thresholded at 0.2 mm/h, a 60 km Gaussian smoothing kernel, radiosonde CAPE at Camborne, Castor Bay, Herstmonceux and Albemarle, MIDAS rain gauges, radar composites and winds at a 1.4 km model level
origin_and_transport_claim: The British Isles is often subject to convection that has initiated on the European continent, which may occur for example in Spanish plume synoptic scenarios; no plume airstream, origin or transport is analysed
origin_evidence: CITED_ONLY: the plume is invoked once as an example and referenced to Lewis and Gray (2010), with no case identification or diagnosis of the authors' own
capping_or_instability_mechanism: NR for the plume; the paper's general account of non-equilibrium convection requires some inhibiting factor such as a layer of stable air, often indicated by convective inhibition, which allows CAPE to build up over time
capping_or_instability_evidence: NR for the plume: the stable-layer account of non-equilibrium convection is attributed to Emanuel (1994) and Weckwerth and Parsons (2006), and CIN is not calculated in this study
initiation_mechanism: NR for the plume; the study finds that most non-equilibrium convective events over the British Isles are initiated near large coastal orographic gradients or on the European continent, occurring most often at mid-range wind speeds of 5-15 m/s with winds from southerly to westerly sectors
initiation_evidence: DIRECT for the climatology: spatial maps of the convective adjustment timescale and of non-equilibrium frequency, diurnal composites and wind roses by region and wind-speed band from three summers of coarse-grained UKV output, none of it attributed specifically to plumes
hazards_locations_and_event_types: NR for the plume specifically; the study concerns convective precipitation and its predictability over the British Isles in JJA 2012-2014, with 85% of convection in quasi-equilibrium and non-equilibrium events preferentially in the south and south-west
key_supporting_quote: This may occur, for example, in ‘Spanish plume’ synoptic scenarios (Lewis and Gray, 2010).
limitations_or_uncertainty: The UKV overestimates peak precipitation, produces overly circular cells, delays convective initiation by about an hour and can retain CAPE too long, so timescales may be overestimated; the precipitation threshold may still admit stratiform rain, especially over mountains where the seeder-feeder mechanism acts; observational comparison was possible for only one summer at four radiosonde sites; the maritime-versus-continental explanation for the contrast with Germany is stated as a hypothesis requiring global climatologies to confirm

airstream_properties: NR
diagnostic_variables: Published Met Office, NWS/NCEP Ocean Prediction Center, HIRLAM, Meteo-France and DWD surface analysis charts for selected dates in January to March 2016, together with the Meteo-France ANASYG and PRESYG graphical analysis format; no meteorological fields are computed by the author
origin_and_transport_claim: NR
origin_evidence: NR: the plume is named only as one of several possible readings a chart user might place on a warm-sector trough line, with no origin or transport described
capping_or_instability_mechanism: NR
capping_or_instability_evidence: NR
initiation_mechanism: NR
initiation_evidence: NR
hazards_locations_and_event_types: NR for the plume; the article is a commentary on the interpretation of frontal and trough symbols on surface analysis charts over the North Atlantic and Europe, with no weather events analysed
prefrontal_trough: UNCLEAR: the plume is offered as one possible meaning of trough lines drawn within warm sectors, but no case is examined and no association is established
key_supporting_quote: On occasion trough lines appear within warm sectors – what is the user to infer from this? Split front? Spanish Plume?
limitations_or_uncertainty: An opinion piece rather than an analysis; the author argues that troughs on charts have come to mean little more than a line of convection, that fronts yield little information without the associated upper pattern, and that modern charts imply a level of detail and precision that is unjustified; the reproduced charts are screenshots of degraded quality

airstream_properties: Hot, humid air ahead of frontal systems pushing in from the west; on the day temperatures reached 28.4 C at St James's Park and 28.6 C at Gravesend in a warm, muggy south-east England, but no further plume properties, soundings or thermodynamic values are given
diagnostic_variables: Radar-derived surface precipitation rates and hourly composite accumulations, Doppler radial winds from five radars, wind profilers, MSG SEVIRI radiances, GNSS zenith total delay, MOPS three-dimensional cloud and rain-rate analyses, lightning strike counts, a Met Office surface analysis chart, and forecasts from the 1.5 km 4D-Var Nowcasting Demonstration Project, the UKV, UK4 and STEPS/UKPP systems verified with the fraction skill score
origin_and_transport_claim: Severe thunderstorms on 28 June 2012 were associated with hot, humid air from a Spanish plume ahead of frontal systems pushing in from the west; no source region, trajectory or transport path is described
origin_evidence: ASSERTED_ONLY: the plume label is applied in a single introductory sentence of the case description with reference only to the surface analysis chart, and no plume diagnosis is carried out
configuration: UNCLASSIFIED: the only synoptic information given is that the hot humid air lay ahead of frontal systems approaching from the west
capping_or_instability_mechanism: NR
capping_or_instability_evidence: NR
initiation_mechanism: NR for the plume; the paper's interest is in whether the assimilation systems could initiate the storms, and it reports only that one line originated near Cardiff in the early morning and moved east-north-eastwards across the UK
initiation_evidence: NR for the plume: the forecast comparisons are DIRECT model output but concern predictability rather than any physical initiation mechanism
hazards_locations_and_event_types: Several distinct lines of thunderstorms with rainfall exceeding 20 mm/h and vigorous lightning, almost 60 000 strikes recorded across the UK in 13 hours, one death, widespread flash flooding of roads and properties, railway closures and a train derailment from landslides, school closures, power loss, and golf-ball sized hail damaging cars and greenhouses in central England; central and northern England and Northern Ireland, 28 June 2012
prefrontal_trough: NR: only frontal systems approaching from the west are mentioned, with no prefrontal trough described
key_supporting_quote: severe thunderstorms associated with hot, humid air from a ‘Spanish plume’ ahead of frontal systems pushing in from the west
limitations_or_uncertainty: The plume is invoked only as scene-setting for a forecast-verification case study with no supporting analysis; more generally the authors note the NDP domain was small so skill converges to that of the driving UKV by T+6, radiosonde and GNSS data usually arrived too late for the NDP, the STEPS nowcast is partly verified against its own input radar data, forecast convective precipitation at 1.5 km is patchy and too intense, and the reason for the misplaced convection band in the UKV runs was not identified

airstream_properties: A deep dry convective boundary layer with nearly constant potential temperature and water vapour mixing ratio with height, formed over arid elevated terrain (chiefly the Iberian Peninsula, with northern Africa and the Atlas Mountains and, further east, the northern Sahara and Turkey as other sources) and advected off the plateau atop cooler air as an elevated mixed layer; it appears as a maximum in 850-700 hPa temperature lapse rate and as a thermal ridge at 850 hPa, supports large CAPE and is often topped by altocumulus castellanus where ascent occurs
diagnostic_variables: WRF-ARW 3.5.1 at 30 km grid spacing with 35 stretched levels, Kain-Fritsch convection and the YSU boundary-layer scheme driven by GFS, 850 hPa potential temperature and 500 hPa geopotential, 850-700 hPa temperature lapse rate, surface velocity convergence, Q vectors with their isentrope-normal (Qn) and isentrope-parallel (Qs) components and their convergence, axes of dilatation, vertical cross-sections of horizontal divergence, MSG visible-infrared imagery, three independent surface analyses, and a three-year composite of NCEP-NCAR Reanalysis-1 850 and 700 hPa fields over 19 cases with and 19 without a prefrontal convergence line
origin_and_transport_claim: Over Europe the main source for elevated mixed layers is the Iberian Peninsula and the resulting EML is sometimes called a Spanish plume, while more recently the whole synoptic pattern involving an EML has been given that name; the deep boundary layer is advected off the plateau over cooler air and drawn into the warm sector by southerly 850 hPa flow
origin_evidence: DIRECT: the authors track the EML plume in their own WRF simulations of 29 July 2009, 2 August 2012 and 1 August 2013 using 850-700 hPa lapse rates and the 850 hPa thermal ridge, and their composite shows both steeper midlevel lapse rates and a stronger southerly 850 hPa component in warm sectors that contain a convergence line
configuration: UNCLASSIFIED: no classic-versus-modified typology is used; the configuration analysed is an Atlantic cold front with an EML plume drawn into the warm sector on southerly 850 hPa flow, summarised in a four-stage conceptual model of the plume's progression
capping_or_instability_mechanism: The EML overlies cooler air, giving steep midlevel lapse rates and the potential for large CAPE, with altocumulus castellanus at the EML top where ascent is present; the paper treats the EML's 850 hPa thermal ridge as the dynamically active feature rather than analysing a lid directly
capping_or_instability_evidence: INDIRECT: the 850-700 hPa lapse rates showing the EML are computed by the authors, but the link to large CAPE and severe convective weather is attributed to Carlson and Ludlam (1968), van Delden (1998) and Lewis and Gray (2010), and neither CAPE nor CIN is calculated here
initiation_mechanism: Deformation of the isentropes at the western periphery of the 850 hPa thermal ridge by the cyclone's geostrophic flow produces both scalar and rotational quasigeostrophic frontogenesis; the ascending branch of the resulting ageostrophic circulation coincides with the surface velocity convergence line, which is accompanied by a surface pressure trough and is frequently the focus of convective development, the forcing shifting to the thermal ridge axis once the plume narrows
initiation_evidence: DIRECT: Q-vector convergence with its Qn and Qs decomposition, axes of dilatation, 24-hour isentrope evolution and vertical cross-sections from the authors' own WRF runs, supported by MSG imagery of convection developing along the line and by the three-year reanalysis composite
hazards_locations_and_event_types: Warm-season thunderstorms, including linearly organised deep convection, developing along prefrontal convergence lines that first appear over France or the Bay of Biscay and spread north-eastwards into Germany and Poland, with occurrence peaking in August; western and central Europe, cases of 29 July 2009, 2 August 2012 and 1 August 2013 and composites for 2012-2014
prefrontal_trough: PRESENT: the convergence lines are stated to be accompanied by a trough in the surface pressure field, with a rather expansive closed low sometimes developing in the warm sector, and the subjective surface analysis for 1200 UTC 2 August 2012 shows the prefrontal convergence line
key_supporting_quote: Over Europe, the main source for EMLs is the Iberian Peninsula, and the respective EML is sometimes referred to as a Spanish plume
limitations_or_uncertainty: Quasigeostrophic theory neglects ageostrophic advection and diabatic effects, so only the leading-order large-scale contribution is captured and the analysed pressure trough is sharper than the diagnosed forcing implies; the Q-vector and divergence fields were too noisy to use directly and had to be thinned to 60 km and Gaussian-smoothed, which merges the EML forcing with that of the large-scale occlusion; signals along the north-west Mediterranean coast are called untrustworthy because of proximity to model orography; in some cases the final collapse of the line may not rely on balanced dynamics but on convective outflow

airstream_properties: A well-mixed and hot continental air mass at mid-levels, originally formed over north-west Africa or on the Central Iberian Plateau and advected north-eastwards; when lifted it forms an elevated mixed layer, a well-mixed layer decoupled from the ground at mid-levels, usually between 700 and 500 hPa
diagnostic_variables: NR for the plume itself; the review synthesises hail frequencies from weather stations, hailpad networks, agricultural and property insurance claims, severe weather databases (ESWD, TORRO, sturmarchiv.ch, Keraunos), radar hail proxies including the Waldvogel echo-top criterion, the Mason 55 dBZ threshold and polarimetric methods, satellite overshooting-top and brightness-temperature detections, and model or reanalysis convective parameters such as CAPE, wind shear and the Lifted Index
origin_and_transport_claim: The air mass was originally formed over north-west Africa or on the Central Iberian Plateau and advected to the north-east downstream of an extended trough, a constellation often referred to as a Spanish plume; the authors speculate that a similar mechanism involving warm air from the Anatolian Plateau or the Balkans may operate in eastern Europe
origin_evidence: CITED_ONLY: the description and the name are attributed to Browning and Hill (1984) and Morris (1986), with the elevated mixed layer concept taken from Carlson and Ludlam (1968) and Carlson et al. (1983); the review presents no origin analysis of its own
configuration: UNCLASSIFIED: given only as an extended trough with the air mass advected north-eastwards downstream of it, alongside a more general severe-hail pattern of a trough over the West European Basin or Bay of Biscay with a downstream Mediterranean ridge
capping_or_instability_mechanism: Lifting of the air mass, either by synoptic-scale processes downstream of a trough or by flow over large-scale mountains, creates an elevated mixed layer decoupled from the ground at mid-levels; the review states generally that hailstorm formation requires a trigger to lift parcels over the boundary-layer convective inhibition
capping_or_instability_evidence: CITED_ONLY: the elevated mixed layer is said to have been confirmed as an important factor for the most intense storms by Lanicci and Warner (1991), van Delden (2001) and Lewis and Gray (2010), with no soundings, lapse rates or indices computed by the authors
initiation_mechanism: NR for the plume specifically; the review states that severe hailstorms over western and central Europe occur either at some distance ahead of cold fronts through low-level flow convergence or at the front itself through cold advection aloft and cross-frontal circulation, and it emphasises orographic triggering downstream of hills and mountain ranges
initiation_evidence: NR for the plume: the frontal and orographic statements are syntheses of the cited regional literature rather than new analysis
hazards_locations_and_event_types: Exceptional severe hailstorms in central and north-west Europe, the review naming as elevated-mixed-layer events the Munich hailstorm of 12 July 1984, the Andreas supercells of 27-28 July 2013 in Germany with EUR 3.6 billion insured loss, and Ela of 8-10 June 2014 in France, Belgium and Germany with EUR 2.3 billion; Europe as a whole, reviewed country by country
prefrontal_trough: NR: only the extended upper-level trough is mentioned in connection with the plume; the review separately notes that severe hailstorms often occur at a distance ahead of cold fronts by low-level convergence, but describes no prefrontal trough
key_supporting_quote: advected to the NE downstream of an extended trough, a constellation often referred to as “Spanish plume”
limitations_or_uncertainty: The review stresses that hailstorms are not captured accurately or comprehensively because of the small scale of hailstreaks and the absence of standardized observing systems; station records often fail to distinguish hail from graupel or frozen rain and observers may ignore the 5 mm threshold; insurance data cover only insured and vulnerable objects; radar and satellite proxies give large uncertainties or no estimate for hailstone size; the reviewed studies use different periods, methods and size thresholds with little spatio-temporal overlap, making quantitative comparison difficult; station-derived trends are described as not reliable or robust

airstream_properties: Warm boundary-layer air from the elevated terrain of the Iberian plateau advected north-eastwards, forming an elevated mixed layer atop a sharp capping inversion; in this case the analogous warm plume extended from Spain to central Europe but lay further south-east and the warm air appears to have been advected horizontally from North Africa rather than from Spain, the elevated mixed layer showing as a weakly stable, relatively moist layer above 700 hPa with a near dry-adiabatic virtual potential temperature gradient
diagnostic_variables: ECMWF operational analyses of 500 hPa geopotential, surface pressure and 850 and 700 hPa equivalent potential temperature, the 1200 UTC Munich radiosonde with skew T and hodograph, Austrian radar composites of maximum reflectivity, ESWD hail and severe wind reports, and WRF 3.4.1 simulations on 12.5, 2.5 and 0.83 km nests including two modified-terrain experiments, yielding most-unstable CAPE and CIN, storm-relative helicity, simulated reflectivity, vertical velocity and vorticity, cross-sections and Hovmoller diagrams
origin_and_transport_claim: In classical Spanish plume cases warm boundary-layer air from the elevated Iberian plateau is advected north-east, forming an elevated mixed layer atop a sharp capping inversion and raising the likelihood of severe weather over Great Britain; in this case the plume lay further to the south-east and the warm air appears to have come horizontally from North Africa rather than Spain
origin_evidence: INDIRECT: the plume-like warm advection is inferred from the ECMWF 850 and 700 hPa equivalent potential temperature fields and from upstream radiosondes showing the elevated mixed layer, with the classical description attributed to Carlson and Ludlam (1968), Lewis and Gray (2010) and Holley et al. (2014); no trajectory calculation is made
configuration: OTHER: the situation is stated to bear only a superficial similarity to the Spanish plume, with the plume displaced to the south-east and the warm air apparently of North African rather than Iberian origin, and is also likened to a warm conveyor belt
capping_or_instability_mechanism: In the classical plume an elevated mixed layer forms atop a sharp capping inversion; here a weakly stable elevated mixed layer with near dry-adiabatic lapse rate lay above 700 hPa over a strongly stratified layer coincident with a sharp specific-humidity gradient that capped diurnal shallow convection, while at the storm's own location the boundary-layer top lay near 800 hPa with no capping inversion and CIN below 10 J/kg
capping_or_instability_evidence: DIRECT: the Munich sounding, simulated skew T profiles and Hovmoller diagrams of the virtual potential temperature gradient and specific humidity show the elevated mixed layer and the stable layer beneath it, with most-unstable CAPE and CIN computed along the whole storm track
initiation_mechanism: Convection was initiated ahead of an approaching cold front by a combination of orographically induced convergence from thermally forced upslope winds and convergence ahead of a cold pool left by earlier convection, with prefrontal convergence lines suggested as a further trigger; strong low-level shear between the synoptic south-westerlies and the thermally driven plain-to-mountain and valley flows then favoured supercell organisation, while slope circulations transported moisture upward, locally increasing CAPE and removing CIN
initiation_evidence: DIRECT: the control simulation and two terrain-modified experiments, with 850 hPa equivalent potential temperature and wind, relative vorticity and vertical velocity fields, CAPE, CIN and storm-relative helicity time series along the track, and vertical cross-sections of the pre-storm environment
