hazards_locations_and_event_types: A supercell lasting more than 8 hours and travelling over 400 km eastward along the Alpine main crest across several 2000 m ridges, producing large hail with locally high accumulations and severe wind, damage estimated at 650 000 euro and precipitation mostly below 50 mm because of the storm's speed; eastern Switzerland, Tyrol, the Salzach valley and eastern Austria, 2 August 2007
prefrontal_trough: NR: convection developed ahead of a cold front and prefrontal convergence lines are mentioned as a possible trigger, but no prefrontal trough is analysed
key_supporting_quote: In classical Spanish plume cases, warm boundary-layer air from the elevated terrain in the Iberian plateau is advected northeast
limitations_or_uncertainty: Limited radar availability makes the supercell character hard to verify with certainty, terrain shading obscured the earliest development, and neither a hook echo nor a bounded weak echo region is visible in the observations; simulated convection initiation occurs about 30 minutes late and 100 km north-east of the observed point, the trailing convective line forms almost two hours early, and after 1500 UTC the simulation diverges strongly from the observations, limiting comparability

airstream_properties: Hot and humid air advected northwards from the Iberian peninsula; no thermodynamic or kinematic properties are given
diagnostic_variables: NR for the plume; the paper's own diagnostics are neighbourhood-based verification scores (continuous ranked probability score, ranked probability score, Brier score and skill score, ensemble bias) for 1.5 m temperature, 10 m wind speed, hourly precipitation, total cloud amount, cloud base height and visibility from MOGREPS-UK, its control member and the UKV, verified against 119 or 205 UK synoptic stations, plus reliability diagrams, rank histograms and a radar comparison
origin_and_transport_claim: During a Spanish Plume event hot and humid air is advected northwards from the Iberian peninsula, creating an increased risk of convective thunderstorms over the United Kingdom; no source mechanism or trajectory is described
origin_evidence: ASSERTED_ONLY: the plume is defined in a single footnote and named as an example of convection originating outside the model's inner domain, with no citation and no analysis
capping_or_instability_mechanism: NR
capping_or_instability_evidence: NR
initiation_mechanism: NR for the plume; the paper's concern is that convective systems originating outside the inner domain need a longer spin-up, which motivated extending the variable-resolution zone of the domain
initiation_evidence: INDIRECT: a subjective blind-test evaluation by operational meteorologists on the deterministic UKV is cited (personal communication) as showing that the larger extension zone improves forecasts of convection originating outside the original domain
hazards_locations_and_event_types: Convective thunderstorms over the United Kingdom; the paper's own case illustration is the severe thunderstorms in south Wales on 5 July 2015, which caused injuries and two fatalities from lightning strikes in the Brecon Beacons, though these are not attributed to a plume
key_supporting_quote: During a Spanish Plume event, hot and humid air is advected northwards from the Iberian peninsula creating increased risk of convective thunderstorms
limitations_or_uncertainty: The plume appears only as a motivating example with a footnote definition and no evidence; the supporting blind-test evidence for the extended domain is an unpublished personal communication about the deterministic model rather than the ensemble; more generally the authors note that visibility forecasts are poor with fog significantly over-forecast, that the reason for the reduced cloud-amount bias in MOGREPS-UK is not fully understood, that the extended-domain benefit varies by season and variable, and that a single case comparison is not a correct way to judge ensemble performance

airstream_properties: NR: no plume properties are given; the only related description is of days of the warm plume scenario, contrasted with polar maritime days that begin sunny, relatively cool and fresh with excellent visibility
diagnostic_variables: Official lightning-death statistics from the Office for National Statistics, the Northern Ireland Statistics and Research Agency and the National Records of Scotland cross-matched with the TORRO National Lightning Incidents Database, population estimates for risk rates, Lamb weather types from the Climatic Research Unit, and a subjective classification of the synoptic situation and airflow at the time and location of each fatal incident
origin_and_transport_claim: NR: no origin, source region or transport is described; the term is used only to name a synoptic situation and, once, as the warm plume scenario
origin_evidence: CITED_ONLY: the category is defined only by reference to Lewis and Gray (2010) and a Met Office web page, with no meteorological analysis of the days assigned to it
configuration: UNCLEAR: the four days are placed in a combined classic or modified Spanish Plume category, with no distinction drawn between the two
capping_or_instability_mechanism: NR
capping_or_instability_evidence: NR
initiation_mechanism: NR for the plume; the authors note that on the contrasting slack warm days thunderstorms are especially favoured along convergence zones such as sea breezes, and that on polar maritime days forecasts are unlikely to give thunder as high a profile
initiation_evidence: NR
hazards_locations_and_event_types: Widespread severe thunderstorms, for which the plume is called the major scenario; of 19 days on which 20 leisure walkers were killed by lightning, four fell in classic or modified Spanish Plume situations, while the deaths of two hill walkers on peaks 1.7 km apart in the Brecon Beacons on 5 July 2015 were placed in the returning maritime polar category; United Kingdom, 1987-2016
key_supporting_quote: the classic or modified Spanish Plume situation (Lewis and Gray 2010; Met Office, 2017), the major scenario for widespread severe thunderstorms
limitations_or_uncertainty: The synoptic classification is subjective and rests on only 19 days; the activity at death was known for 54 of the 58 fatalities and the location for 54; TORRO records four deaths absent from official statistics and lacks details for four official entries, and coroner delays can misdate official records; the authors state that a larger sample would be needed to explore age-range differences and that gender-related behavioural differences require further research

airstream_properties: A hot, initially dry air mass that originated over the elevated Spanish Plateau two days earlier and was drawn north on a veering southerly medium-level flow; the boundary layer was initially devoid of significant moisture, having come from synoptic-scale descent over the Low Countries and northern France, and moistened over the southern North Sea, with an additional shallow layer of very warm but rather moist air near 850 hPa from the Bay of Biscay boundary layer; an elevated mixed layer formed between about 825 and 500 hPa, with surface dew points of 20-23 C beneath it and CAPE reaching about 3000 J/kg
diagnostic_variables: Met Office surface analyses and upper-level geopotential and wind fields, NAME III 66-hour backward trajectories ending above Leeds at 500, 1500, 3500 and 6000 m, the Nottingham/Watnall tephigram with CAPE and CIN, AMDAR aircraft profiles used to modify Euro4 4 km forecast tephigrams, Doppler radial velocity and dual-polarisation differential reflectivity from the High Moorsley, Hameldon Hill and Ingham radars, ATDnet lightning, water vapour and visible satellite imagery, METARs, Weather Observations Website reports and geolocated social media
origin_and_transport_claim: A plume of very warm air moved north from France and Iberia; the medium-level flow veered southerly and drew a hot, initially dry air mass that had originated over the elevated Spanish Plateau two days previously, and the combined boundary-layer and medium-level sources are said to be characteristic of a classic Spanish Plume
origin_evidence: DIRECT: Met Office NAME III 66-hour backward trajectories at four levels ending above Leeds identify the Spanish Plateau, the Bay of Biscay and the Low Countries as the source regions, with the classification referred to Lewis and Gray (2010)
configuration: CLASSIC: explicitly identified as characteristic of a classic Spanish Plume following Lewis and Gray (2010), in a highly amplified upper pattern with a longwave trough west of the UK and an upper ridge with surface high pressure to the east
capping_or_instability_mechanism: Synoptic-scale ascent lifted the Iberian boundary-layer air to form an elevated mixed layer between about 825 and 500 hPa, a source of the steep lapse rates that support severe convection; a warm nose between 850 and 650 hPa initially required a surface temperature of 35 C for surface-based convection, and its later erosion reduced CIN to about 25 J/kg so that up to 3000 J/kg of CAPE could be released
capping_or_instability_evidence: DIRECT: the 1100 UTC Nottingham/Watnall tephigram with an elevated parcel curve giving 1230 J/kg of CAPE and negligible CIN, an AMDAR-modified Euro4 profile near Leeds at 1800 UTC with 25 J/kg CIN and 3057 J/kg CAPE, and a further AMDAR-modified Shawbury profile at 2100 UTC with 2001 J/kg CAPE
initiation_mechanism: Storm 1 formed from medium-level cloud near Barnsley with no clear trigger, possibly gravity waves from earlier deep convection or vorticity filaments from an earlier French mesoscale convective system; Storm 2 was initiated where an inland-propagating sea-breeze front reached a pool of enhanced low-level moisture over complex orography near Skipton in a boundary layer modified by Storm 1; Storm 3 initiated near Shawbury from the elevated layer beneath a more defined vorticity filament as the shortwave trough approached
initiation_evidence: DIRECT: single-site radar clear-air echoes marking the sea-breeze front, METAR and Weather Observations Website observations mapping its inland progression, AMDAR-verified tephigrams, water vapour imagery showing vorticity filaments and radar sequences; the authors state that the trigger for Storm 1 remained unclear
hazards_locations_and_event_types: Three structurally distinct severe thunderstorms with 5423 lightning strikes over land, a downburst with radar-derived winds near 49 kn and a 32 kn gust at RAF Leeming, surface-water flooding around Newcastle and the A1, a supercell producing damaging hail above 20 mm in a continuous swathe of at least 130 km, an unconfirmed funnel cloud near Scotch Corner, and an elevated supercell that later grew into an areal-merger mesoscale convective system; northern England and Scotland, 1 July 2015, the day a UK July record of 36.7 C was set at Heathrow
prefrontal_trough: NR: a longwave upper trough to the west, an upper ridge with surface high to the east and embedded shortwave features are analysed, but no prefrontal surface trough is described
key_supporting_quote: in addition to the dynamical features described, are characteristic of a classic Spanish Plume (Lewis and Gray, 2010)
limitations_or_uncertainty: The trigger for Storm 1 remained unclear despite extensive analysis, because of infrequent sampling of the medium- and upper-level flow and inconclusive satellite imagery, and modelled perturbations were traced back to simulated convection so their detail is judged unreliable; no surface observations confirmed the inferred 45-50 kn gusts; the funnel cloud report lacked supporting evidence; the absence of a second Doppler radar prevented a full two-dimensional wind field for Storm 2; parts of the storm tracks crossed areas with few surface observations

airstream_properties: Elevated mixed layers originating from the Spanish plateau; no thermodynamic or kinematic values are given for them
diagnostic_variables: Fourteen summer half-years (2001-2014) of cloud-to-ground flash data from the BLIDS/EUCLID low-frequency network on a 10 x 10 km grid with an objective thunderstorm-day threshold of five flashes per day, gamma-distribution fits to daily flash numbers, coefficients of variation and Spearman rank correlations of annual thunderstorm-day series with bootstrap significance tests, the NOAA NAO index, and NCEP/NCAR1 reanalysis 300 hPa wind and 850 hPa equivalent potential temperature at 1200 UTC
origin_and_transport_claim: Elevated mixed layers originating from the Spanish plateau, known as the Spanish Plume, frequently lead to the formation of thunderstorm tracks observed between the Bay of Biscay and the Massif Central
origin_evidence: CITED_ONLY: the plume is attributed to Morris (1986) and the associated thunderstorm tracks to van Delden (1998); the authors' own contribution is the observation of a broad streak of higher thunderstorm-day frequencies running north-east from the Bay of Biscay, not any plume diagnosis
capping_or_instability_mechanism: NR for the plume beyond the elevated mixed layer itself; the paper's general discussion relates convective activity to potential instability measured through 850 hPa equivalent potential temperature and notes that strong capping inversions within deep high-pressure systems may inhibit cell formation during positive NAO phases
capping_or_instability_evidence: NR for the plume: no soundings, lapse rates or stability indices are computed for plume situations
initiation_mechanism: NR for the plume; the study attributes lightning maxima generally to orographic flow deviations, thermally driven wind systems and moisture flux convergence, and on the large scale to quasi-geostrophic forcing ahead of frequent shortwave troughs during negative NAO phases
initiation_evidence: NR for the plume; the large-scale lifting argument rests on NCEP/NCAR 300 hPa wind anomaly composites for the two NAO phases rather than on any plume case
hazards_locations_and_event_types: Thunderstorm tracks between the Bay of Biscay and the Massif Central, appearing in the climatology as a broad streak of higher thunderstorm-day frequencies extending north-eastwards from the Bay of Biscay; western and central Europe, summer half-years 2001-2014
key_supporting_quote: Elevated mixed layers originating from the Spanish plateau, known as the Spanish Plume
limitations_or_uncertainty: The 14-year record falls short of a climatological span; only cloud-to-ground flashes are analysed because intracloud detection efficiency and location accuracy are much lower; the coefficient of variation is unstable where mean thunderstorm-day numbers are small and becomes singular over the Atlantic; some correlation patterns may be spurious or due to random effects despite the significance level; separating large-scale from boundary-layer and land-surface controls on interannual variability is stated to be beyond the scope of the paper

airstream_properties: Warm and dry air lifted from the Spanish plateau and advected towards western Europe ahead of the upper-air trough, appearing as an elevated mixed layer between 800 and 650 hPa in the Bergen-Hohne sounding and giving 800-600 hPa lapse rates of 7-9 K/km above a moist boundary layer with specific humidity of 10-14 g/kg, a mean mixing ratio of 13.1 g/kg and a mean dewpoint of 17.7 C in the lowest 50 hPa, yielding mixed-layer CAPE of about 2000-3000 J/kg with significant CIN
diagnostic_variables: COSMO-EU and COSMO-DE operational fields of specific humidity, 800-600 hPa lapse rate, mixed-layer CAPE and deep-layer shear, the 1800 UTC Bergen-Hohne sounding and a COSMO-DE analysis profile for Essen with CAPE, CIN and shear vectors, Meteosat infrared and high-resolution visible imagery, DWD C-band and Essen volume radar with a mesocyclone detection algorithm, LINET lightning, DWD and MeteoGroup surface stations, ESWD reports, and CCLM 5.0 hindcasts nested to 0.025 degrees driven alternately by ERA-Interim and the ECMWF operational analysis with single-variable exchange sensitivity runs
origin_and_transport_claim: The Spanish plume features warm and dry air lifted from the Spanish plateau and advected toward western Europe ahead of the upper-air trough, and is named as the main contributor to the steep mid-tropospheric lapse rates over central Europe on the day
origin_evidence: INDIRECT: the plume attribution rests on Morris (1986) and van Delden (1998) together with the authors' identification of the resulting elevated mixed layer in the Bergen-Hohne sounding and the COSMO-DE profile, rather than on any trajectory or air-mass origin calculation
configuration: UNCLASSIFIED: the setting is described as an upper-level long-wave trough over the north-eastern Atlantic with a ridge from Algeria to Poland and a diffuse quasi-stationary front from Spain to the North Sea, without any named plume configuration
capping_or_instability_mechanism: The elevated mixed layer produced by the plume capped the 2000-3000 J/kg of CAPE and led to significant convective inhibition, the loaded-gun scenario, and the authors state that a capping inversion induced by the Spanish plume had to be overcome to initiate deep convection
capping_or_instability_evidence: DIRECT: the 1800 UTC Bergen-Hohne skew T with a 50 hPa mixed-layer parcel ascent, its lifted condensation level, level of free convection and equilibrium level, together with the COSMO-DE Essen profile, giving mixed-layer CAPE of 1799 and 2583 J/kg and CIN of -85 and -70 J/kg respectively
initiation_mechanism: The outflow of a decaying multicell cluster over northern France interacted with north-easterly surface winds over Belgium to give low-level convergence, and this forced lifting overcame the convective inhibition, after which deep-layer shear of 15-25 m/s nearly parallel to the deep-layer wind allowed a fast, severe, linearly organised system to develop into a bow echo with a rear-inflow jet and a cyclonic bookend vortex
initiation_evidence: DIRECT: Meteosat infrared and visible sequences, LINET lightning, radar reflectivity and radial velocity cross-sections showing the rear-inflow notches and descending rear-inflow jet, the DWD mesocyclone detection, surface observations at Düsseldorf, and CCLM hindcasts reproducing the same triggering by cold outflow
hazards_locations_and_event_types: Hurricane-force wind gusts reaching about 40 m/s along a narrow 15-30 km wide swath over some 260 km, a peak 39.5 m/s gust at Düsseldorf Airport, large hail reports, six fatalities, more than 50 casualties, insured losses of about 650 million euros, extensive tree and rail damage in North Rhine-Westphalia and temporary closure of Düsseldorf Airport; Belgium and western Germany, 9 June 2014
prefrontal_trough: NR: a diffuse and wavy quasi-stationary front from Spain to the North Sea is analysed within an amorphous, very weak pressure field, but no prefrontal trough is described
key_supporting_quote: the Spanish plume (Morris 1986; van Delden 1998), which features warm and dry air lifted from the Spanish plateau and advected toward western Europe
limitations_or_uncertainty: Most operational NWP models failed to forecast the storm despite the favourable ingredients, and COSMO-DE captured it only once the radar observations had been assimilated; the ERA-Interim-driven hindcast track is displaced 50-100 km to the north-west and overestimates the maximum wind (58 against 40 m/s); the further development of the cyclonic vortex is unclear because hydrometeor attenuation degraded the Essen radar scans until 2000 UTC; the bookend-vortex mechanism is offered as a hypothesis; the sensitivity experiments alter only the initial parent-domain fields and other exchanged variables produced only small changes

airstream_properties: Layers of very high mid-tropospheric lapse rates advected off the Spanish Plateau over western Europe, which in combination with high low-level humidity create high CAPE but are themselves characterised by low mid-tropospheric humidity and often large absolute values of convective inhibition
diagnostic_variables: Six years (2008-2013) of EUCLID cloud-to-ground lightning on a 0.25 degree grid rescaled to 0.75 degrees, and ERA-Interim parameters computed at 1 hPa vertical resolution including CAPE and the equivalent maximum updraft speed, CIN, a generalised lifted index, 850-500 hPa mean relative humidity, the 850-500 hPa lapse rate and maximum bulk shear over 0-6, 0-3 and 0-1 km, all related to the relative frequency of lightning in the two hours following each analysis time
origin_and_transport_claim: Layers of very high lapse rates in the mid-troposphere may be advected off the Spanish Plateau over western Europe, where they are called a Spanish Plume
origin_evidence: CITED_ONLY: the identity and origin of the plume are given only by reference to Carlson and Ludlam (1968) and van Delden (2001); the study analyses reanalysis parameters and lightning statistics and identifies no plume itself
capping_or_instability_mechanism: The high mid-level lapse rates combine with high low-level humidity to create high CAPE, but the low mid-tropospheric humidity and the convective inhibition that often accompany these air masses prevent convective initiation across a large area
capping_or_instability_evidence: INDIRECT: inferred from the study's own reanalysis statistics, which show lightning frequency falling below 0.15 when 850-500 hPa relative humidity is under 50 per cent even with negligible CIN and sufficient CAPE, and the fraction of cases with favourable humidity and CIN falling from 0.53 for moderately unstable to 0.38 for very unstable profiles; no plume case is examined
initiation_mechanism: For such air masses convective initiation is said to occur first along their periphery, where the effects of low mid-tropospheric humidity and large negative CIN are smaller but CAPE remains sufficient; more generally the study finds two shear regimes favouring lightning, very weak shear allowing untilted towering cumulus and strong deep-layer shear near fronts and jets that supplies organised ascent
initiation_evidence: INDIRECT: the peripheral-initiation argument is a physical inference drawn from the paper's humidity, CIN and lightning-frequency statistics rather than from any observed plume event
hazards_locations_and_event_types: NR for the plume specifically; the study concerns the occurrence of lightning-producing storms over central Europe in 2008-2013 and deliberately does not distinguish hail, tornadoes or wind gusts
key_supporting_quote: may be advected off the Spanish Plateau over western Europe where they are called a ‘Spanish Plume’ (Carlson and Ludlam, 1968; van Delden, 2001)
limitations_or_uncertainty: The authors list as limitations the neglect of land surface and orography, a 0.75 degree grid too coarse to resolve the immediate storm environment, unavoidable deviation of the reanalysis from the real atmosphere, restriction of the domain to central Europe, and the omission of storms producing only intracloud lightning because EUCLID detects little of it; lightning occurred in some cases with zero CAPE, attributed to reanalysis error or unresolved local instability; confidence intervals are large at the highest CAPE and the most negative lifted-index values

airstream_properties: Moist air capped by warmer but dry air moving into north-western Europe from the south-west; the elevated mixed layer is generated over the Iberian Plateau and advected by south-westerly flow over a warm moist boundary layer, appearing in the 1800 UTC Bergen sounding as a warm dry well-mixed layer between 800 and 650 hPa with a nearly dry-adiabatic lapse rate, with COSMO-EU mean-layer CAPE of 2000-2500 J/kg and peaks to 3000 J/kg, a 0-6 km bulk wind difference of 15 m/s and 0-3 km storm-relative helicity of about 200 m2/s2
diagnostic_variables: The 1800 UTC Bergen radiosonde, COSMO-EU analyses of mean-layer CAPE, deep-layer bulk wind difference and 850 and 500 hPa winds, a Germany-wide 3D polarimetric C-band composite at 1 km horizontal and 250 m vertical spacing every five minutes, the BoXPol polarimetric X-band radar with genuine RHI and birdbath scans, a collocated ceilometer, and at JOYCE the JOYRAD-35 Ka-band Doppler cloud radar, a 1.5 micrometre Doppler lidar, a microwave radiometer and a total sky imager, supplemented by polarimetric WSR-88D observations in Oklahoma
origin_and_transport_claim: Elevated mixed layers are generated over the Iberian Plateau and advected by south-westerly flow, as was the case during the Pentecost event, over a warm moist boundary layer; the Spanish plume refers to a weather pattern in which moist air capped by warmer but dry air moves into north-western Europe from the south-west
origin_evidence: INDIRECT: the elevated mixed layer is identified by the authors in the 1800 UTC Bergen sounding, while the plume label and the Iberian Plateau origin are taken from van Delden (1998), Lewis and Gray (2010), Benjamin and Carlson (1986) and Schaefer (1986); no trajectory or air-mass origin calculation is made
configuration: UNCLASSIFIED: named only as a Spanish plume synoptic weather pattern with south-westerly flow, with no classic, modified or other type assigned
capping_or_instability_mechanism: Steep mid-tropospheric lapse rates associated with the elevated mixed layer allow high CAPE to develop, while a cap at the base of the layer holds it in place, giving so-called loaded-gun soundings; the elevated mixed layer is also said to keep storms isolated
capping_or_instability_evidence: DIRECT for the case: the 1800 UTC Bergen sounding shows a moist boundary layer with little temperature-dewpoint spread beneath a warm dry well-mixed layer between 800 and 650 hPa with a near dry-adiabatic lapse rate, with COSMO-EU mean-layer CAPE of 2000-3000 J/kg
initiation_mechanism: Low-level convergence, for example along a frontal boundary, can push boundary-layer parcels through the layer of convective inhibition at the base of the elevated mixed layer, and diabatic heating in the boundary layer can also remove the inhibition and allow surface-based convection; the accumulated energy is said to be released when air is lifted by low-level colder air approaching from the Atlantic
initiation_evidence: ASSERTED_ONLY: the initiation mechanisms are stated generically in the synoptic overview and no analysis of the actual trigger for the Pentecost storms is presented in this paper
hazards_locations_and_event_types: A series of severe supercell storms over northern France, Belgium, Luxembourg, the Netherlands and especially Germany, with one of the region's most violent storms in decades crossing North Rhine-Westphalia causing six fatalities, gusts up to 42 m/s, hail and a flash flood in Düsseldorf, together with long-lasting and widespread anvil mammatus; 9-10 June 2014
prefrontal_trough: NR: low-level convergence along a frontal boundary is mentioned generically as a possible trigger, but no prefrontal trough is described or analysed
key_supporting_quote: following a heatwave in early June in combination with a Spanish plume synoptic weather pattern
limitations_or_uncertainty: The nearest available sounding lay about 380 km from the observing site; no radiosonde passed through the mammatus region so a stable layer weakening the downdrafts cannot be ruled out; frozen cloud droplets at high concentration cannot be excluded from radar and lidar alone; no polarimetric lidar was available at JOYCE; the ZDR signals in the trailing anvil could not be clearly attributed to mammatus rather than gravity waves; low signal-to-noise near the anvil base makes the ZDR maxima uncertain; the study covers only a few supercell cases and cannot be generalised to other cloud types

airstream_properties: Successive plumes of very warm, humid air moving north from Iberia and France and repeatedly overrun by cooler air at higher levels; the 1200 UTC Brest ascent of 17 July 2014 showed a conspicuous warm nose between 850 and 700 hPa typical of the Spanish Plume, a deep layer of latent instability above 700 hPa and a moist layer from 700 to 600 hPa capped by much drier air, while on 28 June 2012 the plume came with a potent upper trough to the west and a 40-50 kn south-westerly mid-level flow
diagnostic_variables: Met Office ATDnet lightning fixes compiled separately for the UK service area and a newly defined UK land area on daily, monthly and annual scales for 2008-2016, with assessments of detection efficiency and location accuracy, 500 hPa and surface synoptic charts, the Brest and Nottingham upper-air ascents, and the TORRO National Lightning Incidents Database with official fatality statistics and population estimates
origin_and_transport_claim: From late on 17 July 2014 successive plumes of very warm humid air moved north from Iberia and France and were repeatedly overrun by cooler air at higher levels; for 28 June 2012 the plume accompanied a potent upper trough to the west and a strong south-westerly mid-level flow
origin_evidence: INDIRECT: the plume days are identified from synoptic charts and upper-air ascents, with the modified type referred to Lewis and Gray (2010) and the July 2014 episode to a Met Office account; no trajectory or air-mass origin analysis is performed
configuration: CLASSIC+MODIFIED: 28 June 2012 is called a classic Spanish plume, the 17-20 July 2014 episode is identified as the Modified Spanish Plume of Lewis and Gray (2010) with an upper trough extending as far south as Iberia and a south-south-easterly mid-level flow, and 22-23 July 2013 is described as a plume scenario in a more blocked pattern with a greater upper trough extension
capping_or_instability_mechanism: A conspicuous warm nose between 850 and 700 hPa, described as typical of the Spanish Plume, would have inhibited surface-based convection while a deep layer of latent instability lay above 700 hPa and a moist 700-600 hPa layer capped by much drier air gave considerable potential instability; storms on the nights of 17 and 18 July 2014 were therefore elevated and unrelated to surface heating, and on 22-23 July 2013 the elevated plume was destabilised at mid-levels
capping_or_instability_evidence: DIRECT: the 1200 UTC Brest ascent for 17 July 2014 is described in terms of its warm nose, its latent instability above 700 hPa and its moist layer capped by drier air, a few hours before lightning storms affected south-west England
initiation_mechanism: On 28 June 2012 the incursion of the very humid unstable air mass coincided with maximum insolation over central and eastern England, and very high CAPE with strong wind shear produced violent supercells; on 23 July 2013 storms became focused on a waving cold front across northern and eastern England; on 19 July 2014 a rippling inner frontal zone was the main focus of activity
initiation_evidence: INDIRECT: inferred from synoptic descriptions and the spatial and temporal pattern of ATDnet fixes, with supporting references to Clark and Webb (2013), Suri and Page (2014), Rothwell (2014) and Webb (2016) rather than new analysis
hazards_locations_and_event_types: Violent supercell thunderstorms across the English Midlands with a severe hail swathe more than 100 km long and an MCS causing lightning damage and severe flash flooding in north-east England on 28 June 2012, which gave 44 502 land-area fixes in 24 hours; a slow-moving multicell depositing more than 100 mm of rain near Nottingham on 23 July 2013; and several outbreaks on 17-20 July 2014 including an intense supercell over the south Midlands on 19 July and French mesoscale convective systems clipping south-east England; United Kingdom
prefrontal_trough: NR: upper troughs, a waving cold front and a rippling inner frontal zone are described, but no prefrontal trough is identified
key_supporting_quote: The exceptional lightning counts of 28 June 2012 (Figure 5) were a consequence of a classic ‘Spanish plume’.
limitations_or_uncertainty: ATDnet detects about 90 per cent of cloud-to-ground flashes but also up to 25 per cent of cloud flashes and cannot yet discriminate between them; it is some 15-20 per cent less sensitive at night because of modal interference; typical location accuracy is 1-3 km over the UK and 2-10 km elsewhere in Europe and can be worse where sferics overlap; some fixes are rejected by quality control and sensor outages can reduce efficiency; the counts of significant non-injury incidents are acknowledged to be only a fraction of the true number; the authors state that comparison of risk per lightning count between countries would not currently be valid

airstream_properties: A tongue of moist air extending from the Tropics; no thermodynamic properties, source region over Iberia or capping structure is described, and the term is treated as interchangeable with atmospheric river
diagnostic_variables: Historical flood chronologies from the British Newspaper Archive and Environment Agency records back to before 1800, gauged 15-minute river level and discharge series with rates of rise, peak flows and median annual floods at stations on the Wear, West Allen, Wansbeck and South Tyne, rain gauge totals and short-period intensities, and published accounts of individual events
origin_and_transport_claim: The thunderstorms of 28 June 2012 were caused by a tongue of moist air extending from the Tropics, often called a Spanish Plume or Atmospheric River; no Iberian or plateau origin is mentioned
origin_evidence: ASSERTED_ONLY: the attribution is a single clause supported only by a citation to Lavers et al. (2013) on atmospheric rivers, conflating two distinct concepts, with no meteorological analysis in this hydrological paper
capping_or_instability_mechanism: NR
capping_or_instability_evidence: NR
initiation_mechanism: NR for the plume; the paper attributes extreme rainfall generally to convection from highly localised individual cells or from mesoscale convective systems, and notes that the 28 June 2012 storms were associated with a series of cold fronts
initiation_evidence: NR for the plume; the meteorological statements are taken from the cited literature rather than analysed here
hazards_locations_and_event_types: Pluvial flash flooding in Newcastle upon Tyne and surrounding areas on 28 June 2012, the Toon Monsoon, with about 50 mm of rain in two hours from 1630, gridlocked traffic and abandoned cars, 23 000 properties without electricity and about 500 properties internally flooded, two thirds of them for the first time, and record rates of rise on the Team and Ouse Burn; north-east England
key_supporting_quote: were caused by a tongue of moist air extending from the Tropics – often called a ‘Spanish Plume’ or ‘Atmospheric River’ (Lavers et al., 2013)
limitations_or_uncertainty: The plume is invoked only in passing and is conflated with the atmospheric river concept, with no meteorological evidence offered; more broadly the authors note that low rain-gauge densities and the small extent of convective cells mean measured intensities are unlikely to be the maximum over a catchment and that floods often occur where no ground-based rainfall is measured, that stilling-well lag damps gauged rates of rise so that a wall of water cannot be confirmed from 15-minute data, and that historical newspaper accounts are qualitative

airstream_properties: NR for the plume; the situation the authors compare it with is warm southerly mid-tropospheric air transporting large amounts of water colliding with cool air arriving from the north and north-east at low levels
diagnostic_variables: Daily precipitation totals from almost 70 stations in the Polish Carpathians for 1951-2015 with areal means and thresholds of 5, 10, 20, 30, 50 and 100 mm, the Niedzwiedz local circulation-type catalogue and the Grosswetterlagen classification, NCEP/NCAR reanalysis airflow direction and strength at 850, 700 and 500 hPa chiefly for the grid point 50N 20E, and supporting synoptic charts and aerological diagrams
origin_and_transport_claim: NR: no origin, source region or transport is described for the plume, which is invoked only as a partial analogue for the collision of warm southerly mid-tropospheric flow with cool northerly low-level air over the Carpathians
origin_evidence: CITED_ONLY: the analogy rests on citations to Webb et al. (2001) and Webb (2011), with no plume case, chart or diagnosis in this study
capping_or_instability_mechanism: NR
capping_or_instability_evidence: NR
initiation_mechanism: NR for the plume; the authors explain their own extremes by the collision of warm moist southerly mid-tropospheric flow with cool northerly low-level air, giving intensive condensation and sometimes local thunderstorms, together with dynamic ascent over the mountain barrier and the Vb cyclone track
initiation_evidence: INDIRECT: based on frequency distributions of 500 hPa airflow direction during northern-sector low-level flow, for the areal mean and for the Krakow and Poprad stations, rather than on any case analysis
hazards_locations_and_event_types: NR for the plume; the study concerns extreme daily precipitation and consequent floods in the Polish Carpathians, including a record 300 mm at Hala Gasienicowa on 30 June 1973 and areal means above 100 mm, 1951-2015
key_supporting_quote: this situation reminds us of the situation with the so-called Spanish Plume extreme events over the United Kingdom (Webb et al., 2001; Webb, 2011)
limitations_or_uncertainty: The authors report that 700 and 300 hPa reanalysis data provided no substantial information so only the 500 hPa level was used; they stress that undetectable inhomogeneities in precipitation data could lead to completely false conclusions; very local short-duration torrential rainfall capable of producing flash floods was excluded because sufficiently high-resolution long series are unavailable; much of the airflow analysis rests on a single reanalysis grid point

airstream_properties: A warm humid cyclonic southerly flow; no thermodynamic values, source region or capping structure is given
diagnostic_variables: The Theeuwes et al. (2017) diagnostic equation for the daily maximum urban heat island from sky-view factor, vegetation fraction, downward shortwave radiation, diurnal temperature range and rural wind speed, 15 summer half-years (2002-2016) of hourly data from the Rotterdam WMO station, lidar-derived sky-view factors and NDVI vegetation fractions gridded at 100 m, KNMI'14 climate scenarios transformed to 2050, and verification against nine citizen weather stations
origin_and_transport_claim: NR: no origin, source region or transport is described; the plume is named only as a label for a warm humid cyclonic southerly flow with an upper-level trough west of the European continent and approaching fronts
origin_evidence: CITED_ONLY: the label is attached with a single reference and no plume diagnosis, chart or case analysis is presented in this urban-climate study
capping_or_instability_mechanism: NR for a cap; the authors note only that these situations are unstable
capping_or_instability_evidence: ASSERTED_ONLY: instability is asserted in a single clause with no soundings, indices or model fields
initiation_mechanism: NR
initiation_evidence: NR
hazards_locations_and_event_types: NR for direct hazards; the plume situation is associated with tropical nights, defined as minimum temperatures above 20 C, in rural areas around The Hague, and is said to carry a high chance of thunderstorms and squall lines bringing in colder air so that such situations do not usually last long; The Hague agglomeration, 2002-2016
prefrontal_trough: NR: an upper-level trough west of the European continent and approaching fronts are mentioned, but no prefrontal trough is described
key_supporting_quote: with an upper level trough west of the European continent and approaching fronts, sometimes referred to as a Spanish plume
limitations_or_uncertainty: The diagnostic equation omits anthropogenic heat, albedo, thermal admittance and proximity to open water, so coastal parts of the study area carry larger uncertainty and caution is advised where anthropogenic heat production is large; the fixed 0.46 conversion factor from maximum urban heat island to the minimum-temperature heat island is probably not constant across percentiles; the Rotterdam rural reference station is itself affected by urban heat advection; crowdsourced verification covers only two summers at nine stations and shows a cold bias at the lowest percentiles; the residence-density relationship had to be extrapolated for the densest planning strategy

airstream_properties: Warm, dry air from the Iberian plateau moving northwards and rising over a layer of cool, moist air from the Atlantic; in the forecast guidance the associated high impact events are linked to CAPE of roughly more than 350 J/kg
diagnostic_variables: Subjective one-to-five-day probabilistic thunderstorm risk forecasts for the London Terminal Manoeuvring Area produced from UKV, global, gridded post-processed, MOGREPS and ECMWF deterministic and ensemble output using CAPE, cloud top temperature, wind shear and the Boyden and Rackliff instability indices, verified against UK Air Navigation Service Provider weather delay minutes and arrival flow rates with relative operating characteristic curves, areas under the curve, reliability diagrams and economic value plots for the 2014 and 2015 seasons
origin_and_transport_claim: Warm, dry air from the Iberian plateau, the Spanish plume, moves northwards and rises over a layer of cool, moist air from the Atlantic
origin_evidence: ASSERTED_ONLY: the definition is given as background to the forecast guidance with no citation, chart, sounding or case analysis
capping_or_instability_mechanism: As the surface temperature rises, the cool air beneath the Spanish plume layer heats up and stores energy that cannot be released convectively while the lower layer remains cooler than the plume layer; if daytime heating raises the lowest layer above the temperature of the plume layer, the stored energy is released and severe thunderstorms are induced
capping_or_instability_evidence: ASSERTED_ONLY: the mechanism is stated in the introduction with no sounding, index or model evidence
initiation_mechanism: Daytime heating raising the temperature of the lowest layer above that of the Spanish plume layer releases the stored energy and induces severe thunderstorms
initiation_evidence: ASSERTED_ONLY: no case study, chart or diagnostic is presented for the mechanism
hazards_locations_and_event_types: High-impact aviation disruption in the London Terminal Manoeuvring Area, said to arise for example from summertime supercells or Spanish plume events, with heavy flow-rate regulation of more than five fewer arrivals per hour at an airport and significant weather delays; aircraft hazards listed include violent up and down draughts, icing, hail, lightning and severe wind shear
key_supporting_quote: A Spanish plume is a meteorological phenomenon in which warm, dry air from the Iberian plateau (the Spanish plume) moves northwards
limitations_or_uncertainty: The forecasts are subjective and produced by several meteorologists with individual interpretations of impact; the observed impact can be masked where the forecast itself prompted mitigating action and depends on staff decision-making and willingness to regulate; events bridging the 1200Z boundary have to be double counted; high impact events are rarely forecast with more than 30 per cent confidence, so measuring their performance is challenging and the analysis is said to require caution; the user's cost/loss ratio cannot be determined precisely

airstream_properties: A warm moist plume of air advected north-eastwards from Iberia, capped by warmer but very dry well-mixed air from the Spanish plateau, from which conditional instability is released; in this case warm moist air from over the North Atlantic flowed inland over the Iberian Peninsula and then turned north-eastwards, with CAPE of 1000-1600 J/kg where the first MCS began to develop, about 1800 J/kg once it organised and around 800 J/kg by 1200 UTC
diagnostic_variables: Met Office synoptic analysis charts and infrared satellite imagery, rainfall radar and lightning reports, 12 km North Atlantic European MetUM analyses of CAPE, and MetUM 8.2 simulations in the 4.4 km convection-permitting Euro4 and 25 km convection-parametrizing Global configurations, compared through potential vorticity and geopotential height at 250 hPa, vertical PV cross-sections, coarse graining to 25 and 100 km, MCS wind and potential temperature perturbations inserted by incremental analysis update, and root mean square differences over five-day forecasts
origin_and_transport_claim: Warm moist air from the North Atlantic flowed inland over the Iberian Peninsula and then turned north-eastwards towards France and the UK, and conditional instability is released from a warm moist plume advected north-eastwards from Iberia that is capped by warmer but very dry well-mixed air from the Spanish plateau
origin_evidence: INDIRECT: the environment is matched to the modified Spanish Plume category of Lewis and Gray (2010) using Met Office synoptic analyses, satellite imagery and model CAPE fields, without any trajectory or air-mass origin calculation
configuration: MODIFIED: explicitly identified as consistent with the modified Spanish Plume environment of Lewis and Gray (2010), a slowly moving mature frontal system with a forward-tilting trough and possible cut-off low at 500 hPa evolving according to idealised baroclinic life cycle 2
capping_or_instability_mechanism: The warm moist Iberian plume is capped by warmer, very dry well-mixed air from the Spanish plateau; considerable convective inhibition initially limited release of instability from the lower troposphere, and once that inhibition had gone convection initiated from near the ground
capping_or_instability_evidence: INDIRECT: based on the 12 km MetUM analyses of CAPE and convective inhibition for the case, which are quoted but not shown, together with the cited Lewis and Gray (2010) description of the environment
initiation_mechanism: A cut-off low west of the UK was almost stationary for four days with blocking high pressure over Scandinavia; a cold front through central France with a weak upper-level trough provided the trigger through vertical motion forced by upper-level positive vorticity advection, with convection initiating around 0000 UTC on 5 July in southern France and further triggering at 0900 UTC
initiation_evidence: DIRECT: Met Office synoptic charts, infrared satellite imagery, rainfall radar and lightning reports document the initiation and organisation, supported by the model CAPE and inhibition analysis
hazards_locations_and_event_types: Two mesoscale convective systems with precipitation rates exceeding 10 mm/h and abundant lightning, one tracking northwards to the UK and interacting with a developing frontal cyclone and the other moving east towards Italy and Germany; France, the UK and central Europe, 5-6 July 2012
prefrontal_trough: NR: a cold front with a weak upper-level trough and a forward-tilting 500 hPa trough are described, but no prefrontal surface trough is identified
key_supporting_quote: The synoptic environment in which the MCSs formed is consistent with the modified Spanish Plume environment identified by Lewis and Gray (2010)
limitations_or_uncertainty: The Euro4 grid spacing lies in the grey zone where showers are typically too sparse, too intense and initiated too late, and its simulated precipitation rates exceed those observed by radar; the MCS perturbations are attributed to explicit convection but other processes may have contributed during the 15 hours since downscaling; the perturbations are deliberately unbalanced and are initially damped, partly because their scales are finer than the effective resolution of the Global configuration; the perturbation region may have been too small since the differences extend to its edges; the authors note the approach provides an alternative plausible trajectory rather than a more accurate forecast

airstream_properties: NR: no plume properties are given, the case description being confined to a mature low west of the UK, convective initiation over southern France, a cold front in a slack low pressure region and a later warm front
diagnostic_variables: Met Office synoptic analysis charts and infrared satellite imagery for the case, and MetUM 8.2 simulations in the 4.4 km convection-permitting Euro4, 25 km convection-parametrizing Global and 60 km MOGREPS-G configurations, with MCS wind and potential temperature perturbations inserted by incremental analysis update into six downscaled ensemble members, evaluated through 250 hPa potential vorticity, precipitation rate and mean sea level pressure using root mean square difference and error and the correspondence ratio
origin_and_transport_claim: NR: no origin, source region or transport is described; the case environment is simply named as the modified Spanish Plume of Lewis and Gray (2010), with the full description left to the companion paper
origin_evidence: CITED_ONLY: the classification is stated with reference to Lewis and Gray (2010) and to Part 1, with no plume diagnosis in this paper
configuration: MODIFIED: the environment is named as the modified Spanish Plume of Lewis and Gray (2010), without further description here
capping_or_instability_mechanism: NR
capping_or_instability_evidence: NR
initiation_mechanism: NR for the plume; the paper's interest is in how misrepresented mesoscale convective system potential vorticity anomalies alter downstream ensemble forecasts rather than in convective initiation
initiation_evidence: NR for the plume; the initiation description is deferred to the companion paper
hazards_locations_and_event_types: NR for the plume specifically; the case involves two mesoscale convective systems forming over France on 5-6 July 2012, one tracking to the UK along a cold front, with the study concerned with downstream ensemble forecast skill and spread over Europe and the northern hemisphere
prefrontal_trough: NR: a cold front in a slack low pressure region and a later warm front are mentioned, but no prefrontal trough is described
key_supporting_quote: The MCSs developed in a synoptic environment termed the modified Spanish Plume by Lewis and Gray (2010).
limitations_or_uncertainty: The study rests on a single case study and specific model configurations; the Euro4 grid spacing lies in the convective grey zone and produces showers that are too few, too intense and too organised, raising the question of whether the perturbation amplitudes are realistic; the unbalanced perturbations are damped after insertion and the Global model may not retain their energy when they are added over a single hour; the MCS perturbations are inserted only over a limited region while the initial condition perturbations cover the globe, so the comparison between them is not like for like; no discernible change in ensemble mean forecast skill was found

airstream_properties: An elevated mixed layer advected on southerly flow aloft over western France, producing a conditionally unstable environment favourable to severe convective storms; no thermodynamic values are given for the plume itself
diagnostic_variables: EUCLID/BLIDS cloud-to-ground lightning for 2001-2014 defining thunderstorm days and widespread thunderstorm days, NCEP/NCAR R1 reanalysis 300 hPa winds and 850 hPa equivalent potential temperature, the 24 km coastDat-2 COSMO-CLM hindcast for 1958-2014, a new convective weather type classification built on 850 hPa equivalent potential temperature, precipitable water, surface lifted index and 500 hPa vertical velocity, rotated T-mode principal component analysis of 500 hPa geopotential, NOAA NAO, EA and SCAND indices, NOAA OI sea-surface temperature over the Bay of Biscay, and bootstrap significance testing
origin_and_transport_claim: Warm moist air reaches central Europe along two pathways, from south-westerly subtropical regions via Spain and France, possibly in combination with an elevated mixed layer associated with a Spanish plume event, or from the Black Sea region via Poland and north-eastern Germany; southerly flow aloft during positive Bay of Biscay SST anomalies raises the likelihood of the elevated mixed layer known as the Spanish Plume over western France
origin_evidence: CITED_ONLY: the plume and the elevated mixed layer are attributed to Carlson and Ludlam (1968), Carlson et al. (1983), Lanicci and Warner (1991), Morris (1986), van Delden (2001), Lewis and Gray (2010) and Kunz et al. (2018); the authors' own work consists of geopotential, equivalent potential temperature and SST anomaly composites with no plume diagnosis
capping_or_instability_mechanism: The advected elevated mixed layer is said to produce a conditionally unstable environment favourable to the development of severe convective storms; the study's own stability measures are the surface lifted index together with 850 hPa equivalent potential temperature and precipitable water anomalies
capping_or_instability_evidence: CITED_ONLY for the plume's conditional instability, which rests entirely on the cited literature; the authors' own thresholds and composites describe general convection-favouring conditions and no soundings or cap diagnostics are examined
initiation_mechanism: NR for the plume; the study finds convection-favouring conditions occur chiefly ahead of upper-level troughs with large-scale lifting from quasi-geostrophic forcing and embedded shortwave troughs, and in some regions in association with closed upper lows or ridges
initiation_evidence: DIRECT for the climatology: rotated T-mode principal component analysis of 500 hPa geopotential on convection-favouring days and composite anomalies of 300 hPa wind and 850 hPa equivalent potential temperature for each teleconnection and SST phase, with two-sided bootstrap significance tests
hazards_locations_and_event_types: NR for the plume specifically; the study concerns widespread thunderstorm activity over central and western Europe in the summer half-years of 1958-2014, with the plume named as the mechanism linking warm Bay of Biscay sea-surface temperatures to convection-favouring conditions over western France
key_supporting_quote: the advection of an elevated mixed layer (EML), known as the Spanish Plume over western France, which produces a conditionally unstable environment
limitations_or_uncertainty: The lightning record spans only 14 years and thunderstorm days are contaminated by scattered unorganised cells, so statistical significance is low over most sub-regions; the convective weather type scheme was developed and evaluated on the same period without a separate verification sample, has a probability of detection of only about 22 per cent for widespread thunderstorm days, and cannot capture local triggering such as flow deviations at mountains; coastDat-2 does not resolve orographically induced convergence zones, especially around the Alps; the anomaly-based thresholds under-represent northern Italy; the classification is described as sufficient but not necessary for widespread convection

airstream_properties: NR for the plume; the analogous pattern described is warm southerly air transporting large amounts of water in the mid-troposphere colliding with cool air from the north, the humid southern air lifting slowly over the colder layer in what the authors call a typical warm front structure
diagnostic_variables: Daily discharges at 21 gauging stations on Sudeten rivers for 1971-2015, daily precipitation totals at 43 stations, NCEP/NCAR reanalysis sea level pressure, 500 hPa geopotential height and total precipitable water on a 2.5 degree grid with standardized anomaly composites, Ward's method clustering of 17 flood cases into five circulation types, and 72-hour NOAA HYSPLIT back trajectories at 500, 2000 and 5000 m
origin_and_transport_claim: NR for the plume; the paper's own transport finding is that warm humid air from the Mediterranean in the middle troposphere overlaps cool air arriving from the north or north-east in the low troposphere
origin_evidence: CITED_ONLY: the plume is invoked as a partial analogy with references to Wypych et al. and two further sources, and no plume case, chart or diagnosis appears in this study
capping_or_instability_mechanism: NR
capping_or_instability_evidence: NR
initiation_mechanism: NR for the plume; the authors attribute their own extreme rainfall to slow-evolving deep low-pressure systems of Mediterranean or Atlantic origin, meridional northward moisture transport, warm-front ascent of humid southern air over colder northern air, and orographic enhancement
initiation_evidence: DIRECT for the case set: composite sea level pressure, 500 hPa height and precipitable water anomaly maps for six, four, two and zero days before each flood culmination, together with HYSPLIT back trajectories at three levels
hazards_locations_and_event_types: For the plume, extreme high temperatures, intense rainfall with potential for flash flooding and damaging hailstorms over the United Kingdom in summer; the paper's own subject is 17 extreme summer floods in the Polish Sudeten Mountains between 1971 and 2015, with weekly precipitation totals reaching 412.6 mm
key_supporting_quote: Such pattern reminds to a certain degree, the conditions of so-called Spanish Plume over the United Kingdom, which appears in the summer months
limitations_or_uncertainty: The reanalysis grid is 2.5 degrees, described as sufficient only for locating synoptic-scale pressure centres and humidity source regions; extreme floods are rare, so the classification rests on 17 cases split into five almost equally sized groups and the number of clusters is acknowledged to be a subjective choice; the authors note that their meridional moisture transport differs from atmospheric rivers in being non-filamentary and less intense and call for closer investigation of integrated water vapour transport

airstream_properties: NR for the plume itself; the associated flow is described only as advection of warm air masses at low levels from south-westerly regions from Spain to France and central Europe in combination with an elevated mixed layer
diagnostic_variables: EUCLID/BLIDS cloud-to-ground lightning for May to August 2001-2014 with thunderstorm days defined as at least five flashes in a 10 x 10 km box, ERA-Interim blocking identified as persistent vertically averaged 500-150 hPa negative potential vorticity anomalies below -1 PVU lasting five days, odds ratios from autoregressive logistic regression with bootstrap significance, and anomaly composites of 500 hPa geopotential, potential vorticity on the 335 K isentrope, deep-layer shear, surface lifted index, CAPE, 700-500 hPa lapse rate, precipitable water and 500 hPa vertical motion
origin_and_transport_claim: Flow patterns associated with advection of warm low-level air from south-westerly regions from Spain to France and central Europe, combined with an elevated mixed layer and a Spanish plume event, often produce an environment conducive to severe thunderstorms
origin_evidence: CITED_ONLY: the statement rests on citations to Carlson et al. (1983), Lanicci and Warner (1991), Morris (1986), van Delden (2001), Piper (2017), Kunz et al. (2018) and Piper et al. (2019); the study itself analyses blocking and thunderstorm-day statistics and diagnoses no plume
capping_or_instability_mechanism: NR for the plume beyond the elevated mixed layer being named; the paper's own stability diagnostics are the surface lifted index, CAPE and the 700-500 hPa lapse rate composited over blocking days
capping_or_instability_evidence: CITED_ONLY for the plume; the authors' own composites describe general stability and moisture anomalies during blocking rather than any plume cap
initiation_mechanism: NR for the plume; the study finds convection-favouring conditions on the western flank of Baltic Sea blocks through southerly to south-westerly advection of warm moist unstable air, and convection-inhibiting northerly advection with large-scale subsidence on the eastern flank of eastern North Atlantic blocks
initiation_evidence: DIRECT for the blocking analysis: odds ratios between blocking and thunderstorm days for 132 grid points, two case studies and bootstrap-tested anomaly composites of stability, moisture, shear and vertical motion; none of it a plume diagnosis
hazards_locations_and_event_types: NR for the plume specifically; the study concerns warm-season thunderstorm activity over western and central Europe in 2001-2014, its case study being the 10 July 2002 derecho over Germany with a 42 m/s gust and four deaths in Berlin
key_supporting_quote: an elevated mixed layer (Carlson et al. 1983; Lanicci and Warner 1991) and a Spanish plume event
limitations_or_uncertainty: The odds ratio establishes co-occurrence rather than causality, as the authors state explicitly; only 14 years of lightning data are available and monthly analyses become much less significant because of the reduced sample; ERA-Interim is noted as tending to underestimate vertical wind shear; crossover cases with blocking over both regions are too few to give widespread significance; blocking is stated to be unsuitable as a single predictor for convection, and correctly predicting blocking position remains a challenge for global models

airstream_properties: Warm air advected polewards from North Africa west of Algiers or the south of Spain; 850 hPa wet-bulb potential temperature about 18 C rising to 20 C at Herstmonceux and 19-20 C at Idar-Oberstein; low-level southerly to south-south-easterly flow at Herstmonceux on 24-25 July beneath overnight inversions near 950 hPa
diagnostic_variables: 850 hPa wet-bulb potential temperature read visually from Herstmonceux 0000 utc and Idar-Oberstein 1200 utc soundings; NOAA ESRL composite mean sea level pressure, surface temperature anomaly, 250 and 500 hPa geopotential height and 500, 700, 850 and 1000 hPa vector winds; HYSPLIT 5-day backward and forward trajectories with vertical motion at about 950, 900, 850, 700 and 500 hPa; 1800 utc synoptic maximum temperatures; lightning archives
origin_and_transport_claim: Advection of heat from the subtropics to the British Isles is sometimes referred to as a Spanish Plume, defined after Meteorological Office (1991) as potentially warm air flowing from Spain towards France ahead of a slow-moving upper trough; on 25 July the London Heathrow back trajectories developed a Spanish Plume pattern originating from North Africa west of Algiers or the south of Spain
origin_evidence: DIRECT: HYSPLIT backward trajectories at London Heathrow and Idar-Oberstein plus five-day forward trajectories from Algiers, supported by the soundings and composite vector winds; the glossary definition itself is cited to Meteorological Office (1991)
capping_or_instability_mechanism: NR for a plume cap; the paper reports only subsidence-induced near-dry-adiabatic lapse rates, overnight radiative inversions near 950 hPa typically below subsidence level, and superadiabatic surface layers at Idar-Oberstein at 1200 utc
capping_or_instability_evidence: NR for the plume: no capping or instability claim is made for it; the inversions and subsidence warming are DIRECT from the Herstmonceux and Idar-Oberstein soundings and trajectory vertical-motion traces
initiation_mechanism: NR: no convective initiation analysis; scattered thunderstorms over England on 24-25 July are said only to be consistent with the Spanish Plume definition of thunderstorms over France moving northward to England, while afternoon thunderstorms at Idar-Oberstein accompanied an approaching cold front
initiation_evidence: INDIRECT: lightning location archives matched to the glossary definition and to the trajectory dates; no initiation diagnosis is attempted
hazards_locations_and_event_types: Extreme heat 22-26 July 2019 with national records (France 43.1 C, Germany 42.6 C, Belgium 41.8 C, Netherlands 40.7 C, UK 38.7 C at Cambridge on the 25th, Edinburgh 31.2 C) over France, Germany, Benelux, Scandinavia and the British Isles; scattered thunderstorms with considerable lightning over England on 24 and 25 July
key_supporting_quote: the heat over the British Isles was a combination of both processes, which was boosted by the Spanish Plume event on the 25th
limitations_or_uncertainty: Wet-bulb potential temperatures were determined visually from plotted soundings so the results are stated to be somewhat subjective; preferred 1200 utc soundings were unavailable at Herstmonceux so 0000 utc ascents were used; Herstmonceux is only a proxy for London Heathrow; several trajectory levels and dates are not shown; the authors note there is no single internationally accepted definition of a heat wave

airstream_properties: Relatively hot dry air heated over the Iberian Peninsula and advected north over the Pyrenees in a deep south-westerly flow, about 20 C at 850 hPa from Spain, overrunning already present warm moist air and acting as a lid; cold dry Atlantic air above in upper westerlies, giving CAPE of about 3000 J/kg and 20-30 m/s vertical wind shear
diagnostic_variables: GFS surface and upper-air reanalysis (surface pressure, 500 hPa temperature and geopotential height), 850 hPa potential and equivalent potential temperature, 500-1000 hPa thickness, radiosonde-based CAPE and shear from cited case reports, KNMI Doppler radar rainfall and maximum reflectivity, KNMI and amateur station rainfall and wind, and WRF-ARW simulations at 2 and 4 km of CAPE, CIN, LCL, LFC, accumulated rainfall and wind speed with soil-moisture ensembles
origin_and_transport_claim: Air above the Iberian Peninsula was heated in the preceding days and a deep south-westerly flow transported relatively hot air (20 C at 850 hPa from Spain) towards the Netherlands over already present warm moist air; this warm air advection is referred to as the Spanish Plume
origin_evidence: INDIRECT: the synoptic description rests on GFS reanalysis charts showing a steep potential temperature and geopotential gradient from Spain to Denmark and on WRF 850 hPa equivalent potential temperature fields, while the plume label and Iberian source are attributed to reference 8 (Morris 1986); no trajectories were computed
capping_or_instability_mechanism: The advected hot dry Iberian air acted as a lid over less warm but moist air, producing an inversion that held a potentially highly unstable atmosphere in a loaded-gun state until the convective inhibition could be overcome; upper westerlies carrying cold dry Atlantic air aloft further increased the potential instability
capping_or_instability_evidence: INDIRECT: the lid and loaded-gun description is asserted with citations to radiosonde-based case reports (references 9 and 10), while the paper's own CAPE, CIN, LCL and LFC evidence comes from WRF simulations compared with an Essen sounding adjusted to observed Eindhoven surface values
initiation_mechanism: Frontogenesis and surface heating supplied sufficient energy to break the inversion and overcome the convective inhibition so that the CAPE was released, producing the mesoscale convective system
initiation_evidence: CITED_ONLY: the trigger statement is attributed to reference 10 (van Delden 2001); the WRF experiments compare simulated CIN and CAPE evolution between convection schemes rather than testing the trigger mechanism
hazards_locations_and_event_types: Mesoscale convective system on 23 June 2016 over Noord-Brabant in the Netherlands with hail about 10 cm in diameter, lightning, heavy precipitation (65 mm observed in south-east Noord-Brabant), downbursts and gusts (15 m/s at Ell), peaking near 18:45 utc at Luyksgestel and causing 675 million euros of damage
key_supporting_quote: The extreme weather was a result of a Mesoscale Convective System (MCS) formed by a Spanish plume over Europe.
limitations_or_uncertainty: The Betts-Miller-Janjic scheme activates too early and predicts no MCS, Grell-Freitas and Kain-Fritsch underestimate its intensity, and explicit convection is delayed by about an hour at 4 km and overestimates intensity; 4 km lies in the grey zone where neither parameterised nor resolved convection is clearly valid; boundary conditions were updated only 6-hourly; a deliberately simple WSM3 microphysics scheme was used; the narrow 25 km storm track cannot be simulated in the exact location so area maxima were compared; the accuracy of the amateur weather station is hard to assess

airstream_properties: NR for the plume airstream; it is characterised only as an important variety of UK convection associated with elevated convective instability and an elevated mixed layer, usually accompanied by moderate to strong flow aloft and not usually containing surface-based convection over the UK
diagnostic_variables: 15 min Environment Agency and Natural Resources Wales rain gauge data from about 1100 gauges converted to rolling hourly accumulations; Met Office GPS-derived integrated water vapour (precipitable water); 6-hourly Met Office surface pressure and frontal analyses; UK weather radar rainfall; radiosondes; ArcGIS spatial and temporal interpolation; linear and non-linear least-squares regression with squared correlation coefficients; box-and-whisker plots; UKV 1.5 km model forecasts
origin_and_transport_claim: NR: no origin or transport claim is made for the plume
origin_evidence: NR: there is no origin claim to support; the term is used only as a case-selection category cited to Morris (1986)
capping_or_instability_mechanism: NR for capping; the events are characterised only by elevated convective instability with convection often released from medium levels, in contrast to the surface-based deep instability of the 20 cases analysed
capping_or_instability_evidence: CITED_ONLY: the characterisation rests on Morris (1986) and operational experience, and plume cases were deliberately excluded so no soundings or stability diagnostics are presented for them
initiation_mechanism: NR: plume convection is said to be released from medium levels rather than surface-triggered, which together with the wind-speed constraint is the stated reason for excluding such cases; no initiation analysis is offered
initiation_evidence: NR: no plume case was analysed
hazards_locations_and_event_types: Intense short-period convective rainfall and surface water (pluvial) flooding across England and Wales in 20 daytime convective cases between July 2012 and April 2017, with thresholds of 20 mm in 1 hour for localised and 30 mm for severe flooding; Spanish Plume events are excluded although very high precipitable water above 35 mm is often associated with them
key_supporting_quote: “Spanish Plume” events (Morris, 1986)—an important variety of convection in the UK associated with elevated convective instability
limitations_or_uncertainty: Spanish Plume, elevated-instability, mesoscale convective and frontal cases were excluded so the relationship is not demonstrated for them; all England and Wales gauges were used for each event rather than only the convective area, so the derived percentage thresholds may be too low; data are sparse above 26 mm precipitable water and only one case supplied points above 35 mm; only the largest hourly total per gauge per event was retained; the extreme-totals line rests on a very small sample and is sensitive to the choice of precipitable water intervals; gauges tend to miss the largest point totals

airstream_properties: NR for the plume itself, which is described only as hot, moist and unstable southerly airflow; the paper's own composites show positive dewpoint, column water vapour and integrated vapour transport anomalies arriving from the south, south-east and south-west
diagnostic_variables: Quality-controlled hourly rain gauge records 1979-2014 aggregated to 3-hourly peaks-over-threshold (POT3) samples for six UK regions; ERA-Interim dewpoint temperature, mean sea level pressure, surface evaporation, 200 hPa geopotential height, column-integrated water vapour and integrated vapour transport; pentad-anomaly composites with two-tailed t-tests at the 90% level; a Newfoundland to central-north-Atlantic geopotential ratio index; Met Office daily weather summaries for event corroboration
origin_and_transport_claim: Thunderstorm activity that can become organised mesoscale convective systems is often enhanced during hot, moist and unstable southerly airflows referred to as Spanish Plumes when they influence the UK; the single heaviest event (Rhydymain, 3 July 2001) is attributed to a mesoscale convective system within a modified Spanish Plume synoptic pattern
origin_evidence: CITED_ONLY: the plume attributions rest on Gray and Marshall (1998) and Lewis and Gray (2010) together with Met Office daily weather summaries; the study's own composites diagnose anomalous southerly moisture transport but establish no plume origin
capping_or_instability_mechanism: NR for the plume; the paper notes only that the associated airflows are unstable, and speculates that drier anticyclonic conditions four days earlier may reduce soil moisture, shift the surface energy balance towards sensible heating and so modify the boundary layer in a way that favours the most extreme events
capping_or_instability_evidence: NR for the plume: no stability diagnostics are computed; the anticyclonic-precursor suggestion is INDIRECT, inferred from composite geopotential, pressure and moisture anomalies
initiation_mechanism: NR for the plume; individual heavy events are associated with cyclonic southerly flow, convergence lines ahead of cold fronts, a static cold front, or mesoscale convective systems, and atmospheric blocking is said to promote or suppress thunderstorm activity depending on its position
initiation_evidence: INDIRECT: the heaviest events were cross-referenced against Met Office daily weather summaries and nearby gauges and interpreted through ERA-Interim composites rather than analysed for initiation
hazards_locations_and_event_types: The most intense 3-hourly summer rainfall and associated flash and surface water flooding across six UK regions 1979-2014; heaviest event 148.8 mm at Rhydymain (north-west England and Wales) on 3 July 2001, with other cases including Ringway on 6 August 1981, the Boscastle convergence line of 2004 and Thornwood
key_supporting_quote: probably associated with a mesoscale convective system as part of a “modified” Spanish Plume synoptic pattern (Lewis and Gray 2010).
limitations_or_uncertainty: Several extreme gauge totals could not be corroborated in independent records and some remain suspect despite quality control, while manual screening risks removing genuine highly localised events; the six regions were chosen pragmatically rather than objectively; the geopotential tripole index shows only weak association with heavy rainfall, with just 1.8% of high-index days preceding a heaviest event, so it is judged not to be a useful predictor; dynamical precursor signals are weak and incoherent for south-east England

airstream_properties: NR for the plume beyond southerly to south-westerly winds advecting unstable, warm and moist air masses from the Mediterranean on the downstream flank of a mid-tropospheric trough; no thermodynamic properties of the plume itself are reported
diagnostic_variables: 2-D radar reflectivity at 1 km and 5 min from DWD and Meteo France processed with a modified TRACE3D cell-tracking algorithm using the Mason Z>=55 dBZ hail criterion; ESWD hail reports matched within 10 km; ERA-Interim surface lifted index, 0-500 hPa deep-layer shear and 0-3 km storm-relative helicity composited in 800 km moving windows; coastDat-3 10 km reanalysis lapse rate and shear; thermal-front-parameter cold-front detection on 850 hPa equivalent potential temperature; 500 hPa mean wind against radar-derived storm motion
origin_and_transport_claim: Hailstorms usually occur downstream of the eastern flank of a mid-troposphere trough where southerly to south-westerly winds are frequently associated with advection of unstable, warm and moist air masses from the Mediterranean, a constellation often referred to as the Spanish plume
origin_evidence: CITED_ONLY: the plume label is attributed to Morris (1986) and the advection statement to Graf et al. (2011), Wapler and James (2015) and Piper et al. (2019); the study's own composites locate troughs and shear maxima but diagnose no air-mass origin
capping_or_instability_mechanism: NR for a plume cap; the study's own instability measures are the surface lifted index (mean -3.8 K, falling to about -4.5 K for large hail on long tracks) and the 700-500 hPa lapse rate, with cold fronts raising CAPE and reducing CIN through cold-air advection aloft, frontal cross-circulations and along-front low-level moisture advection
capping_or_instability_evidence: DIRECT for the paper's own ERA-Interim and coastDat-3 composites of surface lifted index and lapse rate around 985 hailstorm tracks; NR for any plume-related capping, which is not examined
initiation_mechanism: NR for the plume; convection initiation is said to require additional lifting to overcome boundary-layer inhibition, supplied by synoptic cold fronts (about a quarter of all storms, locally up to 50% over flat terrain), by large-scale ascent downstream of the trough, or by orographic and low-level flow convergence over complex terrain
initiation_evidence: DIRECT: 26012 radar-derived storm tracks matched to objectively detected ERA-Interim cold fronts within a search radius of half the track length plus 200 km, combined with environmental composites for nine hail-size and track-length classes
hazards_locations_and_event_types: Severe convective storms and hailstorms over Germany, France, Belgium and Luxembourg from April to September 2005-2014 (26012 storm tracks, 985 hailstorm tracks); hail diameters from below 3 cm to 5 cm and above with tracks exceeding 150 km; cited loss events include the 27-28 July 2013 supercells (EUR 3.6 billion) and storm cluster Ela of 8-10 July 2014 (EUR 2.6 billion)
key_supporting_quote: This constellation is often referred to as “Spanish plume” (Morris, 1986).
limitations_or_uncertainty: Reliance on ESWD eyewitness reports biased towards populated regions and daytime with strong under-reporting in France; the Mason 55 dBZ criterion has a 35-40% false-alarm rate so the sample includes some heavy-rain events; maximum diameters of non-spherical hailstones add uncertainty; fixed frontal-detection thresholds may discard fragmented or distorted fronts near mountains; ERA-Interim is too coarse to resolve subgrid variability; sample sizes prevented further subdivision; the operationally more relevant reverse question of footprint probability given an environment could not be evaluated quantitatively

airstream_properties: NR for the plume beyond the displaced elevated mixed layer; the paper reports that European EML development is confined to the Iberian Peninsula, the Alps, Turkey and north-western Africa and is comparatively rare without a favourable southerly wind component, and that European 0-3 km lapse rates and 0-3 km CAPE exceed those of the United States while 2-4 km lapse rates are similar
