diagnostic_variables: ERA5 on 137 hybrid-sigma levels at 0.25 degrees and hourly steps giving mixed-layer CAPE, 0-3 km CAPE, LCL, LFC, CIN, equilibrium level, mixing ratio, precipitable water, 0-3 km and 2-4 km lapse rates, effective and 0-6, 0-3 and 0-1 km bulk shear, storm-relative helicity, low-level jet, SCP, STP, SHIP and WMAXSHEAR; NLDN and ATDnet lightning converted to thunderstorm hours; SPC Storm Data and ESWD reports; conditional probabilities and return periods
origin_and_transport_claim: So-called Spanish plume events displacing the elevated mixed layer from the Iberian Peninsula are typically linked to severe weather outbreaks over western Europe, and enhanced composite-parameter values in a corridor from central France to western Germany are said to correspond to Spanish plume synoptic patterns
origin_evidence: CITED_ONLY: the EML source regions are attributed to Carlson and Ludlam (1968) and the plume-outbreak link to Hamid (2012), Mathias et al. (2017) and Antonescu et al. (2018); the authors' own ERA5 analysis measures lapse rates and composite indices rather than air-mass origin
capping_or_instability_mechanism: NR for a plume-specific cap; the paper attributes the discrepancy between low- and mid-level lapse rates to the presence of an elevated mixed layer, and reports that weak CIN over Europe permits more frequent convective initiation whereas stronger CIN over the United States can delay initiation until CAPE is maximised and so favour discrete supercell modes
capping_or_instability_evidence: DIRECT for the ERA5 CIN, LCL, LFC and lapse-rate distributions computed for 818689 report-matched unique profiles plus millions of thunderstorm hours; CITED_ONLY for the elevated mixed layer and plume attribution
initiation_mechanism: NR for the plume; the study instead quantifies the likelihood of convective initiation given a severe environment, about 7-12% over central and eastern Europe against 3-6% over the Great Plains, and attributes the European advantage to weaker convective inhibition
initiation_evidence: DIRECT: conditional probabilities derived by combining hourly lightning detections with collocated ERA5 environments on upscaled conditional-probability subdomain grids over 1979-2018
hazards_locations_and_event_types: Lightning, large hail (2-5, 5-8 and 8 cm and above), severe convective wind (25-32 and above 32 m/s in warm and cold types) and tornadoes (F0-F1, F2-F3, F4-F5) across Europe and the United States 1979-2018; plume-linked severe weather outbreaks are placed in a corridor from central France to western Germany
key_supporting_quote: However, so-called Spanish plume events displacing EML from the Iberian Peninsula are typically linked to severe weather outbreaks over western Europe
limitations_or_uncertainty: Severe weather report quality, local reporting practice and spatiotemporal biases differ between the ESWD and SPC datasets, with probable under-reporting of severe wind and 2-5 cm hail in Europe; differing NLDN and ATDnet detection efficiencies introduce inhomogeneity in thunderstorm hours; ERA5 still requires convective parameterisation and is known to be biased in the lowest part of the atmosphere, and its resolution cannot represent orographic shear enhancement; calibrated composite indices such as STP, SCP and SHIP transfer poorly from the United States to Europe

airstream_properties: A warm plume of air with 850 hPa wet-bulb potential temperature of 18 C or more, showing potential instability (theta-w decreasing with height) between 850 and 500 hPa above a comparatively stable boundary layer, dry air below 700 hPa, a high freezing level, strong unidirectional flow aloft and precipitable water of 30-35 mm
diagnostic_variables: Met Office 1800 utc surface analysis; CFS reanalysis 500 hPa geopotential height and mean sea level pressure; Meteosat false-colour imagery using channels 2 and 5; Camborne 1200 utc radiosonde; Euro 4 km model forecast tephigram for Jersey adjusted to Dinard maximum temperature and dew point of 32 and 17 C; Met Office Global Model 12-hour forecast 850 hPa theta-w; Jersey 500 m radar; rain gauges; St Aubin's stream hydrograph; lightning maps; anemometer traces; the Fawbush and Miller (1954) downdraught gust technique; precipitable water
origin_and_transport_claim: Strong poleward advection of warm air from Iberia occurs ahead of a slow, eastward-moving amplified upper trough and approaching cold front during the summer, the setup of 25 June 2020 being described as displaying Spanish Plume type characteristics
origin_evidence: CITED_ONLY for the Iberian origin, which is supplied as the general definition with citations to Morris (1986), Lewis and Gray (2010) and Holley et al. (2014); the authors' own support is the Met Office analysis chart, the CFS 500 hPa reanalysis and the Global Model 850 hPa theta-w field showing the warm plume, with no trajectory analysis
capping_or_instability_mechanism: Radiosonde profiles displayed potential instability, with wet-bulb potential temperature decreasing with height between 850 and 500 hPa above a comparatively stable boundary layer, and cumulonimbus bases were observed above 6000 ft (1800 m) with the potential for very large CAPE; low sea surface temperatures of 15-17 C around the islands later inhibited further development
capping_or_instability_evidence: DIRECT: the Camborne 1200 utc radiosonde ascent and a Euro 4 km forecast tephigram for Jersey adjusted to the observed Dinard maximum temperature and air mass dew point, together with observed cumulonimbus base heights
initiation_mechanism: Storm development was triggered by high temperatures over northern France (32-34 C, with high dew points around Dinard), likely aided by frictional low-level convergence around a surface trough and an associated shallow low and possibly a sea-breeze front; strong unidirectional flow aloft then decoupled the storms from their generation area around Dinard and carried the cells swiftly across Jersey
initiation_evidence: DIRECT: surface temperature and dew point observations at Dinard and Jersey, the Met Office surface analysis showing the surface trough and shallow low, satellite and 500 m radar tracking of cells from Brittany, and the adjusted forecast tephigram
hazards_locations_and_event_types: Severe thunderstorms across northern France and the Channel Islands between 1700 and 2300 utc on 25 June 2020; torrential rain (30.0 mm in 20 min and 20 mm in 10 min at Route du Sud, radar-derived rates to 120 mm/h), localised surface water and flash flooding with a small number of properties flooded, river flow rising from 0.1 to 4.3 m3/s in 30 minutes, lightning peaking at about 80 strikes per minute, a 45 kn gust at St Helier harbour causing roof damage, and reports of large hail above 5 mm
prefrontal_trough: PRESENT: a surface trough with an associated shallow area of low pressure over northern France lay within the warm plume ahead of the slow-moving frontolytic cold front and supplied the convergence for initiation
key_supporting_quote: a ‘Spanish Plume’ event, where strong poleward advection of warm air from Iberia occurs ahead of a slow, eastward-moving amplified upper trough
limitations_or_uncertainty: Many Jersey rain gauges are non-standard or of unknown exposure; radar-derived rain rates can be inflated by the high reflectivity of hail, although one gauge provided ground truth; the 1-in-20-year return period rests on a report based on 2-hour storm durations so the event may have been rarer; land surface temperature is unrepresentative given sea surface temperatures of 15-17 C; several observations are personal communications or social media reports; the authors note the difficulty of predicting the severity of a thundery breakdown at a local level even when the synoptic-scale possibility is well indicated

airstream_properties: NR for measured properties; the plume is described only as warm and moist air flowing northwards from Iberia in strong southerly flow, and in the restated classic model of Lewis and Gray (2010) as warm moist Iberian air capped by warmer but very dry air from the Spanish plateau
diagnostic_variables: The 30 mean sea level pressure weather patterns of Neal et al. (2016) derived by k-means clustering of EMULATE EMSLP data for 1850-2003 and assigned daily by matching regridded ERA5 1200 utc MSLP; ATDnet lightning fixes for 2010-2019 quality-controlled against Met Office radar; a thunder area defined within a 16 km radius on a 2 km grid, plus thunder intensity and duration; significant thunder days of at least 10000 km2; Wilson score intervals; Spearman rank correlations; thunder day fraction maps
origin_and_transport_claim: Strong southerly flow with air from Iberia coupled with a low-pressure system to the west of Ireland are notable features of the Spanish Plume, which occurs when warm and moist air flows northwards from Iberia and is believed to be the predominant mechanism leading to summertime thunderstorms over Britain and Ireland
origin_evidence: CITED_ONLY: the definition and Iberian origin are attributed to Morris (1986), Lewis and Gray (2010), Sibley (2012), Van Delden (2001) and Piper and Kunz (2017); the authors' own evidence is mean sea level pressure pattern matching, and they conclude that a plume cannot be defined by pressure patterns alone
capping_or_instability_mechanism: The only capping statement is the restatement of Lewis and Gray's classic model, in which warm moist air from Iberia is capped by warmer but very dry air from the Spanish plateau in association with a baroclinic wave on a developing low; the authors' own reasoning uses Doswell's three ingredients of instability, moisture and lift together with the CAPE climatology of Holley et al. (2014)
capping_or_instability_evidence: CITED_ONLY: the cap appears only in the restatement of Lewis and Gray (2010); the study measures lightning occurrence and pressure patterns and makes no stability measurement of its own
initiation_mechanism: NR for the plume; thunderstorm occurrence is attributed generally to the coincidence of instability, moisture and lift, with orographic ascent over the Pennines, Scottish and Welsh hills, warm sea surface temperatures, urban heating and convergence in slack-flow patterns invoked for particular weather patterns
initiation_evidence: INDIRECT: inferred from thunder day fraction maps by weather pattern and season set against orography and coastlines, rather than from case analysis
hazards_locations_and_event_types: Lightning and thunderstorm days over Britain and Ireland 2010-2019; the largest and longest-lived summer outbreaks occur in weather patterns 11, 16 and 22, with 90th percentile thunder areas near 250000 km2 (about 24% of the domain) and median durations of 6-8 hours; listed hazards are flash floods, hailstorms and severe storms, with documented cases including the 2004 Boscastle flood, the Birmingham tornado of 28 July 2005 and the 28 June 2011 Spanish Plume case
key_supporting_quote: these patterns are probably more representative of the modified Spanish Plume from the Lewis and Gray (2010) study.
limitations_or_uncertainty: The authors state that it is difficult to define a Spanish Plume by pressure patterns alone, since plumes may fall into more than one surface pressure pattern (the 28 June 2011 case maps to pattern 6, an Azores high extension), so patterns 16 and 22 are relabelled simply as strong southerly flow; mapping an unlimited variety of observed pressure fields onto 30 climatological mean patterns loses intensity and location detail; several summer patterns have wide Wilson score intervals; 2.8% of ATDnet fixes were removed as false alarms and the network cannot distinguish cloud-to-ground from intracloud flashes; instability and moisture are not included in the scheme

airstream_properties: An elevated mixed layer of well-mixed subtropical mid-tropospheric air, typically from the Iberian plateau but in this episode traced to the Algerian Sahara, producing steep mid-tropospheric lapse rates and high potential instability, with foehn-like adiabatic warming north of the Alps further increasing the lapse rate; integrated water vapour of 30-35 kg/m2 and surface temperatures of 30-35 C in the warm air mass
diagnostic_variables: ESWD quality-controlled severe weather reports; EUCLID/BLIDS lightning; DWD radar maximum reflectivity and RADOLAN precipitation; MSG overshooting-top detections and high-resolution visible satellite imagery; ERA5 500 hPa geopotential height; FU Berlin mean sea level pressure analyses; COSMO-D2 assimilation analyses of integrated water vapour, surface lifted index and the significant hail parameter; storm-relative helicity and deep-layer shear; DWD radiosondes; model backward trajectories; station gust and rainfall records; insurance loss and capital-stock data
origin_and_transport_claim: In Spanish plume situations an elevated mixed layer typically originating from the Iberian plateau is advected to western and central Europe and is lifted dynamically or orographically on the way; for this episode an elevated mixed layer plume from the Algerian Sahara crossed the western Mediterranean and the Alps from 9 to 11 June to reach central and eastern Europe
origin_evidence: DIRECT: model backward trajectories (stated but not shown) trace the elevated mixed layer to the Algerian Sahara across the western Mediterranean and the Alps; the generic Iberian-plateau origin is cited to Morris (1986) and Carlson et al. (1983)
capping_or_instability_mechanism: Advection of the elevated mixed layer created steep mid-tropospheric lapse rates and high potential instability, reinforced by foehn-like adiabatic warming north of the Alps; high low-tropospheric moisture, very high thermal instability and sufficient wind shear supplied the ingredients for organised severe storms, but no lid or convective inhibition is quantified
capping_or_instability_evidence: DIRECT: COSMO-D2 assimilation analyses of integrated water vapour, surface lifted index and significant hail parameter at 1600 utc on each of the three days, together with DWD radiosondes and the backward-trajectory identification of the elevated mixed layer
initiation_mechanism: Large-scale lifting from positive vorticity advection increasing with height downstream of the upper-level trough combined with positive layer thickness advection on 10 and 11 June; vertical lifting along a low-level convergence line at the German-Polish border on 11 and 12 June; additional lifting by the advancing cold front of the low-pressure system Klaus on 12 June; initiation over the eastern lower mountain ranges such as the Bavarian Forest and Ore Mountains
initiation_evidence: DIRECT: mean sea level pressure and 500 hPa analyses, vorticity and thickness advection fields (not shown), the 0000 utc 12 June analysis convergence line, and radar and lightning tracking of where cells formed relative to these features
hazards_locations_and_event_types: Three-day severe convective storm episode of 10-12 June 2019 over Germany and neighbouring countries, concentrated in Bavaria and Saxony; hail to 6 cm at Gilching, gusts to 33.2 m/s, 1-hour rainfall to 69.1 mm and 24-hour totals to 95.9 mm, two tornadoes near Dresden (one F1 damaging 30-40 houses) and a nocturnal mesoscale convective complex near Berlin; 217 German ESWD reports and almost EUR 1.0 billion total loss from the Munich hailstorm alone
key_supporting_quote: The general flow constellation during these days resembled the Spanish plume pattern (Morris, 1986).
limitations_or_uncertainty: The backward trajectories, the vorticity and thickness advection fields and the 12 June convergence line are all stated but not shown; overshooting-top detections use a visible channel and therefore miss nocturnal storms such as the Berlin mesoscale convective complex; ESWD reports are quality-graded with about 11% only plausibility-checked; the authors note that the atmospheric setting would generally have allowed even larger hail and that the largest German hailstones fell on the day when instability, moisture and the hail parameter were lower than on the following two days; no reliable data exist for consumption assets in the loss analysis

airstream_properties: NR: no airstream properties are reported; the configuration said to be especially favourable for severe local storms is described only as a warm east or north-easterly surface wind coupled with a veer with height to a broadly southerly mid-level flow
diagnostic_variables: Daily thunder-day records for Oxford 1828-2019 from Radcliffe Observatory manuscript registers, the published Radcliffe Results, the Monthly Weather Report, MIDAS and a private central Oxford record; comparison series from Brize Norton and west London (Kew, Heathrow, Northolt); objective 1200 utc Lamb Weather Types from Jones et al. (2013); thunder-day to non-thunder-day Lamb Weather Type frequency ratios; daily maximum temperature; correlation coefficients and the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test
origin_and_transport_claim: NR: the only transport statement is that summer storms may be imported into the south Midlands on a Spanish plume heatwave event; no origin or trajectory claim is made
origin_evidence: ASSERTED_ONLY: the plume attribution is asserted without citation, trajectory or air-mass analysis, resting only on the association of south-easterly Lamb Weather Types with thundery conditions in Oxford
capping_or_instability_mechanism: NR for the plume; the author notes only that a warm east or north-easterly surface wind veering with height to a southerly mid-level flow is especially favourable for severe thunderstorms, and that the long land track of surface winds in slack cyclonic northerly, north-easterly or easterly situations raises day temperatures around Oxford
capping_or_instability_evidence: ASSERTED_ONLY: these statements are the author's generalisations from the Oxford record and named case dates; no soundings or stability diagnostics are presented
initiation_mechanism: NR for the plume; when the 500 hPa flow is relatively light, storm initiation is said to tend to occur over the downlands to the south, with local convergence zones forming in slack-pressure and col situations and local convective outbreaks on the periphery of anticyclones
initiation_evidence: INDIRECT: inferred from Lamb Weather Type frequency ratios between thunder and non-thunder days for 1871-2019 and from named example dates (24 May 1989, 17 May 1997, 19 May 1999, 3 August 2004 and 29 June 2005) rather than from case analysis
hazards_locations_and_event_types: Days with thunder heard at Oxford 1828-2019, averaging 11.9 per year and ranging from zero in 1829 to 28 in 1925, with August 1878 the most thundery month at 10 days; 75% of thunder days fall in May to August; comparison records at Brize Norton and west London; the 2010-2019 average of 8.1 days per year is the lowest in almost 150 years
key_supporting_quote: the incidence of certain weather types, particularly southeasterly variants often indicative of Spanish plume events, is of greater predictive value
limitations_or_uncertainty: Dates of occurrence are missing for 1936-1970 because the Met Office archive was closed to visitors, so only monthly totals exist for that period; early manuscript entries may have been missed or illegible and the first two decades appear light relative to London; Monthly Weather Report totals are generally lower than the Radcliffe Results because they often exclude thunder heard without lightning; the observing routine was reduced to once daily from 1925 and thunder reporting ceased in 1987, after which a private record about 4 km away is used; background noise can cause missed or false counts and storms spanning midnight can be double counted; Lamb Weather Types give only a broad-brush picture and the winter thunder sample of 57 days is very small

airstream_properties: Hot southerly winds with thunderstorms moving northwards from Africa and Spain; direct surface heating is lost as the air moves into the Bay of Biscay and across northern Europe so convection becomes elevated with cloud bases typically above about 2000 m (observed near 800 hPa, about 1900 m); boundary-layer flow from the east-north-east at 5-10 kn veering to south-west at about 35 kn at 700 hPa, with warm advection between 750 and 650 hPa
diagnostic_variables: Met Office synoptic pressure and frontal analysis; rain radar showing bow echoes and the Herwijnen Doppler radar; MSG 10.8 micron infrared imagery; Trappes, Ijmuiden, Herstmonceux and Beauvechain radiosonde tephigrams; CAPE (619 J/kg at Trappes, up to about 1300 J/kg estimated over Kent) and DCAPE (about 914 J/kg); one-minute surface pressure, wind and temperature records at Langdon Bay, Manston and Herstmonceux and the Sandettie Light Vessel; Cabauw LIDAR; tide gauges and WERA ocean radar; hydrostatic, gravity-wave and Proudman/Froude calculations; UKV 1.5 km model output
origin_and_transport_claim: Spanish Plume events occur periodically over Europe in spring and summer with hot southerly winds and thunderstorms moving northwards from Africa and Spain; for this case the mesoscale convective system is said to have originated over Spain and the Bay of Biscay before running along the English Channel into the southern North Sea
origin_evidence: INDIRECT: the plume attribution rests on the synoptic analysis chart, which shows a broad warm sector with a surface cold front extending south towards Spain and an upper cold front and pressure trough that had overrun it, together with a citation to Lewis and Gray (2010); the storm's Spanish and Biscay origin is traced from rain-radar imagery rather than from computed trajectories
capping_or_instability_mechanism: Conditional instability is released at medium levels beneath an elevated mesoscale convective system; the upper cold front having overrun the surface cold front indicates a potentially unstable air mass running into the rear of the system, direct surface heating is lost over the Bay of Biscay leaving a stable boundary layer with cloud base near 800 hPa, and cold advection at higher levels further destabilises the vertical profile
capping_or_instability_evidence: DIRECT: the Trappes, Ijmuiden and Herstmonceux tephigrams showing a stable boundary layer, marked directional veer above it, an elevated cloud base near 800 hPa and mid-level warm advection between 750 and 650 hPa, supported by the Cabauw LIDAR and by CAPE and DCAPE estimates
initiation_mechanism: The release of conditional instability that drives the elevated mesoscale convective system results from medium-level warm advection with uplift of the plume along isentropic surfaces together with horizontal convergence, with further enhancement from cold advection at higher levels
initiation_evidence: INDIRECT: the mechanism is given as part of the general plume description with a citation to Lewis and Gray (2010) and is supported by the soundings and synoptic charts; the paper's own analysis concerns the rear-flank downdraft and gravity wave rather than convective initiation
hazards_locations_and_event_types: Meteotsunami of 28-29 May 2017 along the English Channel and North Sea coasts from the Channel Islands and northern France to eastern England, the Netherlands and Germany, with measured amplitude up to 0.88 m, estimated Dutch beach run-up of 2 m, damage to boats and shoreline facilities and harbour seiching; the parent mesoscale convective system brought heavy rain, frequent lightning, a squall line, pressure jumps of 4-6.7 hPa in tens of minutes and a gust of 72 kn (37 m/s) at the Sandettie Light Vessel
prefrontal_trough: PRESENT: an upper cold front and pressure trough over northern France and the English Channel lay within the broad warm sector, having evidently overrun the surface cold front
key_supporting_quote: These events occur periodically over Europe in the spring and summer months, with hot, southerly, winds and thunderstorms moving northwards from Africa and Spain
limitations_or_uncertainty: The Trappes and Beauvechain soundings were taken ahead of the storm so they cannot capture the cold advection at its rear, and the Herstmonceux ascent failed above 700 hPa; automated CAPE from Trappes (619 J/kg) differs from the chief forecaster's estimate of up to 1300 J/kg over Kent; the DCAPE, gravity-wave speed and hydrostatic pressure-rise calculations are approximations using several estimated parameters; tide gauges averaged over 10 minutes did not capture the full wave height and the 2 m figure is a run-up estimate; the two UKV runs diverged and neither generated the observed 5 hPa meso-high; no coupled ocean-atmosphere model is operational and ensemble modelling was not assessed

airstream_properties: Low-level south-westerly flow in the prefrontal zone of an approaching cold front, mid-level warm dry air from the Iberian peninsula and westerly upper-level cooler Atlantic air, giving high CAPE and directional wind shear; no measured plume values are reported, and south-westerly flow more generally is said to carry warm, humid Mediterranean air with high CAPE and moisture
diagnostic_variables: The five-radar Swiss Rad4Alp polarimetric C-band network for 2016-2020 supplying 2-D maximum reflectivity and 3-D dealiased Doppler velocity via the R2D2 algorithm; the T-DaTing thunderstorm detection and tracking algorithm; a new mesocyclone detection algorithm requiring vorticity of at least 1e-2 per second, rotational velocity of at least 10 m/s and a 3000 m signature depth; COSMO-1 analyses; the eight-class GrossWetterTypes 500 hPa flow classification; a digital elevation model; a radar network quality index; vertically integrated liquid
origin_and_transport_claim: In the Spanish plume constellation the low-level south-westerly flow lies in the prefrontal zone of an approaching cold front over France, the mid-level flow supplies warm dry air stemming from the Iberian peninsula, and the upper-level flow is westerly with cooler Atlantic air
origin_evidence: CITED_ONLY: the plume description is attributed to Morris (1986) and Peyraud (2013); the study's own evidence is the GrossWetterTypes 500 hPa flow class assigned to each mesocyclone day, not an air-mass origin analysis
capping_or_instability_mechanism: Warm dry Iberian air above the low-level south-westerly flow is said to produce high amounts of CAPE, while the vertical change in flow direction supplies directional wind shear beneficial to mesocyclone development; more generally, afternoon upslope winds cause convergence over ridges that provides the initial lift needed to overcome convective inhibition
capping_or_instability_evidence: CITED_ONLY: the CAPE and shear statements for the plume rest on Morris (1986) and Peyraud (2013); the study itself measures no thermodynamic variables, only radar-derived rotation and synoptic flow classes
initiation_mechanism: In plume situations lifting is provided by the approaching front; across the domain generally, topographically induced valley-wind systems and afternoon upslope convergence over ridges supply the lift needed to overcome convective inhibition
initiation_evidence: INDIRECT: inferred from mapped mesocyclone initiation points and thunderstorm density set against topography and the radar quality index, and from the fraction of days in each flow class producing a mesocyclone; the frontal lifting statement is cited
hazards_locations_and_event_types: Mesocyclones and supercell thunderstorms in the Swiss radar domain from April to October 2016-2020, averaging 690 detections, 80 storm tracks and 22 active days per year, with hotspots in the Southern Prealps and Ticino and secondary maxima in the Napf area, Zurich Oberland and the Bernese Alps; associated hazards are lightning, downbursts, severe precipitation, hail and tornadoes, the latter occurring about once a year in Switzerland and mostly rated F0
prefrontal_trough: UNCLEAR: the low-level south-westerly flow is placed in the prefrontal zone of an approaching cold front, but no prefrontal trough is identified
key_supporting_quote: the mid-level flow supplies warm, dry air stemming from the Iberian peninsula; and the upper-level flow is westerly, with cooler, Atlantic air
limitations_or_uncertainty: Radar beam blockage and terrain lower the quality index, particularly over the Jura and the main Alpine ridge, where confirmed mesocyclones such as the Neuchatel tornado case are missed; the quality index is qualitative and does not correct for detection gaps; range-dependent thresholds lower the vorticity requirement with distance from the radars; only five years of data are analysed, which may explain discrepancies between rotation strength and hail size in the Bernese Alps and Zurich Oberland; the GrossWetterTypes classification uses synoptic-scale 500 hPa flow so the steering-level flow can deviate from it, and a fraction of Spanish plume events may be classified as westerly flow

airstream_properties: NR: no airstream description is given; the only related content is that the summertime quasi-linear composite has high CAPE over continental Europe
diagnostic_variables: 71 tide gauges across northwest Europe for 2010-2017 at 5-15 min intervals processed with manual filtering, automatic peak detection and a stacking algorithm to remove tidal signals against a 6 sigma threshold; a northwest European radar mosaic with derived precipitation used to classify mesoscale systems as isolated cells, nonlinear clusters, quasi-linear systems or open cells; ERA5 0.25 degree composites of sea level pressure, 500 hPa geopotential height, the 850 hPa minus sea surface temperature difference and CAPE; 700 hPa wind speed compared with shallow-water wave speed to infer Proudman resonance
origin_and_transport_claim: NR: no origin or transport claim is made; the plume is invoked only as a resemblance for the summertime quasi-linear synoptic composite
origin_evidence: CITED_ONLY: the resemblance is asserted against Carlson and Ludlam (1968), Morris (1986) and Lewis and Gray (2010); the composite itself shows only pressure, geopotential height, air-sea temperature difference and CAPE fields
capping_or_instability_mechanism: NR for the plume; the paper reports only stronger CAPE over land for the summer meteotsunamis and lower-tropospheric static instability for winter cases, inferred where 850 hPa air is more than 13 C colder than the sea surface
capping_or_instability_evidence: DIRECT for the paper's own ERA5 composites of CAPE occurrence and the 850 hPa minus sea surface temperature difference across 45 French meteotsunami events; NR for any plume-related capping, which is not examined
initiation_mechanism: NR: convective initiation is not analysed; summertime quasi-linear systems are noted to include mesoscale convective systems while winter quasi-linear cases include narrow cold-frontal rainbands
initiation_evidence: NR: no initiation analysis is presented
hazards_locations_and_event_types: Meteotsunamis across northwest Europe 2010-2017: 13080 threshold exceedances at 71 tide gauges, 2339 non-seismic sea level oscillations at tidal timescales and 349 meteotsunamis (54.0 per year), with median wave heights of 0.27-0.40 m by country, the three largest about 1 m at Le Havre and 79% below 0.5 m; most occur in winter and the largest most often in France and the Republic of Ireland
key_supporting_quote: The quasi-linear summertime synoptic composite presented here has high CAPE over continental Europe and is broadly consistent with a Spanish Plume pattern
limitations_or_uncertainty: Tide gauge sampling intervals of 5-15 min are long compared with meteotsunami periods of 2-120 min so wave heights are probably underestimated, and the 15 min UK interval is judged too long for a representative climatology although the analysis cannot say what interval would suffice; the synoptic composites cover only 45 events on the French coastline; the specificity and sensitivity of the radar-only classification are not quantified and 29 of 378 large events could not be linked to a precipitating feature

airstream_properties: NR: the air mass is described only as an unstable continental air mass affecting south-east England; no airstream properties are given
diagnostic_variables: NR: the article is a career retrospective presenting no analysis dataset; the forecasting tools it describes are hand-drawn radio-facsimile charts, teleprinter observations, numerical model output and satellite and radar imagery
origin_and_transport_claim: NR: no origin or transport claim is made
origin_evidence: NR: no evidence is offered; the term is used only to label a remembered forecasting shift
capping_or_instability_mechanism: NR for capping; the author notes only that the continental air mass was unstable
capping_or_instability_evidence: ASSERTED_ONLY: a personal recollection with no charts, soundings or data presented
initiation_mechanism: NR: unexpected cyclogenesis in the unstable continental air mass is given as what produced the storms, with no analysis of convective initiation
initiation_evidence: ASSERTED_ONLY: personal recollection of the shift, with no observations or analyses presented
hazards_locations_and_event_types: A Spanish Plume overnight on 13/14 June 1980 bringing widespread heavy thunderstorms, frequent lightning and torrential rain to south-east England in the early hours, necessitating the diversion of early morning flights at Heathrow and flooding the airport access tunnel
key_supporting_quote: An early solo shift etched in my mind was a 'Spanish Plume' overnight on 13/14 June 1980 involving cyclogenesis that was totally unexpected.
limitations_or_uncertainty: The account is an informal personal retrospective containing no data or analysis; the author notes more generally that thunderstorms and fog remain situations in which forecast detail is difficult even a few hours ahead, and that a key remaining role of the forecaster is spotting where models give misleading guidance

airstream_properties: NR for measured properties; the plume is described only as southerly and south-westerly flow bringing warm moist air to the study area, or as plumes of warm summer air tracking in from the continent
diagnostic_variables: Total lightning (cloud-to-ground and cloud-cloud) from three ground-based lightning location systems, LINET, ATDnet and Meteorage, for 2008-2019; flash density per km2 per year and thunderstorm days; k-means clustering of seasonal flash-density distributions into seven regions; seasonal and diurnal distributions by region and network; the 30 Met Office weather patterns of Neal et al. (2016) assigned to the highest flash-count days; sea surface temperatures
origin_and_transport_claim: Spanish plume mesoscale convective systems are known to travel most often north-eastward from the European continent into the UK overnight, the classic type tracking from the Bay of Biscay into south-east England, the modified type propagating south to north, and the European easterly plume running north-west from northern France to south-east England and occurring less often
origin_evidence: CITED_ONLY: the plume types, tracks and characteristics are taken from Lewis and Gray (2010) with Gray and Marshall (1998) and Holley et al. (2014); the study's own evidence is regional lightning flash density and thunderstorm day distributions, which it interprets as consistent with these tracks
configuration: CLASSIC+MODIFIED+EUROPEAN_EASTERLY: all three Lewis and Gray (2010) types are tabulated as thunderstorm environments in the study's Table 1, but no case in the study is assigned to a particular type
capping_or_instability_mechanism: NR for the plume; instability is discussed only generically, with summer thunderstorms driven by solar heating of the land, winter storms forced by warm sea surface temperatures, and a shallower winter troposphere, reduced ground heating and lower atmospheric moisture limiting winter storm intensity
capping_or_instability_evidence: NR for the plume: no stability diagnostic is computed; the paper's own instability reasoning is INDIRECT, inferred from seasonal and diurnal flash-density and thunderstorm-day patterns and from December sea surface temperatures of 10-12 C
initiation_mechanism: NR for the plume; the paper attributes regional lightning to solar heating of land, sea-surface forcing, sea and land breeze circulations and frontal lifting, as listed in its table of thunderstorm environments
initiation_evidence: INDIRECT: inferred from the correspondence between regional seasonal and diurnal flash-density and thunderstorm-day distributions and established thunderstorm-generating phenomena, and from the weather patterns assigned to the highest flash-count days
hazards_locations_and_event_types: Lightning and thunderstorm days across seven k-means regions covering the UK, Ireland, the English Channel and adjoining northern France, 2008-2019; the highest regional flash counts for regions 4, 6 and 7 occurred on 17 July 2014 and 2 July 2009 under weather pattern 16, labelled Spanish Plume, while on 3 June 2018 a possible Spanish Plume style event was confined to the north-west coast of France by a blocking high; listed thunderstorm hazards are lightning, heavy rainfall, hail, thunder-snow, strong winds and tornadoes
key_supporting_quote: much more intense thunderstorms which are known to travel from France overnight into the UK during Spanish Plume events (Lewis & Gray, 2010).
limitations_or_uncertainty: The three lightning location systems use different technologies and detection efficiencies so flash magnitudes differ between them even where distributions agree; regions 6 and 7 lie at the fringe of sensor coverage where diurnal distributions differ between networks and cannot be interpreted with certainty; using a single network could not reveal such inhomogeneities; the k-means regionalisation is acknowledged to warrant further work; thunderstorm mechanisms are inferred from lightning distributions rather than directly observed

airstream_properties: South-westerly mid-level flow advecting milder air north-eastwards above a cool north-easterly surface flow confined below 900 hPa, with very marked wind shear at the interface, a warm nose between 850 and 650 hPa and wet-bulb potential temperature decreasing gradually with height to about 550 hPa
diagnostic_variables: Met Office surface pressure and frontal analysis for 0000 utc on 19 June 2022; the Camborne 1200 utc radiosonde of 18 June 2022 read for wind, temperature and wet-bulb potential temperature structure; a surface pressure time series from an amateur weather station at Wokingham; tide gauge records including Boulogne-sur-Mer; media video reports; the shallow-water wave speed relation and Proudman resonance
origin_and_transport_claim: The south-westerly mid-level flow above the north-easterly surface flow continued to advect milder air north-eastwards, which the author says can be thought of as a modified Spanish Plume event; no source region is named
origin_evidence: DIRECT for the flow structure, read from the Met Office frontal analysis and the Camborne sounding showing the cool north-easterly flow below 900 hPa with milder south-westerly flow above; ASSERTED_ONLY for the modified Spanish Plume label itself, which is offered without citation, source region or trajectory analysis
capping_or_instability_mechanism: A rearward-sloping cold front with a cool north-easterly airflow undercutting milder air above produced a warm nose between 850 and 650 hPa coincident with gradually decreasing wet-bulb potential temperature to about 550 hPa, indicating potential instability above 650 hPa
capping_or_instability_evidence: DIRECT: the Camborne 1200 utc radiosonde ascent of 18 June 2022, read for wind, temperature and wet-bulb potential temperature structure
initiation_mechanism: The potential instability above 650 hPa was released through forced uplift along the frontal surface, with the resulting convective downdraughts descending to lower levels and hydrostatically generating boundary-layer gravity waves that moved against the surface flow and produced surface pressure anomalies acting on the sea
initiation_evidence: INDIRECT: inferred from the sounding structure and the observed surface pressure oscillations, with the downdraught and gravity-wave mechanism carried over from Sibley et al. (2021)
hazards_locations_and_event_types: Meteotsunamis on 18-19 June 2022 with unusual tidal movements in Cork Harbour, Ireland and at Solva in Pembrokeshire, followed by seiching in Cork Harbour; surface pressure variation of about 4.5 hPa at Wokingham with thundery outbreaks over south-east England; tide gauge oscillations of 50-60 cm along the Channel coast and over 60 cm at Boulogne-sur-Mer
key_supporting_quote: In that sense, it can be thought of as a modified ‘Spanish Plume’ event.
limitations_or_uncertainty: A short spotlight note whose mechanism is stated in consistently hedged terms (waves are likely to have been generated, downdrafts are likely to have descended, seiching appears to have taken place) and which rests on a single radiosonde ascent, one amateur pressure trace and tide gauge records, with no modelling and no quantitative resonance calculation

airstream_properties: NR: no airstream properties are given; the only related attribute sought is a warm 2 m temperature anomaly over western Europe and North Africa
diagnostic_variables: Seasonal 1-day rainfall maxima for 1950-2017 at 125 locations across Great Britain from the CEH-GEAR dataset; daily NCEP/NCAR Reanalysis 1 mean sea level pressure and 2 m air temperature on a 2.5 degree grid over 10-70 N and 100 W to 20 E, standardised by calendar-month mean and standard deviation into 48 by 24 cell anomaly fields and clustered after flattening and concatenation; wind components and 500 hPa geopotential heights for interpretation; NAO and AMO indices; two-sided Student t tests; regional maps for 13 administrative regions
origin_and_transport_claim: NR: no origin or transport claim is made; the study only entertains the possibility that temperatures over North Africa might yield a separate summer cluster corresponding to a Spanish Plume mechanism
origin_evidence: NR: the study deliberately extended its domain over part of North Africa to test for such a cluster but reports that the rarity of these events makes it difficult to link them to any particular class, so no origin evidence is produced
capping_or_instability_mechanism: NR: no instability or capping variable is analysed; heavy rainfall in the classes is instead attributed to fronts and cyclone centres, with the temperature contrast between warm southerly air and colder air to the north-west said to provide ideal conditions
capping_or_instability_evidence: NR: only sea level pressure, 2 m temperature, wind and 500 hPa geopotential height anomalies are examined, with no stability diagnostic
initiation_mechanism: NR for the plume; heavy rainfall in the classes is associated with the fronts of eastward or north-eastward tracking cyclones and with the cold front or low-pressure centre of mid-latitude cyclones
initiation_evidence: INDIRECT: inferred from composite anomaly pressure, temperature, wind and upper-level flow patterns and from the geographical distribution of events, rather than from case analysis
hazards_locations_and_event_types: Heavy daily rainfall events and associated flooding across Great Britain 1950-2017, classified into four summer and three winter classes with occurrence mapped over 13 administrative regions; mesoscale convective systems such as those associated with the Spanish Plume are said to occur mainly in southern Britain
key_supporting_quote: Mesoscale convective systems, such as associated with the Spanish Plume (e.g., Lewis and Gray, 2010), mainly occur in southern Britain.
limitations_or_uncertainty: The authors state that the rarity of these events makes it difficult to link them to any particular class even though some classes have warmer average temperature anomalies over western Europe and North Africa; no seasonal maximum was extracted for each class so a formal frequency analysis could not be performed; spatial dependence means heavy rainfall events co-occur on the same day so only unique dates were used; the daily reanalysis fields precede the rainfall day by several hours

airstream_properties: NR for the plume beyond the displaced elevated mixed layer from the Iberian Peninsula; the paper's own violent-tornado profiles report steep lapse rates, mean mixing ratio of 12.6 g/kg, mean CAPE around 1650-1678 J/kg, mean convective inhibition around -30 J/kg, mean 0-6 km shear around 24 m/s and LCL near 1000 m above ground
diagnostic_variables: ERA5 reanalysis and WRF dynamical downscaling to 3 km grid spacing on model levels for 12 European violent tornado cases between 1957 and 2021; composite-reflectivity screening of warm-sector inflow profiles within 100 km and 3 h of the report, averaged over 15 km circles; convective parameters including CAPE, CIN, 0-6 km and 0-1 km shear, 0-3 km storm-relative helicity, LCL, mixing ratio and hodographs; simulated updraft helicity tracks
origin_and_transport_claim: High-CAPE and high-shear situations are rare in Europe and are typically associated with the Spanish Plume setup displacing the elevated mixed layer from the Iberian Peninsula into western and central Europe
origin_evidence: CITED_ONLY: the statement is supported by citations to Hamid (2012), Mathias et al. (2017) and van Delden (2001); the study's own simulations reconstruct tornado environments and diagnose no plume
capping_or_instability_mechanism: NR for a plume cap; the paper reports a weak resistance to convective initiation with mean convective inhibition around -30 J/kg and steep lapse rates in both WRF and ERA5 mean profiles, and notes that two cases occurred in high-shear low-CAPE environments
capping_or_instability_evidence: DIRECT for the paper's own WRF and ERA5 proximity profiles of temperature, dew point, CAPE and CIN across the 12 cases; CITED_ONLY for the plume attribution
initiation_mechanism: NR for the plume; tornado reports were typically located in the warm sector on the eastern flank of an approaching trough, often in an area of upper-level divergence with mid-tropospheric south-westerly flow, while two high-shear low-CAPE cases involved strong synoptic-scale lift
initiation_evidence: DIRECT: synoptic composites for the 12 cases plus WRF simulations that produced updraft helicity tracks in a favourable convective environment within 50 km and 3 h of the report in 8 of 12 cases
hazards_locations_and_event_types: Violent tornadoes in Europe, about 1-3 per decade, with 12 cases reconstructed between 1957 and 2021 including 1957, 1960, 1979, 2008, 2015 and 2021
key_supporting_quote: typically associated with the ‘Spanish Plume’ setup displacing elevated mixed-layer from the Iberian Peninsula into Western and Central Europe
limitations_or_uncertainty: Only 12 cases could be reconstructed and the older ones rest on reanalysis of sparse historical observations; ERA5 and WRF differ, with hodograph curvature and storm-relative helicity enhanced in WRF (mean 92 against 62 m2/s2); CAPE varies between cases by more than an order of magnitude, from 100-300 J/kg in 2008 to 2500-3500 J/kg in 2021; single-grid profiles can be contaminated by nearby convective cells so 15 km circle means were used; in 4 of 12 simulations no updraft helicity track appeared in a favourable environment

airstream_properties: NR: no airstream properties are reported; the plume is named only as a class of continental weather system that may affect the United Kingdom
diagnostic_variables: Long-range lightning location network data combined with surface observations of thunder to generate gridded days of thunder for the United Kingdom, with a 30-year average for 1990-2019 and rolling 10-year averages; seasonal gridded climatologies; differences between the 1990-1999 and 2010-2019 means; Sen's slope analysis with two-tailed p-value significance; regional aggregation into north land, south land, sea and land
origin_and_transport_claim: NR: no origin or transport claim is made; plume events are suggested only as a possible contributor to the relatively high autumn days of thunder over the English Channel
origin_evidence: CITED_ONLY: the suggestion is explicitly hedged as there may also be some impact, and is supported only by citations to Carlson and Ludlam (1968) and Lewis and Gray (2010)
capping_or_instability_mechanism: NR: no capping or instability variable is analysed; the autumn English Channel maximum is attributed mainly to the relatively higher surface temperature of the sea compared with the land in those months
capping_or_instability_evidence: NR: the study uses lightning and surface thunder observations only, with no thermodynamic data
initiation_mechanism: NR for the plume; regional and seasonal differences are attributed to solar heating of the land in summer and to relatively warm sea surface temperatures in autumn and winter
initiation_evidence: INDIRECT: inferred from the seasonal and spatial distribution of gridded days of thunder rather than measured
hazards_locations_and_event_types: Days of thunder across the United Kingdom and surrounding seas 1990-2019, with a maximum of about 20 per year over France, a minimum of 0-1 per year over the sea and about 10 per year over most UK land; associated hazards listed are lightning, hail, severe wind, tornadoes and heavy rain; there is an overall reduction of about one day with a north-south divide near 54 N
key_supporting_quote: some impact from continental weather systems impacting the United Kingdom, such as “Spanish plume” events (Carlson and Ludlam, 1968; Lewis and Gray, 2010).
limitations_or_uncertainty: The lightning location network data are described as precise but inconsistent and the surface thunder observations as less precise but more consistent, so the two had to be combined and normalised; earlier published climatologies were limited by short records or extrapolation from low-resolution surface data; the attribution of the autumn English Channel maximum to plume events is explicitly hedged; the detected trends are small, around 0.5 to 1 day, relative to the record length

airstream_properties: NR for the plume itself; the associated environment is described only as advection of very warm air with steep lapse rates and an elevated mixed layer, commonly referred to as a loaded gun profile
diagnostic_variables: Cloud-to-ground lightning flashes from the Polish PERUN network for 2002-2019 divided into intensity categories by peak 1-minute flash rate and collocated with proximal ERA5 profiles; most unstable CAPE, convective inhibition, 0-6 km deep-layer shear, 0-1 km low-level shear, 0-3 km storm-relative helicity and the MUWMAXSHEAR composite; ESWD severe weather reports; diurnal, seasonal and spatial distributions with medians and probability tables
origin_and_transport_claim: NR: no origin or transport claim is made; the plume is named only as the synoptic setup with which loaded-gun environments in Europe are often associated
origin_evidence: CITED_ONLY: attributed to Carlson and Ludlam (1968), Van Delden (2001) and Mathias et al. (2017); the study itself diagnoses ERA5 convective parameters rather than any plume structure
capping_or_instability_mechanism: Stronger convective inhibition is said to promote stronger moisture pooling, higher convective instability, better storm organisation and more sudden development of convective updrafts and hence higher flash rates; environments favourable for extreme thunderstorms often involve advection of very warm air with steep lapse rates and an elevated mixed layer, a loaded gun profile, while strong inhibition at night is instead linked to well organised elevated thunderstorms initiating above a stable layer
capping_or_instability_evidence: DIRECT for the paper's own ERA5 convective inhibition, CAPE and shear distributions by flash-rate category, hour and month; CITED_ONLY for the plume attribution
initiation_mechanism: NR for the plume; higher flash rates are attributed to a more sudden development of convective updrafts after stronger inhibition has allowed moisture pooling, while nocturnal extreme thunderstorms are attributed to elevated convection initiating above a stable layer without strong mixed-layer or surface-based inhibition
initiation_evidence: DIRECT: 18 years of PERUN flash-rate categories collocated with proximal ERA5 profiles and analysed by month and hour
hazards_locations_and_event_types: Cloud-to-ground lightning and thunderstorms over Poland 2002-2019, most frequent in July between 1400 and 1600 UTC and over the south-eastern part of the country; higher flash rates are shown to be associated more frequently with severe weather reports of hail, tornado and wind, and derechos and tornadic supercells are noted as causing considerable material losses
key_supporting_quote: These environments in Europe are often associated with “Spanish plume” synoptic setups (Carlson and Ludlam 1968; Van Delden 2001; Mathias et al. 2017).
limitations_or_uncertainty: Differences in deep-layer shear, low-level shear and storm-relative helicity between thunderstorm categories are small, which the authors say demonstrates limited utility in forecasting specific flash rates from kinematic parameters alone; ERA5 proximity profiles are a reanalysis approximation of the storm environment; the flash-rate categories rest on a single national detection network over 18 years

airstream_properties: NR for the plume airstream beyond a brisk south or south-westerly airflow at 500 hPa; for the 20 July 2021 case the paper reports light west or north-west surface winds over the western and south Midlands, light east or north-easterly winds further north-east, and a sharp veer to westerly above 925 hPa with a 23 kn increase in strength between 925 and 500 hPa
diagnostic_variables: Met Office Ingham 1 km radar reflectivity panels at 2 degree elevation for 1711-1741 utc; the Nottingham 1200 utc radiosonde ascent, adjusted for observed afternoon maxima of 29-32 C to give 1000-1500 J/kg of CAPE; 500 and 300 hPa charts showing a short-wave upper trough and discrete cold pool; hourly surface wind observations; a hodograph; rainfall and hail reports; TORRO severe thunderstorm watches and UK hailstorm climatologies
origin_and_transport_claim: NR for the 20 July 2021 case, whose heat is attributed to anticyclonic subsidence and seasonally strong insolation rather than advection of hot air from the south; nearly all previous UK occasions of 50 mm or larger hail are said to have had a synoptic set-up with features of the Spanish Plume scenario, namely a major upper trough to the west of these islands and a brisk south or south-westerly airflow at 500 hPa
origin_evidence: CITED_ONLY for the plume characterisation, drawn from Carlson and Ludlam (1968), Clark and Smart (2016) and the hail climatology of Webb et al. (2009); DIRECT for the contrasting 2021 synoptic description, taken from the author's own reading of the 500 and 300 hPa charts, surface observations and radar
configuration: CLASSIC: the plume scenario referred to is described as a major upper trough to the west of these islands with a brisk south or south-westerly 500 hPa airflow, but the storms of 20 July 2021 are explicitly said to have differed considerably, with a major upper trough further east over Europe and storm tracks from west-north-west to east-south-east
capping_or_instability_mechanism: NR for a plume cap; for the 2021 case the Nottingham ascent showed instability through a deep layer from 850 hPa to above 300 hPa, with a parcel-environment difference already over 6 degC at mid levels, giving 1000-1500 J/kg of CAPE after adjustment for the afternoon maxima
capping_or_instability_evidence: DIRECT for the 2021 case: the 1200 utc Nottingham radiosonde adjusted for observed afternoon maximum temperatures, together with 500 and 300 hPa charts showing a discrete cold pool over the Humber; NR for any plume capping
initiation_mechanism: A shallow heat low developed over the English Midlands within a slack belt of high pressure while a short-wave upper trough with a discrete cold pool drifted south-south-east over eastern England; local convergence and backing of surface winds along convergence zones supplied lift and directional shear, with speed shear of 23 kn between 925 and 500 hPa sufficient for organised multicell and possibly supercell storms
initiation_evidence: DIRECT: hourly surface observations at 1500 and 1600 utc showing the convergent wind field, upper-air charts, the Nottingham ascent, a hodograph and Met Office Ingham radar sequences showing cell splitting into right- and left-moving members
hazards_locations_and_event_types: Severe hailstorms on 20 July 2021 across England from South Yorkshire to Kent and from west Norfolk to Northamptonshire; at Kibworth, Leicestershire, 72 mm of rain fell from 1700 to 1815 utc with prolonged hail of 45-50 mm diameter and local flooding; 30-40 mm hail near Thaxted, Essex, 20-25 mm hail at March and 44 mm of rain at RAF Marham; comparison events include 28 June 2012 (50 mm hail with conglomerates to 90 mm), 24 July 1994 and 11 May 1945
key_supporting_quote: nearly all these occasions (which include the 1945, 1994 and 2012 episodes) had a synoptic set up with features of the ‘Spanish Plume’ scenario
limitations_or_uncertainty: Described by the author as a preliminary analysis; the nearest radar at Ingham is 93 km north-north-east of Kibworth; the left-splitting supercell interpretation is hedged as one that may have been associated with the event and rests on personal communications; CAPE is an adjustment of a 1200 utc ascent for afternoon maxima rather than a measurement; several details derive from personal communications and the TORRO forum

airstream_properties: A tongue of air with high 850 hPa wet-bulb potential temperature above 18 C extending into the UK from the south, against about 14 C in the original Atlantic cold front; a warm continental plume supporting elevated or mid-level instability, with a low-latitude origin in Iberia and further south and very steep lapse rates at medium levels
diagnostic_variables: Operational weather radar network imagery; Meteosat visible, infrared and water vapour imagery with cloud-top temperatures; limited area model 850 hPa wet-bulb potential temperature and 6-hour rainfall totals; 15 km mesoscale model forecasts of dynamic and convective rain, convective cloud tops and 10 m winds; fine mesh model sea-level pressure and precipitation rate; surface analyses, wind observations and streamlines identifying convergence zones; lightning reports; forecast upper air maps
origin_and_transport_claim: The low latitude origin, in Iberia and further south, of the airflows that characterise such events was recognised and described by Douglas and Harding (1946), including the very steep lapse rate at medium levels; the thundery rain develops in a separate warm Spanish plume ahead of the original Atlantic cold front, with convection over Biscay expanding into a large rain area over the UK and France
origin_evidence: CITED_ONLY: the origin statement is attributed to Douglas and Harding (1946), the term itself credited to Carlson and Ludlam (1968) and its revival to Morris (1986), and the supporting figures are reproduced from Morris (1986) and Young (1995) rather than newly analysed here
capping_or_instability_mechanism: Elevated or mid-level instability, typically associated with continental air masses, with very steep lapse rates at medium levels within the warm plume; in the 20 May 1986 case the convection diagnosed over Britain and France was primarily elevated instability within a warm continental plume, in contrast to surface-based instability beneath an upper trough in the cool air mass over Ireland
capping_or_instability_evidence: INDIRECT: the elevated-instability characterisation is taken from Douglas and Harding (1946) and from the reproduced model diagnostics of Morris (1986), supported by the 850 hPa wet-bulb potential temperature field and forecast convective cloud-top chart rather than by soundings presented here
initiation_mechanism: Low-level convergence zones which, when combined with surface-based convection, could provide a trigger; in the 24 June 1994 case a convergence zone extending from southern England into northern France with convective rain likely associated with diurnal heating over France; overnight plume developments are said to be dominated exclusively by convection triggered well above the surface by processes that were poorly understood and remain so
initiation_evidence: INDIRECT: the 1994 example is supported by reproduced mesoscale model convergence-zone forecasts, half-hourly Meteosat images showing rapidly expanding very cold cloud tops, lightning reports and radar echoes from Young (1995); the statement that overnight plume convection is triggered well above the surface by poorly understood processes is asserted without evidence
hazards_locations_and_event_types: Thunderstorms and severe thunderstorms over the UK, France and Biscay in Spanish Plume situations, illustrated by the 20 May 1986 case of Morris (1986) and by the severe thunderstorms of 24 June 1994 that moved north-north-east into south-east England and prompted severe weather warnings (Young, 1995); also unpredicted hailstorms along the south coast of England immediately east of a small upper cold pool (Hill, 1984)
prefrontal_trough: UNCLEAR: a sharpening upper trough to the west and a convergence zone from southern England into northern France are reported, and the plume is placed ahead of the original Atlantic cold front, but no prefrontal trough is identified
key_supporting_quote: The low latitude origin (Iberia and further south) of the airflows that characterise such events was recognised and described by Douglas and Harding (1946)
limitations_or_uncertainty: A historical review rather than a new analysis, with figures reproduced from Booth (1984), Monk (1987), Morris (1986) and Young (1995); the authors note in a footnote that model guidance had been inconsistent in such cases and record one author's recollection of a subsequent model run reverting to a more diurnal convective treatment; overnight Spanish Plume developments are stated to remain particularly problematic because the above-surface triggering processes were and remain poorly understood; mesoscale model products were slow to reach outstations and initial confidence in them was probably low

airstream_properties: NR: no airstream properties are given; the associated instability is described only as elevated instability
diagnostic_variables: Archived Central Forecasting Office surface analyses and 24-, 48- and 72-hour forecast charts with 1000/500 hPa thickness contours; Met Office 10-level model prognoses at 1000 and 500 hPa for 48 and 72 hours, with occasional US and German products; Meteosat imagery from 1977 and earlier polar-orbiting satellite imagery; bogus humidity observations inserted into the model; forecaster recollections and personal communications
origin_and_transport_claim: NR: no origin or transport claim is made; the only structural statement is that an expanding area of medium cloud over western France was a northward-moving internal frontal system associated with a Spanish Plume that gave heavy thunderstorms in south-east England later that day
origin_evidence: INDIRECT: that identification is made from a reproduced Meteosat infrared image and synoptic chart for 0600 utc 30 May 1979 taken from Moore (1980); no air-mass or trajectory analysis is presented, and the term itself is credited to Carlson and Ludlam (1968) and Morris (1986)
capping_or_instability_mechanism: NR for capping; the thunderstorms of 13/14 June 1980 are attributed only to elevated instability
capping_or_instability_evidence: ASSERTED_ONLY: elevated instability is named in the author's recollection of the shift and in a reproduced figure caption, with no soundings or stability diagnostics presented
initiation_mechanism: NR: unanticipated cyclogenesis, occurring some 9-12 hours ahead of expectation and producing a much deeper depression than anticipated, is given as the development that produced the storms; no convective initiation analysis is offered
initiation_evidence: INDIRECT: based on the author's recollection of the forecasting failure together with archived charts and, for the earlier 1979 case, reproduced satellite imagery and a synoptic chart
hazards_locations_and_event_types: Unexpectedly severe thunderstorms linked to elevated instability on 13/14 June 1980 requiring many short-notice warnings and causing major disruption to early morning flights from Heathrow and other south-east England airfields as well as flooding the main road tunnel into Heathrow; heavy thunderstorms in south-east England on 30 May 1979 associated with a northward-moving internal frontal system
key_supporting_quote: cyclogenesis occurred in what would some years later become familiar to forecasters as a ‘Spanish Plume’ (Carlson and Ludlam, 1968; Morris, 1986).
limitations_or_uncertainty: An informal historical account relying partly on personal recollection and personal communications, with figures reproduced from earlier publications; the authors note that major synoptic errors were quite common less than 24 hours ahead in this era, that blocking patterns were very poorly handled at medium range, and that subjective modification of model output was routinely needed

airstream_properties: NR: described only as a thundery Spanish plume arriving from the south
diagnostic_variables: Archived Central Forecasting Office surface analyses and 24-hour forecast charts, some reproduced from The Guardian newspaper; output of the early operational numerical models, which are noted to have been devoid of moisture; ship reports; early satellite imagery from 1966 onwards; personal communications and recollections
origin_and_transport_claim: NR beyond the plume arriving from the south; the authors state that the background to and importance of the Spanish plume are described in a later paper of the series
origin_evidence: CITED_ONLY: the plume is attributed to Salter (1968) and its background explicitly deferred to a later paper in the series; no origin analysis is presented here
capping_or_instability_mechanism: NR: no capping or instability discussion; development in such cases is said only to have been enhanced through latent heat release as well as embedded convection
capping_or_instability_evidence: NR: no stability data are presented, and the model of the time is noted to have been devoid of moisture so that it could not reasonably have been expected to reproduce such developments
initiation_mechanism: NR for the plume; the flooding events are attributed to the combination of cyclogenesis with a thundery plume arriving from the south, with development enhanced by latent heat release and embedded convection
initiation_evidence: INDIRECT: inferred from archived surface analyses and 24-hour forecast charts compared against what occurred, together with the cited account of Salter (1968)
hazards_locations_and_event_types: Serious flooding events of 1/2 July and 10/11 July 1968, the latter affecting a swathe of England from the south-west across to eastern areas with severe flooding and exceptional July winds over East Anglia from strong pressure gradients in the rear of the system; the devastating September 1968 floods in south-east England are also cited
key_supporting_quote: When cyclogenesis combines with a thundery ‘Spanish plume’ (Salter, 1968)
limitations_or_uncertainty: A historical review relying on archived charts, published accounts and personal recollection; the authors note that 24-hour forecasts gave no indication of the exceptional nature of the July 1968 events until they had commenced, and that the moisture-free model of the time could not have been expected to reproduce developments enhanced by latent heat release and embedded convection

airstream_properties: NR for thermodynamic detail; described only as warm air moving northwards from the European continent and Iberia, or as warm air brought polewards from the Equator by southerly winds up and along the English Channel, with summer CAPE highest over land owing to warm 2 m air temperatures over landmasses
diagnostic_variables: A compiled catalogue of UK meteotsunami combining a historical record (1750-2009) with a modern record (2010-2022); UK tide gauge data at 15 min sampling; Met Office C-band radar network imagery used to classify convective systems into open cells, quasi-linear systems, isolated cells and non-linear clusters; Camborne and Lerwick 0000 and 1200 UTC radiosonde CAPE as a marginal-instability test; synoptic charts; air pressure traces with rates such as 4 mbar in 10 min; eyewitness and media reports
origin_and_transport_claim: In Spanish plume situations warm air moves northwards from the European continent and Iberia, bringing warm air polewards with southerly winds up and along the English Channel, during which mesoscale convective weather tends to occur
origin_evidence: CITED_ONLY: the plume characterisation and its association with summer meteotsunami rest on Haslett et al. (2009), Tappin et al. (2013), Sibley (2012), Sibley et al. (2016) and Thompson et al. (2020); the study's own evidence is the correlation between event timing and radar-classified convective systems
capping_or_instability_mechanism: NR for capping; instability is assessed only through whether Camborne or Lerwick sounding CAPE exceeds zero, and summer CAPE is said to be highest over land because of warm 2 m air temperatures
capping_or_instability_evidence: DIRECT for the paper's own use of Camborne and Lerwick sounding CAPE as a marginal-instability test alongside radar classification; NR for any plume-related capping
initiation_mechanism: NR for the plume; quasi-linear multicellular systems with high CAPE, heavy precipitation and strong winds are said sometimes to be called squall lines and to occur within synoptic Spanish plume events, while meteotsunami initiation and amplification are attributed to local bathymetry in harbours, bays and river mouths through resonance and seiching
initiation_evidence: INDIRECT: event times taken from tide gauges are linked to radar-identified convective systems and checked against soundings and synoptic charts, giving a 71% positive correlation between summer events and convective weather, rather than a direct initiation analysis
hazards_locations_and_event_types: UK meteotsunami from 1750 to 2022, some affecting seven or more locations; summer events concentrated along the southern UK coast, with 48% of the long record peaking in July and August, including the 27 June 2011 and 18 June 2022 events along the south-west UK coast and an air pressure fall of 4 mbar in 10 min; winter events cluster around the south-west UK and north-west Scotland; impacts include rapid changes in water level and flow velocity capable of causing injury and loss of life
key_supporting_quote: This is where warm air moves northwards from the European continent and Iberia, during which mesoscale convective weather tends to occur.
limitations_or_uncertainty: The 15 min sampling interval used at UK tide gauges since 1993 cannot detect waves with periods of 2-120 min, so events go unobserved, wave heights are underestimated and events are mischaracterised as seiches, tsunami or surge; there is no central UK database and no standardised identification methodology; the historical record depends on eyewitness reports biased by the number of people at the shoreline in summer; the modern 2010-2022 record is short and shows a contradictory 66% winter prevalence

airstream_properties: NR: no airstream properties are reported for the plume; the associated circulation is described only as predominantly south-westerly mid-level flow
diagnostic_variables: 38 warm-season derechos in France for 2000-2022 identified from severe convective wind reports and station gust data following established derecho criteria; daily averaged ERA5 500 hPa geopotential height patterns with the spatial mean removed to isolate dynamical change; circulation analogues drawn from 1950-1980 and 1992-2022; most unstable CAPE and 0-6 km deep-layer shear computed as the 500 hPa minus 10 m wind vector difference; temperature, precipitation and wind speed fields; event frequency per 200 km by 200 km cell; AMO and ENSO indices
origin_and_transport_claim: NR: no origin or transport claim is made; the plume is named only as a typical configuration that many of the derecho 500 hPa patterns resemble
origin_evidence: CITED_ONLY: the resemblance is asserted with citations to Morris (1986) and Holley et al. (2014); the study's own diagnosis is of 500 hPa geopotential height patterns and analogues, not of any plume structure
capping_or_instability_mechanism: NR for the plume; the study's own thermodynamic proxy is most unstable CAPE, which increases for most events between the distant and recent analogue periods, with no consistent change in 0-6 km deep-layer shear
capping_or_instability_evidence: DIRECT for the paper's own ERA5 CAPE and deep-layer shear composites over circulation analogues for each of the 38 events; CITED_ONLY for the plume resemblance
initiation_mechanism: NR for the plume; derecho-producing mesoscale convective systems are said to develop preferentially ahead of a trough or cut-off low in south-westerly flow, and the authors acknowledge that sub-synoptic environments matter for convective initiation and CAPE release
initiation_evidence: INDIRECT: inferred from daily averaged 500 hPa geopotential height patterns for the 38 events and from the spatial distribution of derecho tracks, rather than from case-level initiation analysis
hazards_locations_and_event_types: Warm-season derechos in France 2000-2022, averaging 1.65 per season with a maximum local frequency of 0.65 per year per 200 km by 200 km cell in the north-east of France; tracks predominantly north-eastward, some reaching Switzerland, southern Germany, Benelux, Denmark and Sweden; the 18 August 2022 event produced gusts over 200 km/h across 1500 km in 12 hours, reaching 225 km/h in Corsica with 12 deaths and over 100 injuries
key_supporting_quote: Many Z500 patterns associated with warm-season derechos in France bear resemblance to the Spanish plume (Morris, 1986; Holley et al., 2014)
limitations_or_uncertainty: The ESWD-based severe wind climatology used for comparison covers only 13 years and lacks spatial and temporal uniformity, with report frequency steadily rising; events over the sea may go undetected because of the limited number of weather stations, as the authors suspect for events like the 2022 Corsica derecho; no one-to-one correspondence exists between synoptic patterns and derecho occurrence; the role of anthropogenic climate change in the detected environmental changes remains uncertain given possible ENSO and AMO influences

airstream_properties: NR for measured properties; the mechanism is given only as a low-level southerly flow bringing warm moist air up from Iberia, with the central and south-east European flow of pattern 27 said to behave similarly in summer by bringing warm moist air to the south of the study area
diagnostic_variables: ATDnet lightning flash data for Northwest Europe (48-65 N, 15 W to 10 E) for 2008-2018, clustered into thunderstorms of at least three flashes by a spatio-temporal proximity algorithm written in R; derived thunderstorm speed, direction of movement, flash count, flashes per minute, duration and distance travelled; track-roses and kernel density maps of initiation points; the 30 Neal et al. (2016) EMSLP weather patterns
origin_and_transport_claim: Weather pattern 16, identified as the Spanish Plume weather pattern, produces summer thunderstorms by the mechanism of a low-level southerly flow bringing warm moist air up from Iberia, with thunderstorms under it originating most frequently from a south-westerly or southerly direction
origin_evidence: CITED_ONLY: the plume identification and its mechanism are attributed to Hayward et al. (2022), Wilkinson and Neal (2021), Gray and Marshall (1998) and Lewis and Gray (2010); the study's own evidence is the track-rose and thunderstorm behaviour statistics for pattern 16
capping_or_instability_mechanism: NR: no capping or instability variable is analysed; seasonal variation in instability is invoked only qualitatively to explain the shift of thunderstorm initiation points from land in summer to coastal and ocean areas in autumn and winter
capping_or_instability_evidence: NR: the study uses lightning-derived thunderstorm statistics and mean sea level pressure patterns only, with no thermodynamic data
initiation_mechanism: NR for the plume; initiation is characterised only by the spatial distribution of thunderstorm initiation points by season and weather pattern
initiation_evidence: INDIRECT: inferred from kernel density maps of initiation points and from the correspondence between track-rose directions and the surface airflow of each weather pattern
hazards_locations_and_event_types: Thunderstorms across Northwest Europe including the UK and Ireland, 2008-2018; weather pattern 16, the Spanish Plume pattern, has the largest mean flash count of all patterns at 597 with the longest duration and greatest distance travelled, consistent with severe storms on some days; the 28 June 2011 Spanish Plume event from Iberia, diagnosed as pattern 6, caused very severe thunderstorms with intense lightning and damage over south-east England; listed hazards are lightning, heavy rainfall, hail, thunder-snow and strong winds
key_supporting_quote: Pattern 16 is identified as the Spanish Plume weather pattern (Hayward et al., 2022; Wilkinson & Neal, 2021)
limitations_or_uncertainty: The authors note that the 28 June 2011 Spanish Plume event does not fit well with its diagnosed pattern 6, which may demonstrate the limitations of classifying very variable synoptic conditions into 30 general patterns; pattern 1 shows a clear mismatch between dominant thunderstorm movement and surface airflow for reasons that remain unknown, possibly transitional stages between patterns during the day; where flow direction varies across the study area so does thunderstorm track direction; ATDnet detects only about 25% of intracloud flashes; the catalogue requires at least three flashes so the smallest storms are excluded
